en: *Wenju gejue*, Volume One, Part Four.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Baiting Shan Yue of Siming.
First Fascicle.
The Preface (xu): This serves to set forth the subject matter and initiate the beginning of a single work.

According to the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*), whenever ancient masters expounded upon a scriptural title, they invariably composed a preface; thus, one knows that the name has a long-standing tradition.
Based on the *Zhijian shi*, it is identified as a separate work—the preface to a scripture preached at another time. The compiler collected it from Xuan.
The "Preface" (xu) belongs to the category of introductory sections; its inclusion here at the beginning of the scripture is likewise for that same purpose.

Therefore, I have explained the "Preface Chapter, First" (Xupin Diyi) within this context, as it follows naturally. This is because the "Private Preface" (Siqu) by Wang was also placed next to it; thus, I know that the former should be placed at the very head.
May readers not reproach me for this act of taking liberties.
The Preface states: "The wondrous name is inconceivable. The Commentary explains: "To cite merely 'one inconceivable' and so forth means that outside of the wondrous, there is no other dharma.
Ah, how profound these words! For this reason, it transcends all dependence; the path of language is cut off.
The wondrousness of this entire treatise is summarized in a single phrase. What further explanation could possibly suffice? Nevertheless, the teaching cannot be...

If one speaks of what is not [the ultimate], there is no way to know its subtlety; therefore, one must present it by citing its essentials. Thus, there are the fundamental and the phenomenal (*honji-kempon*); there are the provisional and the real (*gonjitsu*);
there are the bestowal, the unfolding, and the abolition (*se-kai-hai*); and there are the doctrine and the analogy (*hōhi*).

It is for this reason that the purport of the single title is set forth. Now, that which has been accomplished for a long time is called the "fundamental," while that which has been accomplished recently is called the "phenomenal. Thus, as for the Tathāgata...
This establishes the gateway of transformation. It is not through the fundamental that traces can be manifested, nor is it through traces that the fundamental can be revealed.

Although the fundamental and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one; this is what is meant by "the wondrous. What is this "wondrous"? It refers to the wondrousness of the dharma of the identity of the provisional and the real.
Because it is wondrous, it is able to be deployed as the function of the provisional and the real. Now, regarding these two—provisional and real—...
The Dharma is that which is to be employed, and its applications are threefold: bestowing, opening, and abandoning. Thus, both the fundamental and the derivative each further open into three aspects;

these are what are known as "establishing the provisional for the sake of the real" and so forth. However, without the provisional there is no means to manifest the real, and without the real there is no means to employ the provisional.
Therefore, "establishing the provisional for the sake of the real" is precisely the provisional of the real; it is the opening of the provisional to reveal the real.

This is precisely the reality of the provisional; thus, the provisional and the real function in mutual dependence. Since the provisional and the real are identical, both the provisional and the real are appropriate.
Because they are appropriate, they are one; because they are one, they are wondrous. Thus, the transformation of the original and the trace establishes the teaching of the Tathāgata.
Using the trace as an analogy for the original, and employing parables to illustrate the Dharma—all are like this. This is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma).
This is the supreme teaching of the ultimate *amṛta*.
The six difficulties set forth below demonstrate that encountering a Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and so forth, are all not easily attained;

they are intended to inspire in future generations a mind of faith, reverence, reflection, and cultivation, so that one may know from whence the compiler derived [this teaching] and set one’s resolve upon the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*), thereby aspiring toward it.

The underlying intent of this is significant. In his commentary on the words regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, [Zhiyi] briefly indicates: "One must open up the provisional and the real at the stage of fruition across the three teachings.
Now, that which constitutes the fruition of the three teachings is the Buddha; the two types of wisdom, the provisional and the real, are wisdom itself.
Were it not for the opening and revealing of the provisional and real nature of that fruition-attainment, how could the partial and perfect, the great and small of the four flavors be brought forth?

How is it sufficient to clarify the Buddha-wisdom of the present? "To develop" (fa) is also "to open" (kai). Is the perfection of these four flavors also something that must be opened? Therefore, the question is asked at length. The meaning in the answer is as follows:

if the reality of the Perfect (yuan-shi) is not different [from the past], then the Perfection of the present and the past are identical; this is from the perspective of the meaning of the teachings (jiao-yi).

However, regarding that which has not yet been opened and revealed, the "Perfection of the past" refers to that which has not yet been opened and revealed; this is from the perspective of the meaning of the sections (bu-yi).

Regarding "people of initial resolve," there are four types of people listed below, which refers to the four teachings. Categorically, there are three [levels], yet those of initial resolve enter the reality (the ultimate truth).
As for the people of the first three teachings, they are called "of initial resolve" because they are separated from the Perfect by means of the Partial;

speaking according to the present text, since this is contrasted with "entering reality," everyone from the stage of the Ten Faiths downward is included. This is because they have not yet heard the teaching on the opening [of the provisional].

When [the teachings] are manifested, they have not yet reached the source of transformation; thus, the partial and the perfect remain separated. Therefore, in the past, those of the Perfect Teaching were not without the sentiment of regarding the Partial as inferior;

this was merely a matter of their personal realization and did not concern the nature of the Dharma-teachings themselves. As for those of the Perfect capacity, they perceive all four types [of teachings] as equally secret and wondrous.
With the exception of those Bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm and stable, no one else falls within this category. Only...

The current text is thus; whether it advances [the teaching] further or not shall be examined in detail. As for the opening of the three teachings at the ultimate fruit-stage (*phala-koṭi*), the ancients all considered this a difficult point regarding the divisions and teachings of the *buddhāvatamsaka*, as discussed at length in the separate treatise (etc.).

In this school, there are established rules for all those who penetrate the sutras and explain their meanings; therefore, one first explains the title and its purport through five points, and subsequently interprets the scriptural text through the three divisions and four methods of explanation.
Thus, at the beginning of the text, the characteristics of the detailed explanation are first demonstrated.

Regarding the two gates of "Original" (hon) and "Traced" (jaku), and the three and one [divisions], the following section of the text summarizes the general meaning, as that previous section was profound and concise.
It is not that we do not speak of the Great; rather, there is nothing that surpasses what is called the "Original and the Traced" (*honji-kempon*).

That which is termed the "Original Ground" (*honji*)—both in its general and specific aspects—transcends all other expositions. This refers to the fact that he attained Buddhahood long ago and possesses an immeasurably vast lifespan;

this is the "Original. Not only was it unheard of in the past, but even within the "Traced" scriptures it remained secret; for these reasons, it transcends all other expositions. Furthermore, it is said that among the three [realms] within the Traced, the One is of preeminent merit.

"Period" (*qi*) refers to the three cycles of the Trace Gate (*jìmén*) that reveal and manifest [the Truth], which is unprecedented in the entire course of a single transformation; thus, its merit is supreme within this single period.
Furthermore, the "three *kalpas*" (*sāṃkhyeya-kalpa*) are specific, while the "one *kalpa*" (*eka-kalpa*) is general—they differ only in name.

Not only are the three and the one fused into a single essence, but they also stand forever apart from previous teachings, as they originate from our own school (*ekagṛha*). This is truly because they are based upon [the ultimate reality].
This is because it is the fundamental source (*mūla*). Regarding the phrase "the trace is equal to the fundamental," this is based on the intent of the section on revelation and manifestation:

because the inconceivable is one, the trace and the fundamental, and the fundamental and the trace, are thus mutually identical. Now, first clarifying the trace, it says: "For instance, within the trace, they share the same essence.

This refers to the principle of the single true reality (*ekābhisaṃbodhi-tattva*). This principle is neither delusion nor awakening; it is not something attained through cultivation; it is the ultimate unity of all phenomena.

Because it encompasses all meanings, it is neither cause nor effect; yet, while it is neither cause nor effect, it does not exist outside of cause and effect. To discern [the truth] by relying upon this is the "thesis" (zong).
To manifest the essence first and subsequently employ its function is the "function" (yong). If one discusses the *Sūtra on the Three Dharmas*, it already contains this;

however, because this [text] reveals and clarifies it, it is given the name "Wondrous" (Miao), and all other aspects are likewise wondrous. That which is wondrous in its capacity to reveal is identical [to the essence].

This embodies the provisional and the real. If one does not know their identity, how can one distinguish their difference? If one does not recognize the subtle, how can one clarify the coarse? Therefore it is said:

"If one does not first understand that names are equal, they are still to be distinguished. To distinguish the coarse and the subtle is merely a matter of the characteristics of the teaching; thus these two phrases refer to the characteristics of the teaching.
This is because the subtlety of the trace and the subtlety of the source have not yet been manifested; therefore, [the former] is distinguished in contrast to the trace.
This present work elucidates the ultimate meaning; thus it says "and so forth.

The intention behind showing this beforehand is that when the teachings are expounded in future generations, one may universally apply this intent throughout every sentence and phrase of the entire text, ensuring that the subtle purport is not lost.

The reason why only the textual passages are cited is precisely because the detailed explanation of the title's meaning is already provided. Siming said: "If one examines the commentary on the sutra..."
The Great Meaning is not slight; it does not merely consist in dividing the text by phrases. To speak of "phrases" is likely a humble expression;
this commentary is precisely intended to exalt it. If one were to immediately disparage it, how could such a person be said to understand discourse?

If it were merely to divide the phrases and show what each describes, while simultaneously manifesting the intent of broad indication, it is therefore said that "it points to the Mysterious together."

The "Exposition" (*Vyākhyāna*) and other sections do not depart from those five chapters; when assigned to practice, four chapters pertain to practice, while when categorized by teaching, they constitute the characteristics of the teachings (*śāstra-lakṣaṇa*).
Some, failing to understand this, offer many convoluted explanations that are not worth mentioning. Furthermore, I admonish those who propagate the sutra:

you should take contemplation according to principle (*yili*) as primary and ritual phenomena (*shixiang*) as secondary; keep great compassion in your heart and do not obstruct it with fame or profit.
Having thus transmitted and propagated [the teaching], it may be said that the task is accomplished.
Regarding the essential meaning of this sutra, there is both the general and the specific. In its general sense, every phrase and every chapter is without exception wondrous;

this is what is meant by "all embodying the equality of the Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*). Specifically, four chapters constitute the core theme, and thus they are called the "Expedient Means," "Peace and Bliss," and so forth.
The foregoing refers to the Expedient Means and the Life Span as the fundamental and derivative sources; the Peaceful Medicine and the Universal Gate constitute the pivotal keys of this sutra.

These may also be discussed generally through four propositions. Someone might raise a doubt: "While the other three [sections] may be so, it is not known what the significance of the Universal Gate being the essential point is.

[The response is: In the text of the Entrustment and Propagation, there are eight chapters, and the Universal Gate occupies the central position, penetrating and encompassing all that precedes and follows.

The following section is likewise essential for the circulation [of this teaching], as the text states at length. Furthermore, how could the Great Master’s explanation of the ten pairs regarding the "Universal Gate" (Pumen) and the "Distinct Practice" (Bie xing) chapter not be considered essential?
Otherwise, what would it mean for him to point toward the "Exhortation by Samantabhadra" (Puxian quan fa)? [As stated at length.]
In this, we see that the faults of the ancient masters’ interpretations of the sūtras—namely, being either overly prolix or too concise—are cases of "excess" and "insufficiency.

At first, when the scriptural teachings were in their infancy, they merely expounded upon the broad principles of meaning without dividing them into chapters and sections; consequently, there arose criticism that they failed to distinguish the beginnings and endings [of topics].
Thereupon, topical outlines (*pijiu*) were established later on. Nevertheless, as there were still sūtras and śāstras to rely upon, matters did not yet reach an extreme state.

From the time of Shi [Tongxuan] until the final age, matters became increasingly complex; during the Guangzhai period, they grew even more refined, and thus for the first time there arose the affliction of "excess" and "insufficiency.

Had these complexities not been exhausted by weariness, there would have been no need for the rebuke regarding "smoke rising and dust flying. Now, our school says that human sentiments have their natural divisions and should not involve contentious strife;

yet, this causes one to lose the three benefits and forfeit the One Way. Furthermore, Jingxi composed [the following]: *Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Tiantai or Huayan doctrine, likely discussing the evolution of ritual and doctrinal complexity from the Tang through the Song dynasties, specifically critiquing the loss of simplicity and the resulting scholastic disputes.*

Regarding the granting (*yǔ*) or refuting (*duò*) of the meaning of "allowing" (*zòngxǔ*): to say that the Buddha accords with the capacities of sentient beings when he teaches is what is meant by "granting.

To stubbornly insist on this and thereby give rise to dispute—wherein neither advancing nor retreating is correct—is what is meant by "refuting. Furthermore, it is said: even if there are similarities and differences, just as various chrysanthemums and mugworts are still permitted to be called "flowers" by those who grasp their essential meaning, this is "granting.
Even if one does not entirely contradict the Sage’s intention, it remains the conceptual vision of a human being; this is also "refuting."
As for what may be done later, how could it be possible? Therefore, I have concluded by saying that if one can roughly achieve general utility, there is no need to exhaustively debate their words.
Those who evaluate right and wrong in the future should take this as a mirror.
In other sutras, the three divisions are treated as a single set of textual classifications; however, only the *Lotus Sūtra* and Tiantai’s system employ a two-fold classification.

This distinction arises from the fact that the "True Teaching" (*zhengzong*) possesses two gates—the "Original" (*ben*) and the "Tracable" (*ji*)—which represent different aspects of its transformative function (*huayong*).
Therefore, they cannot be unified. Yet, if they cannot be unified, why must there still be a general division? This, too, ultimately returns to the Introductory Division (*xufen*).
Because this is the sole circulating version of the sutra, the textual divisions can be listed side by side; however, the interpretations of the sutra’s meaning cannot both be retained.
Since these meanings cannot coexist, there must be a distinction between what is primary and what is secondary in their application.

When explaining the *nidāna* (introductory) section, the primary application follows the general division (*sāmānya-bhāga*), while the secondary application concurrently includes the specific division (*viśeṣa-bhāga*). Because the primary application follows the general division, this record states that it proceeds from the preceding [section] to analyze the text.
Thus, when explained by means of the four methods of interpretation (*catasraḥ vyākhyāḥ*), these four methods are employed in their entirety to penetrate the entire Root Section (*mūla-mukha*).

However, in explaining the Main Teaching (*samyak-siddhānta*), one primarily employs the "distinctive division" (*bhedavibhāga*) while secondarily incorporating the "comprehensive division" (*samudāyavibhāga*). Because it primarily employs the distinctive division, it is said:

"Now, for the time being, we shall follow the immediate and proceed to divide the Trace [Section] into two categories. Thus, when explained by means of the four methods of interpretation, the Root and the Trace each have three [divisions], arranged vertically.
Regarding the use of the "root and trace" (honji-suijaku), it merely borrows the framework of essence and function (tai-yō) for the root and trace;

in the Root Section (Honmon), there is no need to apply the categories of the teachings, as it is already encompassed by the distant root. For the other sections, they are simply divided according to their respective gates.

However, when explaining the final section on the Propagation (Ryūtsū), one must divide them collectively. Thus, regarding the question [in the *Juki*], the commentary states: "The meaning of the question exists because there are two explanations," etc., referring to the text.
Since this follows from the preceding three sections and further poses a separate question by dividing the introduction into two parts, the intention lies in these two interpretations.
What prevents us from taking the text of the question according to the latter?

Thus, while both interpretations exist, choosing either the former or the latter is merely following the meaning for the time being; therefore it is said [as above], with the intent as explained previously.
If one wishes to know this in full detail, it is as explained in other treatises (and so forth).
Regarding the interpretation of the "sack of scriptures," throughout ancient and modern times, Tiantai alone has exclusively excelled in this mastery.

This is because his great synthesis is rich and comprehensive, and he proceeds with ease through the Middle Way. For instance, a single explanation of *idappaccayatā* (dependent origination) encompasses the four *satyans* (the fourfold benefit); what dharma would it not include?
How much more so when these three interpretations are added—reaching the source and exhausting the root, with both teaching and contemplation—what principle would not be clarified?
Furthermore, speaking in terms of this sutra, among all phenomena and dharma-gates, none exceed the Trace Gate of causes and conditions;
therein, the opening of the provisional to reveal the real corresponds to the teaching aspect, while the Opening of the Root Gate to reveal the remote corresponds to the long-standing origin.
Having examined each and every phrase so that it enters the mind and forms contemplation, one realizes that the contemplation is itself the mind;

therefore, one knows that the current fourfold explanation of the sutra is not intended to refer to anything outside the text. Although various topical sections may arise, none of them departs from the essential purport of this single sutra. Thus it is said:

"Only now do we know that the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation) in its entirety is the fishing trap for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. Is this not the contemplation of the mind in the present?
Because one contemplates the Dharma by surveying the essential purport of the sutras in their entirety, one is able to manifest the Samādhi of the Lotus Sutra;
this is precisely why [the sutra] serves as a "trap" (quánzhì). It is merely like this: while sound constitutes the substance of the teaching, its meanings do not follow a single path.

As for entering [the path], it depends on the person, and the difference between success and failure is vast. Now, sound is one and the same, yet there is that which elucidates principle and that which does not elucidate principle. That which elucidates principle...
What is now called "teaching" (jiao) refers to this; that which does not explicate principle (li) is precisely that which possesses sound.

If one enters the Way by means of it, then even if it does not explicate principle, it is still like teaching. If one does not enter [the Way] thereby, then even teaching is not [true teaching], let alone that which does not explicate principle.

Therefore, regarding sound and teaching, there are those who take them as the substance of the teaching, such as Avalokiteśvara entering the Way through the faculty of hearing (karṇendriya). There are also...
"Attainment" refers to that which is like what Ājñātakauṇḍinya heard from the oral teachings—that is, selecting that which is not the Perfect Penetration (yuan-tong).

Thus, we know that the present clarification of the substance of teaching (*dharma-deha*) is precisely discussed in terms of "entering" or "not entering," rather than being explained by "signifying" or "not signifying. This is because that which enters resides here and not there.
As for the ten directions of the world, the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) can all serve as the substance; if this were not so...
Regarding what is received through sound and teaching, the current text states:

"Although there are the extinction [of the Buddha], the form-body, the sutras, the Pure Name, the assembly, the dharma-food, practice, contemplation, and awakening, these all pertain to the six sense objects; yet they all trace back to sound and teaching, for their benefit arises from this land through the medium of words.
By making this distinction, the points of gain and loss become clear.

Those who study today are said to seek only the lofty and vastness of others' original and manifested traces, exhausting themselves in vain without ever observing the lofty and vastness of their own minds.
How could they not fall into the reproach of "counting treasures" (neglecting the true essence) while performing acts for self-benefit?

Nevertheless, if one were to exclusively employ this censure, I fear those who practice contemplation would become indolent; therefore, since both the teaching and the practice arise together, I shall now record them.
It is further said: "If one takes faith and practice as the vehicle," and so forth; thus we know that the capacities of sentient beings cannot be treated by a single path.

Now, considering what is appropriate for them, I shall offer this explanation: Since these two cannot be practiced simultaneously, rather than merely understanding them in theory, would it not be better to observe how they might both be neglected and abandoned?
Is it not preferable to favor one over the other? This is still a discussion of the "best among the mediocre."

Furthermore, regarding the reason why the commentary on the "Contemplation of the Mind" specifically cites the passage "I believe what you have said": the words spoken therein encompass the entire treatise.
Since one sees the Buddha through the Dharma, one also sees it in you; and since you are the Sangha Jewel, these three are of one essence.
The Three Jewels are to be recognized at their very locus within a single thought-moment; as the recorded text states:
"To recognize the Three Jewels as one essence within one's own mind—this principle is perfectly complete. How could this be anything other than contemplative practice (*guanxing*)?

Thus, it is logically appropriate to establish a comprehensive section on the Contemplation of Mind throughout the entire treatise. It is just as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Wherever this scripture is located..."
The existence of Buddhas and so forth is also of this same category; if one extrapolates and clarifies this, what dharma would not be the single essence?

Furthermore, wherever the Three Jewels reside, how could it be merely a matter of universally establishing the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*)? Is it not therefore appropriate to cite this passage?

In the discourse on the ultimate and the non-ultimate, there is the theory of phenomena and the theory of principle. In principle, the non-ultimate is valued; if it is non-ultimate, then it is principle.
Wherever a matter is debated that is improper, it leads to an infinite regress; yet if one pursues it to its limit, what end could there possibly be?

Thus, whenever the scriptural teachings provide an answer that leads to an infinite regress, they do so from the perspective of practical application (*yōji*). If one were to exhaustively investigate the underlying principle until it reaches infinity, who could say it is not correct?
For example, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, six successive rounds of inquiry into the source of delusion culminate in "non-abiding" (*amūla*) as the fundamental basis.
This is precisely its underlying principle. Furthermore, the ultimate limit of phenomena must reach the realm of principle;
that which reaches the realm of principle is "exhausted" yet inexhaustible, and being inexhaustible is itself exhaustion. Thus, exhaustion and inexhaustibility are both equally inexhaustible.

Now, in this present text, one wishes to discuss how the various Buddhas have successively received the teachings, ultimately resulting in there being a single Buddha at the beginning—is this, then, truly existent?

If one asks whether the ultimate limit is finite or infinite: if it were finite, it would fall into the error of having no cause; if it were infinite, then reason could not be established as a basis. To this, the answer is given:

"To seek the source by erasing its traces is merely returning to the original tenet to seek further benefit. What benefit is there in seeking the beginning? This is what is called an evasive answer (*sthāpanīya-praśna*).
Next, the questioner follows upon the previous point and asks again regarding the absence of an initial teaching, leading once more to [the same conclusion].

The answer regarding the absence of formal instruction culminates merely in internal permeation and self-awakening. Indeed, "internal permeation and self-awakening" refers to reaching the ultimate principle.
Nevertheless, to claim that one must wait for internal permeation to achieve self-awakening is simply to abandon the matter;
this is profoundly at odds with the Way of the Teachings. Therefore, the analogy of the hundred blind men is further established in order to reprove this.
Those who preserve their ignorance and abandon themselves may now be said to have reached the ultimate limit.

Furthermore, if one is cautioned that the more one receives the teachings, the more one should attend to them, yet instead indulges in useless discourse, then even the remaining methods of Buddhist transformation—whereby the six sense-objects can all lead one into the Way—are available;
why must one insist on seeking the initial stage and thereby indulge in self-deception? Alas! Such are the repeated and earnest admonitions.
Consequently, students study superficially without adding any reflection; how regrettable!

To contemplate the mind (*citta*) is the essential core of this single scripture and also the subtle, essential method for simultaneously understanding the commonalities and differences of other scriptures.

What is called "contemplating the mind" is, in the words of the people, the most expansive [of doctrines]; in principle, it is extremely pertinent, as its status universally encompasses all contemplations.
Third, for the time being, this is intended to establish the path for beginners; such is the purport of this single passage.

Although people of the past have often understood this only as a text on "contemplating the mind" (*guanxin*), with the exception of the "Peaceful Practices" (*anle xing*) which involve the cultivation and gathering of the mind, all other sections are established through doctrinal meaning.
Furthermore, why was the "Parable Chapter" (*yupin*) cited above as a clear exposition of contemplative practice (*guanxing*)? This is because it serves as the reason for [this].
To state the essential point: although we do not concern ourselves with this matter, we shall nevertheless provide a brief response.

Is it not the case that what is called "the practice of peace and bliss" (anraku-gyō) refers specifically to the contemplation of mind through practice (*gyōkan-shin*) alone, and thus cannot be taken as the primary text? All other instances are established by way of meaning (*gi-ri*).

This is because when one speaks of the contemplation of mind regarding phenomena (*ji-hō kan-shin*), in comparison to the contemplation of mind through practice, they are all established by way of meaning; hence, the *Girui* (Examples of Meaning) states that there are two types of contemplation: that of phenomena and that of meaning.

Establishing the contemplation of the mind is precisely this. However, if we now cite scriptural evidence regarding phenomena (*dharmas*), would it not be a clear textual authority for "reaching the principle by touching upon phenomena" (*tuo shi jian li*)?

Since each text has its own specific application, how can one treat them all with a single standard? Furthermore, the previous text’s demonstration of the characteristics of contemplating the mind consists of two levels;
this is also a statement regarding the structural framework of the teachings and practices of our school, which students should [understand].
One must not fail to know this; I shall now briefly point it out to show the method for its practice. Throughout ancient and modern times, many have explained it in this way.
Tell me, is it truly radiant? If it is still not so, there is great cause for doubt. Consider this:
regarding what is called "the purport of the entire scripture shining clearly before one's eyes," after all, what is that which shines so radiantly?
Even if you perceive it with intimacy, if you understand it as something before your eyes, it is still not correct.
According to the literary style, one should simply say "resplendent" (*bingran*) and stop; yet there is a gateway for further inspiration.
It is simply not right to say "not so," for how could there be an order for seeing off a guest? To do otherwise would be like the wind blowing a different tune. Truly, this is difficult.
Regarding those points in the textual meanings of the doctrinal gates that were subject to doubt, the Master of Records (Jikishu) resolved them all;
yet, those who have spoken since then, unaware of this, have continued to debate them, so that their explanations have ultimately failed to approach the truth.

Thus, the meaning of whether the Secret Teaching is transmitted or not may be said to be clarified herein. Nevertheless, there remain further doubts, for as long as this teaching has not been put into practice, it remains impossible to fully grasp.
Since it is known that Ānanda already utilized [the teachings] and compiled them, how can one say that Ānanda was unable to receive them?
Now, what is meant by "Ānanda received only that which is manifest" is precisely this: that which was employed in the secret [teachings] was entirely manifest to him.
As for the hidden intent (*saṃdhyāya*), however, Nāgārjuna inferred it by deducing the meaning from the various texts; at that time, [he understood it].
At the time of the assembly, Ānanda himself could not fathom it; indeed, for one who has not deeply penetrated its meaning, it is difficult to understand.
This point has already been demonstrated in the *Xuánqiān* (Profound Commentary), [as stated] at length.

The difficulty of establishing teachings and interpreting their tenets cannot be surpassed by anyone other than those who personally received the Buddha’s instructions during his assemblies and deeply realized the Sage’s intent, or those whom the Tathāgata foresaw and entrusted with this responsibility—surely it is Master Tiantai who is such a person.

Yet he still modestly compared himself to others, fearing that future generations might fail in their duty to fully adapt the teachings to the capacities of beings; how much more so for those who are merely ordinary? Therefore, it is said: [and so forth].
Furthermore, the preceding text states: "One should not attempt to open the many doors of the Eight Teachings with a single spoon from among the various masters;
it is just like this. Yet Jingxi says: "The categories of Sudden and so forth constitute the great outline for the judgment of teachings within this school.

However, without the *Lotus Sūtra*, one cannot know where the intent of the transformation lies; and without the principles of the teaching, one cannot know the grand method of judgment and interpretation. Regarding this—
These words are indeed well-founded.
One who clarifies the nature of the teaching must understand that the entire Great Canon of the Buddha’s teachings first exists as sound and subsequently takes on form;

because of this form and sound, the three—name (*nāma*), phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*)—are able to be maintained. This is truly a provisional synthesis of conditions, which is why it is capable [of functioning].

This establishes the essence of all teachings. If one does not allow that form exists as scripture after [the Buddha’s] passing, then why should sound not also be accepted as scripture during the Buddha’s lifetime?

Therefore, it is said, etc. This uses the case of after the passing as an analogy for the time of the Buddha's life to raise an objection; thus, it uses "form" (*rūpa*) as an analogy for "sound" (*śabda*).
It must be amended by correcting the reason based on principle, stating: "One should know that both were previously perceived by the eyes and ears..."

That which is called "attaining equality" refers to the fact that the words of the harmonious assembly cannot be deceived; as it is said in the treatises: "The Muni taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (dharmaskandha);
their substance is either speech or names, both of which are subsumed under the aggregates of form (rūpaskandha) and formations (saṃskāraskandha). This is what is meant.

Regarding Ānanda ascending the high seat and the assembly arising with three doubts: some of the ancients have raised various objections on this point, such as the so-called "doubts of expediency" (*upāya-kāṅkṣā*) and "doubts of reality" (*tattva-kāṅkṣā*).
This is because at the time of the Council, the assembly of Dharma-reciters was originally entirely free of doubt;
as Arhats, they should not have been subject to further instances of the three types of doubt. I have discussed this elsewhere. Now, as for what is called "non-" [existence]...
Regarding those who harbor doubts, their words vary in degree—some being minor and others major.

What is stated here refers specifically to attaining freedom from doubt within the limited scope of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and the Vedic scriptures; it does not mean that one is entirely free from doubt regarding all things.
Furthermore, the reason for such doubt is precisely because the three objects of doubt all contradict what was previously known, leading to uncertainty or indecision.
If one truly knows this, one simply declares it to be real; what further cause for doubt could there be? Judging by this, there is nothing at all that warrants difficulty.
When the single utterance of the words "Thus have I heard" dispels all doubts, how can one still debate between the provisional and the ultimate within it?
Such is the general outline.

I have long harbored a doubt regarding the two types of time discussed in Indian treatises: namely, that *kāla* is real time because it is shallow and easy to understand, while *samaya* is conventional time because it is profound and difficult to grasp.
Furthermore, it is said that real time is taught for the disciples of our own school (*śāsana*), whereas conventional time is used to refute the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This being so, time is in fact one; yet it is spoken of as having difficulties and ease, and as being either conventional or real.
Why is this? All of these are not easily understood; I now venture to offer the following reflections. As for the statement that "time has two distinct types," my intention is as follows:

the "real" refers to the time when the inner teachings are shown to disciples, and the time of the protective luminous signs (*rakṣā-vidyā-rūpa*), where the divisions of the day and night do not deviate, and thus its characteristics are easy to discern.
The "provisional," however, is characterized by momentary impermanence; it initially lacks fixed characteristics, and is intended to subvert [false attachments].
Because non-Buddhists cling to the notion of permanence, the principle is not easily perceived; is this not indeed difficult?
Speaking from this perspective, although it is a single moment, its application may be either provisional or ultimate; thus, the difficulty does not lie merely in the verbal expression.
Regarding the explanations in the treatises, there are further points concerning the meaning of long and short durations, which may involve progress or lack thereof.

Some maintain that both long and short are merely provisional time, as the treatise states; this means that "long" and "short" are all conventional designations arising from the conceptual calculations of ordinary minds.

By extension, one might also hold that both long and short are real, such as the "time for eating" (*kālabhojana*) and other practices observed by followers of our own tradition (the Buddhist insiders). Or...

Regarding the pairing of the two names based on length and brevity, the so-called "Four Clarifications" state that when following the Buddha’s regulations, the time of birth and death is short, and so forth;

yet in reality, all three explanations are universally applicable and do not apply specifically to this particular discussion. As for the question concerning whether length and brevity are both provisional or real:
since length and brevity are mutually relative, they are not fixed; how could they not be provisional? This is because [the measurement] depends upon the relationship between the sun and the moon.
If one looks at it from the perspective of permanence, how can it not be real? Someone asked: "What do you say regarding the doctrine of long and short durations? I replied:
"For a disciple of the Buddha, if they awaken to the Way through time, they transcend birth and death; how can this not be 'short'?

As for those outside the Way who cling to permanence and are submerged in craving, sinking long into the sea of suffering—how can this not be 'long'? If one takes a single moment to clarify the contemplation of the mind, then the contemplation and the object merge."
Because this principle is particularly intimate, it is said that "time and the Way coincide," which also possesses a profound significance.

When the proper season arrives, the principle manifests of itself; thus, when the ancients awakened to the Way and clarified the mind, there was invariably a specific time, much like the simultaneous pecking and hatching of a chick—a matter difficult to describe.
However, such is merely a general discourse and is insufficient to distinguish between shallow and deep realization; one should rather speak in terms of "contemplating the mind."
First emptiness, next the provisional, and finally the middle—this is the sequence of the three periods.

When the mind is contemplated as simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle, this is the perfect and wondrous unity of a single moment; its principle is thus direct. Therefore it is said: "When contemplation and the object coincide, it is called 'one period'."

Now, the Buddha is but one; how could there be four? It is precisely because the four teachings are expounded that we distinguish the responsive manifestations (*nirmāṇakāya*) according to those teachings;

thus, the characteristics of these four responsive Buddhas are clarified. Although we do not explicitly state here which teaching’s Buddha-characteristics are being discussed, by examining the body through the lens of the teaching, we know this to be the responsive manifestation of the Perfect Buddha (*yuanfo*).
Furthermore, when discussing the revelation and clarification of the teachings, it does not stop at the Perfect alone.

The Buddha is characterized by these marks alone; yet, when the small is opened to reveal the great, and the partial manifests as the perfect, one attains the perfectly marvelous, absolute, and ultimate Buddha-marks.
Therefore it is said that the previous three marks are concealed and spoken of according to their predominance; this does not mean that the "Great Void" is itself named the Perfect Buddha.
Thus, one should know that the Teacher of the present sutra is not distinct from those three Buddhas to constitute a separate Perfect Buddha, nor is he apart from them.

If one holds that the Dharma-body exists as a result of retribution, it is further said that prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the three Buddhas were separated from clarity and obstructed by the partial and inferior;
thus, upon arriving at the present sutra, the inferior is distinguished as superior, and the three are realized as one.

It is not apart from the six-foot body in its soiled robes that there is nothing which is not the essence of the jeweled necklace; this retributive body is precisely the Teacher of the present sutra. Once this is understood, one also understands what preceded it.
Since all these marks of response are not the work of any single Buddha alone, it is further said:
"If one attains the true meaning, one will know that while the essence of the four Buddhas is identical, their functions differ; such is the subtle excellence of the provisional teachings.

How could it be otherwise than erroneous to fail to discuss this from the perspective of the general principles of capacity and teaching, but instead to focus narrowly on the superiority or inferiority of the auspicious marks? It is for this reason that I have made this distinction.
It is clear that they are not fit for discourse.

All explanations based on the provisional teachings merely distinguish the four teachings; they do not clarify the revelation and manifestation [of the ultimate truth], and thus are insufficient to reveal the intent of this present section.

Therefore, it is said that this sutra is the Perfect Teaching, and only through further revelation and manifestation can one perceive the subtlety of the intent of this sutra’s section; this should be understood.

The two meanings of "division" (*bu*) and "teaching" (*jiao*) are implicit and concise in their phrasing; I shall now provide a brief explanation of them. One should say that the statement "the present sutra is Perfect" (*yuan*) refers to the meaning of the teachings (*jiao*), while the further necessity of "opening and revealing" (*kaixian*) refers to the meaning of the divisions (*bu*). This is the established principle here, which actually applies throughout both the beginning and the end [of the teaching]. Failing to see this, people harbor doubts, wondering: "If the present Perfect [teaching] still requires opening and revealing, would that not be an error? As it is said: [Text omitted for brevity] ...if one does not understand the intent of the division and teaching, one will surely fall into such errors. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the three vehicles are all the Buddha’s true teaching," this is a provisional statement based on the meaning of the divisions; it is not a definitive statement based on the meaning of the teachings. If one were to interpret it as a definitive statement based on the meaning of the teachings, then the Lotus Sutra would be no different from the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and other such texts. If one were to interpret it as a provisional statement based on the meaning of the divisions, then the Lotus Sutra would be no different from the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other such texts. Therefore, one must know that the meaning of the divisions and the meaning of the teachings are distinct. For this reason, the *Lotus Sutra* is called the "Perfect Teaching" (*yuanjiao*) based on the meaning of the teachings, yet it is also called the "Sutra of Opening and Revealing" (*kaixian jing*) based on the meaning of the divisions. Thus, the two meanings of division and teaching are indeed distinct. If one does not understand this, one will surely fall into error. Furthermore, regarding the passage "the three vehicles are all the Buddha’s true teaching," this is a provisional statement based on the meaning of the divisions; it is not a definitive statement based on the meaning of the teachings. The subsequent text states: "Among the preceding four teachings, this is precisely the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). Furthermore, one should know that this Perfect Teaching of revelation and manifestation differs from the current [teaching] only in its degree of detail;
were it not for the classification of the divisions and teachings, who could clarify this?"
The passage concerning the city of Rājagṛha below appears quite concise, dignified, and substantial; if all texts were like this, they could entirely serve as a model.
Since the reality of the Dharma-realm is fundamentally without the four [elements], yet the four views differ, it is clear that the Dharma has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, it says: "The quiescent principle of the Buddhas is divinely without fixed location; whether there be sand and stones or the seven treasures, it arises accordingly."

That which is deluded is summoned and responded to within the mind; this can also be known. Because phenomena originally lack inherent characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), they have never failed to be wondrous.
Because summoning and responding occur within the mind, the distinction between the coarse and the wondrous arises from the person and does not originate from the phenomena themselves.

Nevertheless, it is necessarily through the phenomena that one is able to respond to stimuli accordingly, and thus there has never been any partiality. Therefore, the first two views are observed according to specific circumstances.

Thus, one perceives distinctions of superior and inferior. Furthermore, it is said that regarding the realm of the Buddha, the latter two contemplations observe according to principle (*li*), whether existence is immediate or separate.

Now, since it is both said to be "originally wondrous" and said to be "within the mind," and some say it is "following affairs" while others say "following principle"—which of these accords with the truth?
We reply: Generally speaking, there is nothing that does not accord with the truth. To speak from the perspective of the origin, they are one.
It is simply a matter of the subtle skill in verbal concealment.

To clarify the principles and categories, there are three types of contemplation on phenomena (*dharmas*). Regarding "contemplation based on phenomena" (*tuo-shi guan*), as indicated by the text at length below, this particular case is cited as an example for several reasons:
first, because the object and the contemplation are complete; second, because the object is proximate and essential.

Third, because the observation is clear; fourth, because it manifests both by relying on phenomena to perceive principle, and so forth. The *Ji* (Commentary) states: "The consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) acts as the sovereign;

among the various minds that create karma, there must be mental concomitants (*caitta*). Although this point of Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is close at hand, many people are ignorant of it.
This, too, is a obscuration caused by practitioners' failure to see their own [defects]. Now, when one speaks of the consciousness-aggregate, it refers directly to the mind-king (*cittarāja*).
Your mind-king (*citta-rāja*) does not necessarily create karma; the creation of karma must necessarily proceed from the mind.

What is meant by "receiving" (*vedanā*), "perception" (*saṃjñā*), and "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*) arising as good or evil is precisely the meaning of "creating" (*karoti*). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) also refers to this as the "mind that can attract retribution.

To say that the mind-king creates [the city] is merely a convenient way of speaking based on the text of "Rājagṛha" (King’s House); in reality, that which creates is necessarily the mental factors (*caitta*).

Therefore it is said: "Now, if one wishes to eliminate [the notion of] 'kings' (i.e., sovereign minds) such as yours, one must consider that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is fundamentally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Now, for the sake of eliminating [this misconception], we combine the wholesome and unwholesome with the mind-king; thus it is called the 'wholesome and unwholesome king. In reality, however, the wholesome and unwholesome are fundamentally mental factors (*caitasika*).
According to the treatises, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) pervade all three natures; yet, if spoken of in terms of what they produce, they are merely indeterminate."

It has not yet been distinguished whether this is good or evil; I have often seen scholars treat these teachings with negligence, such that the profound meaning of Jingxi remains obscure and unclarified—only Siming truly understood this.

Furthermore, it is said: "Being different from other sutras, it should be like the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation)," for the *Zhi guan* takes the ten profundities (*shimiao*) as its entirety to form the fundamental substance of the contemplative method. If it were not thus, [it would not be so].
How could this be any different from other sutras? Since all subsequent contemplations and explanations fully embody this principle, it is said that "all that follows is likewise.

Generally, regarding the characteristics of the contemplation of all phenomena, one interprets the meaning according to the text; thus, there is the opening and closing of names and characteristics, with the meanings being either detailed or concise.

The distinction between identity and difference is one and the same in terms of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Therefore, although the present explanation of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is the same as that concerning the aggregates (*skandha*), there is a difference in their synthesis and analysis.
Above, they were combined because they were treated in contrast; now, they are explained separately because they concern Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Furthermore, it is said that here, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, for the sake of convenience in treating the aggregates, they are spoken of by way of the *skandhas*; this refers to the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, which is identical to that [previous] text.
Furthermore, in various texts, it is sometimes said that "objects" (*viṣaya*) and "wisdom" (*jñāna*), and so forth, are all merely different names for the same thing;

or that according to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun jiao*), one directly reaches the rational nature (*li-xing*) and thus does not permit the establishment of the aggregates (*skandha*). How is this to be understood in relation to the present text?

And how about the *Zhi-guan*? Moreover, although the gate of contemplating phenomena (*shi-fa guan-men*) is a brief contemplation, it can nonetheless be practiced and entered—this refers to what is called "not depending on the contemplated object. This is the case here.
To say that the broad meaning is intended to correspond to the literal text implies that there would be obstructions in practice;

therefore, it is said that the broad clarifies the brief, rather than being strictly dependent upon the latter. Speaking from this perspective, the principle is fundamentally universal—why do people remain so stubbornly attached? I do not know.

How great is the Middle Way! It is that which both ordinary beings and sages alike follow. Therefore, the Buddha always abides in the Middle Way; there has never been a time when he was not in the Middle.
If one discusses this principle, what could possibly not be the Middle? It unifies the entire Dharma-realm as nothing but the Middle alone.
Why must one ascend to the heavens or descend to the Middle Kingdom, or be born at midday and extinguished at midnight, before it can be considered the Middle? Nevertheless...
Thus, what is spoken here is specifically intended to manifest the principle within the phenomenon; if one attains the principle within the phenomenon, what phenomenon would not be the mean?
There is no error therein. This is what is meant by "all manifesting the Middle Way.

As for the Sage, he acts spontaneously and remains ever thus, not dwelling in anything through deliberate selection; he simply serves as a model for all things. As for ordinary people, although they may ultimately...
One follows this daily yet remains unaware of it; this is what is meant by "being unaware of what one uses daily," which is the opposite of the *Zhongyong*.

Furthermore, regarding the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), there is the sense that it possesses a substantial essence (*sabhāva*) and the sense that it lacks a substantial essence. This meaning arises from the following: the Mahāyāna teachings speak of a Middle Way that possesses a substantial essence, whereas the *Āgamas* speak of a Middle Way free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism that lacks a substantial essence.

Moreover, the Middle Way with a substantial essence is divided into two types: the limited and the non-limited. It is precisely because it is free from these [extremes] that it is called the Middle Way.

The "Middle within the extremes" is simply the Middle; it is the Middle that is identical with the extremes, not merely the Middle alone. This is what is called the wondrous Middle of absolute transcendence (*juedai*).
Some, regarding every phenomenon (*dharma*), insist on grasping only the Middle; this is to know only the mere Middle. How could they recognize what is meant by "absolute transcendence"?
Furthermore, it is said that "the identity of emptiness and the Middle" possesses two kinds of Middle; this refers to the aforementioned "having substance."
The two [types of] "non-substantiality" are also [included in] the middle.

Regarding the old treatise’s statement that the Śrāvakas are fundamentally small and thus subsumed under the indeterminate nature—because they emerge from within the determinate nature—it records that the second half-verse belongs exclusively to the present sutra. However, I maintain this is incorrect; it is based on the treatise.
The eight reasons for listing the assembly with the śrāvakas first are clearly set forth; regarding the second reason, it states:

"To encompass those of indeterminate nature who turn their minds to enter the Great Vehicle. As for the term "encompass" (*she*), there are two meanings. Here, I take it to mean "guiding and encompassing.

Thus, the reason the assembly is listed before the śrāvakas is precisely to guide and encompass those of indeterminate nature who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle, leading them back to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
How could it ever be said that those who were not yet fixed are being subsumed and returned to the category of the fixed?

Thus, the text states: "Still lacking half of what is obtained in that land. Is this not precisely because among the śrāvakas there are both those who are fixed and those who are not; since we are now subsuming the half who are not fixed, they do not belong to the category of the fixed.
Therefore, the text makes this distinction for that reason. Generally, when examining such convoluted explanations, they are all like this—truly pitiable.
[The Master] laughs.

Regarding the "Exegesis by Way of the Provisional Teachings" (*yàojiào shì*), the citation from the *Śāstra* and the subsequent explanation of the text appear to lack coherence. Since the *Śāstra* passage has already been cited, one ought first to explain that passage;
yet here, it immediately states that "those who abide in the fruit are divided into two," which seems to omit the preceding list and lacks an explanation for what follows.
To attempt to explain this further would be difficult to express; one should refer to the subsequent text. It is appropriate to first cite the treatise to enumerate the four types:
namely, those of fixed overweening pride (*abhimāna*), those who regress from the Great Vehicle, and those who are transformational (*nirmāṇa*).

Now, by combining those of fixed regression from the Great Vehicle with those who abide in the fruit with overweening pride—since the latter have not yet entered the stages and are thus not discussed separately—and adding to these the Buddha-vehicle and the transformational ones, there are three.

If one further divides each of these two categories—namely, those who respond to the teaching through citation and interpretation—into two sub-types, they are as follows: "causing the opening" and "abiding in the fruit," making four in total.

These refer to the "breaking of the dharma" (which is the definitive nature of the dharma) and the "retrogression from the Great [Vehicle]. As the *Jiwen* (Record of Texts) states, these are distinguished by whether they have "turned back" or "not yet turned back. Regarding those who have turned back:
upon reaching the Vaipulya (*fangdeng*) period, they receive censure, transform the Tripiṭaka, and achieve the Universal [Vehicle]; this is what is called the "transformed body" (*biànyì tǐ*).
The "Dharma-abiding fruit" (dharmasthitiphala) is this; the other two open up two [other] understandings without any difference in their paths.

When explained in this combined manner, not only can the text of the *Śāstra* (commentary) be seen clearly as it is, but it also allows the text of the *Vṛtti* (sub-commentary) to flow with joy and accord with reason. Explaining each passage in correspondence with the other is like meeting a blade at its edge.
As for the statement that "the meaning of the Śrāvaka is vast," this concludes the enumeration of names and categories, opening up various types as set forth in the record.
This refers to the four types within each of the eight gates of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings; speaking from the perspective of the Shared [Teachings], these are also discussed as four types.

Furthermore, it is said that "each gate has its own Buddha-way," where "traces" (*ji*) refer to the manifestations and transformations (*yinghua*) appearing before us, which are spoken of in terms of their traces (*jibian*).

According to the fundamental reality (*ben*), there should also be stages such as the *bhūmi* and *vihāra*, which are spoken of from the perspective of the fundamental. Since it is said that these are "corrupted by overweening pride" (*shangman*), this means they are confused with those actual [stages].
The number of practices is also as previously enumerated; because one cannot finish counting them, they are called "vast" (*ābhoga*).

Since that [text] lacks explanations regarding the provisional and definitive teachings, the fundamental and the manifested, or their opening and closing, it merely knows of abiding in the fruit; therefore, it asks: "Why is it said that they abide in *nirvāṇa*?
Even if one were to employ the teachings, saying that Mahāyāna *śrāvakas* [abide there], this would still not constitute thorough understanding; thus, it is criticized.

You say: "That which is most ultimate is none other than emptiness; that which is most manifold is none other than the provisional; that which is most supreme is none other than the Middle. Therefore it is said: 'Most ultimate, most manifold, and most supreme—these are none other than emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle.
One should also say that all three are named 'emptiness,' and so forth; furthermore, all three contemplations are equally great."
Because they are equal, the statement "one mind is all minds" is merely a conventional designation; that "all minds are one mind" is emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

and that "neither one nor all" is the Middle Way (*madhyamā*). These three contemplations and their three meanings revolve and interpenetrate so clearly that, like a pearl rolling on a platter, there is nothing that cannot be manifested.
