It may be said that none of these are one's own; yet, when a single Buddha attains enlightenment, the entire dharma-realm is nothing other than the Buddha’s environment and essence (the *śāśrita* and *āśraya*), so it may also be said that all are already one's own.
How could there ever be a fixed conclusion? This principle can be discussed with those who understand it, but it is difficult to speak of with worldly people;
let us therefore set it aside for now.
When King Aśoka paid homage to the various stūpas of the arhats, he offered twenty cowries at the stūpa of Pukkusāti;
yet the cowries flew out from the stūpa. Is this not the power of the habitual cultivation of few desires that can reach such a state?
What is called "not perishing even in death" is seen here. This is also different from those who remain greedy until the moment of their death.
However, the disposition toward greed and that toward few desires are one and the same; why is it that people of the world do not understand this essential point?
Is the teaching of the Buddha truly different from the teaching of the non-Buddhists, or is it truly not different?
If one cannot attain even a single dharma to enter the mind, how can one say that when I sat at the site of enlightenment, I attained nothing at all? In truth, what is there to be attained?
Furthermore, it is said: "If all dharmas are not accepted, how does this differ from the Buddha’s teaching of non-acceptance?
Nor is there acceptance. Therefore, one knows that difference does not reside in words; ultimately, where does it lie? Let students try to determine this for themselves.
When Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra wished to return to his native land to benefit others, he practiced patience at this moment. Contemplating these words, one should accept them with patience.
This refers to the ultimate limit of patience (*kṣānti*). How, then, does one achieve such patience? It can be said that nothing more than this is required:

patience is the state of being at peace with the meaning [of reality], and because one can analogize from its ultimate point, when encountering insult or humiliation, one remains at peace with the insult and humiliation;

when subjected to being struck, beaten, flogged, or even facing the edge of a blade, one is able to remain at peace with all of these. If so, by what means is one able to remain at peace? It is by means of non-self (*anātman*).
Furthermore, why is it that there is no self? It is simply because of "correspondence" (pratisaṃyukta).

Now, as for this correspondence, if one has not practiced for a long time and accumulated merit through conduct, it cannot be achieved. Therefore it is said: "Only those who can practice patience may be called powerful great beings.
Among all sages and worthies, there are none who did not come from within the midst of forbearance. How is it that people today cannot endure even small things?
The Buddha’s Dharma-body is immovable, yet it manifests traces among humanity.

Knowing well that worldly people are largely attached to signs, he relied upon the story of being born from a stone cave and attaining enlightenment by contemplating emptiness as a means to manifest his arrival.

This was intended to lead worldly people to contemplate emptiness within form and to profoundly penetrate the wondrousness of the Dharma-body. If you wish to see the Buddha, you should see him in this way. Thus it is said.
To truly see the Buddha in this manner means that seeking the Buddha merely through form and sound is practicing a deviant path;
how could such a thing be called seeing the Buddha? Nevertheless, from the perspective of the Buddha’s own teaching, it is permissible;

yet if we consider the capacity of sentient beings, one ought to pay reverence even to clay shrines and molded images—how much more so for the true perception of the Buddha’s form and sound? How, then, could one not pay reverence? Thus, one knows the principle.
It is not the case that there is no single way to categorize them.
"Learning increases daily" refers to study; "the Way decreases daily" refers to non-study (*aśikṣā*). These refer to worldly learning and non-learning.
However, regarding supramundane learning and non-learning, there are further distinctions of depth and shallowness; therefore, the words of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) state:

Regarding "those in training" (*śaikṣa*) and "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*): it is said that those in training do not necessarily exhaust the principle, while those beyond training do not necessarily reach the ultimate;

this is merely a one-sided description. According to the Great Teaching, the principle is actually the reverse: not only do those beyond training reach the ultimate, but those in training also exhaust the principle.

Therefore, five propositions are established to distinguish them, so that their relative magnitude may be compared, their degrees of depth may be clarified, and the distinction between the ordinary and the sage may be elucidated.
It is because they are distinct. Thus, "learning through non-learning" (*xué wúxué*) is that which defines the fixed stages [of cultivation].

Between learning through non-learning and non-learning through learning (*wúxué ér xué*), it is better to practice non-learning through learning; therefore, non-learning through learning is superior, while learning through non-learning is secondary.
"Neither learning nor non-learning" (*fēi xué fēi wúxué*) is yet another stage below that. If one is not subsumed under any of these, one is merely a commoner of the lowest sort. This is the measure.
Are these five phrases not sufficient to cause one to awaken?

The *Yuanlun* (Complete Treatise) states that within the single mind, the ten realms are fully present; each of these ten realms possesses its own hundred realms, and each of those possesses ten suchnesses (*tathatā*), thereby forming one thousand realms.
When expressed in terms of matter and mind, this amounts to two thousand. Now, the current text further states: "Discussing suchness in relation to the realms... and so forth.
As for the treatise stating that the realms (*dhātu*) constitute two thousand, this is yet another example. However, this is still merely a singular enumeration.
If one were to speak of them in their full extension, one should say "a thousand within a hundred realms," or "ten suchnesses (*tathatā*) of suchness," and so forth;

why would there be only one thousand realms and one thousand suchnesses each? Thus, they would amount to twelve thousand, and when combined with the previous [calculation], these constitute three examples. If one were to discuss...

The "three thousand" (sanqian) should properly be a singular number; why then does it now differ from the common usage? Is there perhaps another meaning intended? It is said: It is not that there is no reason for this.
Rather, each follows the specific intent of its respective text, as the numbers may be expanded or contracted, more or less.

For example, Siming once employed this very principle, saying: "the hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses" (baijie qianru) and "the hundred suchnesses and the thousand realms" (bai ru qian jie). Thus, one knows this to be a dharma-gate.
The perfect interfusion of the myriad phenomena in infinite layers is what is called the inconceivable; therein, nothing is impossible, and thus it is a matter of variable numerical categories.

As for what is termed the "three thousand [realms]," however, this is a constant number that cannot be increased or diminished. This distinction is as discussed in the *Jianrui lun* (Treatise on Discerning Categories).

Although it has already been clarified previously that the teacher and disciples encompass and transform one another as principal and attendant, striking up and proclaiming their renown—whether provisional or real, raw or mature, internal or external, close or distant—and though their manifested traces are myriad and their skillful means are manifold, they have all remained scattered without a unifying principle;
thus, the reason why they are fundamentally one in principle and return to a single Way has not yet been made clear. Therefore, herein...
He reveals the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama to serve as its foundation, elaborates upon it by means of the five periods of the Lotus Sūtra,

subsumes it through the "half" and "full" teachings of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, and brings it forth by relying on the true path of the Latter Gate. Only then does one come to know that all the transformations previously established—
whether as teachers or disciples, and whether through skillful means or expedient wisdom— are all established based upon the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
There is no other dharma and no other path; it is simply this.

Although the various great disciples each relied on the specific names and meanings of their respective texts to demonstrate their contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*), they still did not exhaust the subtle refinements of contemplative practice (*guan-xing*).
Therefore, from among all the mental factors (*citta-saṃskāra*), ten wholesome mental factors were selected in general to represent the ten great [virtues].
The Dharma-gates in which my disciples abide each rely upon a single virtue to assist the intention of the Mind-King;

thus, for those at the initial stage of the path, contemplative wisdom is easily aroused. Those who can abandon evil and follow good, transform the mundane into the sacred, and penetrate deeply into the ultimate reality within a single thought-moment do so through the power of the present King-number (the mind-consciousness).
Furthermore, the ten mental factors are employed to correspond to and manifest various practices.

Using these signs to demonstrate the visualization, the King [of Mind] and the Numbers [of Phenomena] support one another to jointly attack the evil numbers and transform all afflictions (*kleśa*) so that they together enter the realm of reality.
That which is neither King nor Number clearly elucidates the essential principle of visualizing the mind. By means of this, one performs the visualization;

whether the visualization succeeds or fails, and its varying degrees of depth, are like passing through the five flavors until reaching the *amṛta* (clarified butter). When both King and Numbers are exhausted, the mental conceptions come to an end.
One who does not practice while practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* is one who contemplates the ultimate perfection of its accomplishment.
Mental factors (*caitta*) may, by means of this, accomplish contemplation, yet they cannot enter the Path;

if one wishes to enter the Path, it is necessary to transform and transcend them until they are utterly exhausted, and only then can one enter the Path. Therefore, the text of the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* is cited as proof.
It is said that if the mental factors (*caitasika*) of affliction (*kleśa*) are not exhausted, then contemplation will not be impartial;
thus we know that if one wishes to enter the Way and realize the Principle, the subject-object mind must be exhausted. To augment subject and object is the beginning of the arising of delusion;

as long as this mind has not perished, the source of delusion remains unexhausted. How, then, could one wish to enter the Principle? Therefore, Siming said: "When both object and contemplation are simultaneously severed."

The principle that the three thousand worlds, in their subtle fusion, manifest simultaneously at every moment is precisely this. Now, whenever one raises a thought or stirs a念 (nian), one immediately falls into the realm of subject-object duality and emotional conceptualization.
Even if one speaks of "Mind-Only" as being beyond all dependence, such a view is merely words;

I have yet to see anyone who attains true resonance with it, let alone achieves awakening. Furthermore, it is said: [The text continues: ...that which is spoken of... (Note: As the source text provided ends mid-sentence, the translation reflects the available portion.)
If that which is exhausted is because the mind exhausts it, then the fruit-mind is likewise exhausted; when cause and effect both do not abide, how could the mental factors (caitta) not be exhausted?
Furthermore, if one gives rise to fixed views by contrasting exhaustion with non-exhaustion, this is merely subject and object—how then could they ever be extinguished?
It is said that as soon as there is even a single thread of hair, there is [a world].
The "silk-head" (the introductory phrase) is precisely this.

In the commentary on the passage praising the virtues of the Bodhisattva, there is an exposition of the sections on the upper and lower branches (*ūrdhva-aṅga-adhara-aṅga*), which includes explanations of their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), as stated in the text at length.
Regarding the mention of "upper and lower branches," it refers to the initial general statement which is able to encompass all that follows; thus it is called [the "head"].
The upper branch (shang zhi) and lower phrase (xia ju) are still assigned to the upper [section], which is called the lower branch (*xià zhī*).

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the "Gate of Gathering Matters" (*shèqǔ shì mén*), it is said that Tiantai based this to provide both horizontal (*héng*) and vertical (*shù*) interpretations; this is not a mere fabrication, for its principle is inherently profound.

However, the horizontal and vertical explanations concerning the stages (*wèi*) are somewhat difficult to comprehend: the vertical is explained according to the meaning of the ten stages (*shì dì*), while the horizontal is explained according to the first dwelling (*chū zhù*).

Regarding the sequential order of the exegesis of the meanings, although the progression from beginning to end is consistent, there are horizontal and vertical distinctions in their significance. I now maintain that this does not constitute an error;

rather, it is what I have spontaneously expressed according to my own understanding. Thus, when the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are explained vertically, they represent the culmination of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*);

whereas when the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) is explained horizontally, it represents the beginning of partial realization. If the beginning and end mutually support one another and the upper and lower levels are revealed in alternation, it is nothing other than this.
In the first case, the horizontal lines below the top cap are all horizontal, while those below the bottom are vertical; in the second, the vertical lines above the top cap are all vertical.

While this interpretation is skillfully constructed and does not contradict the general principle, I fear that such an explanation—claiming it was created because human nature delights in novelty—is not the orthodox doctrine.
If this were the case, what would happen when someone else who delights in novelty appears after the time of Tiantai? It would merely serve to open the door to further heterodox views.
Duan also holds the old view that since [the Buddha] has already been granted a place among the "eyebrows and eyes," he is then deprived of it by being excluded from the "essence and substance.
When such granting and depriving are inconsistent, it is better not to grant him a place at all. The Book of Documents says, "Impartiality gives rise to clarity;

lack of impartiality leads to obscurity. It also says, "In practicing benevolence, one does not yield. If one yields, how can the principle of impartiality emerge? I have spoken these words simply to rectify this matter.
The numerical calculations regarding the calamities and transformations of yin and yang are already somewhat difficult to clarify;
how much more so when secular classics and scriptural teachings offer divergent arguments that become entangled amidst one another—this is precisely why their explanations are inconsistent.

Now, in explicating the single instance of Rāhu’s obstruction, which involves the eclipsing of the sun and moon, this record deliberately refutes the worldly claims that solar and lunar eclipses are ominous or strange portents.

The text further states that while one must critically evaluate and synthesize these views, it is impossible to claim that the principles of calendrical calculation (*kalpa-gaṇanā*) are entirely devoid of reason;
thus it says, "Because the phenomena of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) accord with the laws of yin and yang," and so forth.
Tiantai’s refutation of this view is intended to correct it based on its general principle, not to discard it entirely. This is as if [he were to say]: "As for the sun and moon..."
Zhao et al. should know that this explanation is entirely identical to what is stated in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*:
"Suppose the people of a single country collectively encounter adverse conditions and behold all manner of inauspicious phenomena; yet, within that same land, some see them while others do not.

The meaning of this is remarkably consistent with the principle that when one part [of consciousness] unites with yin and yang, it does not contradict conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), whereas another part relies on the multitude [of conditions].

The power of one's livelihood ensures that one does not lose the correct principle. Nevertheless, if one were to provide an exhaustive explanation for every single case, there might come a time when one reaches an impasse;
therefore, it may suffice to set them aside without further discussion.

The four dharmas of person, principle, teaching, and practice are all one; this is the great purport of the sutra. In the preface, this orthodox lineage is manifested, this circulation is shown, and this propagation is nothing other than this.
Furthermore, in the *Yuanlun* (Treatise on Perfection), regarding the three contemplations and the three virtues that are contemplated, each virtue necessarily encompasses the person;

thus, they too constitute the "fourfold one. Consequently, throughout the stages of the six levels of realization—from beginning to end—every single stage possesses these four. Thus it reaches its conclusion.
Within the mind of every thought-moment, among the objects of form and fragrance, what dharma is not [contained within] the four?
The first is the Lotus Samādhi, which pervades all places and encompasses all dharmas; ultimately, it is spoken of as being simply "one. This one is not merely one;
the one necessarily possesses the four, and while the four are not fixed as four, they are in fact just this one principle. To recognize this one principle is to find the wondrous within it.
If it were not so, the Dharma would reside within the mind; the essential governance of observing the mind lies precisely here.

Only one who possesses illumination understands that this cannot be fully grasped through mere verbal explanation. When the text emerges as the meaning, the text is primary and the meaning secondary; when the meaning emerges as the text, the meaning is primary and the text secondary.
Since these two alternate in being prior and posterior, which must be considered primary? One must say that meaning is primary, for it further clarifies the meaning.
The substance is the reality; the literary expression is the form. If there were no substance in the first place, what would the expression have to apply itself to?

If one understands this principle, then more than half of the reflection on the four propositions will already be complete. As for those who claim that what possesses meaning but lacks expression is unreliable: if it lacked meaning, that would be the end of it;
however, if it does possess meaning, it is perfectly acceptable even without expression. Furthermore, how can one know for certain that there is meaning but no expression?
While this may indeed be what the commentators find difficult to reconcile, to apply these four phrases to the four individuals can be said to exhaustively capture their underlying principle.

Furthermore, his citation of the Four Reliances from the scriptures to corroborate this is also appropriate. However, as for the phrase "neither words nor meaning," it cannot be entirely attributed to those who are deluded;
from the perspective of ultimate truth, it refers to a realm that lies beyond the reach of words and meaning, which is not without its own excellence.
This message may also be described as the ford for those who are deluded to attain awakening; were it not for delusion, how could one attain awakening?
It is also not far removed from this—consider it.
Generally, that which is called a "preface" (xu) must share a relationship of either identity or difference with the primary doctrine (zhengzong). Why is this? If they were identical...
If it were entirely identical to the *samanvāgama* (the sequence), what would be the distinction? If it were entirely different from the sequence, the meaning would not be established;
it must necessarily occupy a position between the two to be considered a sequence. This is why the *Anantaparyāya-sūtra* serves as the introduction (*nidāna*) to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:

first, because their substance is the same while their names differ, it can serve as an introduction. Because their substance is the same, they share the fundamental single *dharmatā* (true mark); because their names differ, [the introduction clarifies this].

It is called either "The Sublime Lotus" or "The Immeasurable Meanings. It is named "The Lotus" because it primarily refers to that which can produce [the teaching], while also encompassing that which is produced;
thus, it constitutes the Main Body (śarīra). It is named "The Immeasurable Meanings" because it primarily refers to the meanings produced, while also encompassing that which produces them;
thus, it forms the Introduction (nidāna). Therefore, it is said: "The Buddha directly spoke these names," and so forth. Second, it is because many emerge from one.
To provide a preface for this sutra, it is said that "from one pure path, two, three, and four are produced.

This merely states that many emerge from one, without yet mentioning the convergence of the many back into the one; therefore, this serves as the preface. To further state that the many are gathered back into the one constitutes the main teaching (*samyak-artha*).
Thus it is said: "From the locus of the single meaning, immeasurable dharmas emerge," and so forth. Regarding these two meanings:
The latter interpretation is most closely aligned with the truth; if one adopts this, the purport of the introduction becomes clearly evident and can be readily observed.

When verified against various texts, there is nothing that does not accord with it. As for the discussion of the provisional means employed—whether they constitute the same or different entities—this is fully detailed in other chapters (etc.).

The words of the Ambrosial Dharma have often already been implemented through official documents and edicts, such that they are no longer subject to alteration.

This is acceptable; however, to insist that [the Master] was necessarily the one taught by his own teacher is likely an error. Even if one wished to correct the record of his lineage, why must it be done in such a manner?

When the text treats all phenomena through the four lines [of the verse], then all phenomena have never been different; yet, it again uses all phenomena to encompass [the whole].

Regarding the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), the four propositions have never been identical; because they have never been identical, they are not one. They have never been different; because they have never been different, they are not different.

Thus it is said: "When one is empty, all are empty," and "when all are real, etc. This is not a distant contemplation of the profound mystery.

Among those who contemplate the vast and lofty, who is capable of participating in this? It is further said that one must understand that the four phrases refer to nothing other than the single *dharmatā*.
This means that the "single *dharmatā*" is the principle (*li*), while the "four phrases" are the meanings pertaining to its essence (*ti*).
Since the essence of *dharmatā* does not conflict with any phenomena and neither accepts, abides in, nor enters them, its essence is therefore devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Conventionally they are all provisional, and ultimately they are all real. When one contemplates the dharma-nature through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), the dharma-nature has never been one;

when one subsumes the four propositions under the dharma-nature, the four propositions have never been different. Since it cannot be sought through oneness or difference, it is neither conjoined nor dispersed.
Because it is neither conjoined nor dispersed, it is omnipresent throughout all dharmas—this is what is meant by "each and every name is one."
A single phrase of a verse and so forth are all non-different from the Dharma-realm because they are the Dharma-realm; because the Dharma-realm is one, and because it is one, there is no obstruction.
This is as explained in the "Ten Gates of Non-duality. When expressed through the ten gates, all may be spoken of;
when expressed through non-duality, all are ineffable. To speak while not speaking—where forgetting and illumination occur simultaneously—is simply the wondrous.

Since all sutras employ skillful means (*upāya*), the magnitude of these skillful means is truly vast. This is because "skillful means" refers to the transformative function (*nirmāṇa-vyāpāra*) of the fruition;

and among transformative functions, none is greater than the three aspects of identical essence, provisional application, and the opening, establishing, abolishing, and restoring [of teachings]. These constitute the skillful means of the present sutra. Therefore, it is said in the introduction:

"The skillful means of the testimony of faith and the incitement," and so forth. Thus, as for "means" (*fang*): *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the full context of the preceding passage.)*

yet it is specifically not mentioned here because this chapter is the very beginning of expedient means, and thus requires no further explanation. Since its essence is identical to reality (*tattva*), it is not an expedient that exists outside of that essence;
how, then, could it be subject to difficulty through being contrasted with expedient means? Thus, it is said: "The Lotus [Sūtra] is one..."
Regarding the fact that the contents of this section can be understood within a mere square inch: as per the previous intent, nothing transcends the single mind (*ekacitta*).
If one understands a single thought-moment (*cittakṣaṇa*), then the essential purport of the entire scripture must be realized within one's own mental consciousness (*svacitta-vijñāna*).

As for why anyone would be willing to take the tainted (*sāsrava*) consciousness of the triple world as the "expedient means" (*upāya*) praised in this sutra—it is precisely because [the truth] does not depart from the *skandha*-mind of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

This is because it can reveal the wondrous principle of the true reality (*tathatā*). Thus, throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, there has never been anyone who sought anything else;
all who seek do so for this alone. As for the ten modes of contemplation, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, and the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood—all are unified within this very principle.

The myriad dharmas arise from the fundamental principle, and the ten pairs begin with non-abiding; therefore it is said that "from the fundamental principle of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.
Now, this fundamental principle is True Suchness (*tathatā*). Because True Suchness does not abide in its own nature, the mind, intellect, and consciousness arise from it.
It is through this that pure and impure karma undergoes endless transformation, thereby forming the first aspect within the realm of phenomena.

Because all dharmas are thoroughly cut off, phenomena (*vastu*) are termed provisional and essential. There is no way to establish phenomena apart from principle (*li*), nor can principle be manifested apart from phenomena.

Yet, within a single word regarding phenomena, there are two aspects: first, the phenomena of deluded defilement; these phenomena emerge from principle, and once they have emerged, they are not the principle itself.
Although they are not the principle, one still relies upon these phenomena to perceive the principle. Second, the phenomena of cultivation and manifestation.

The matters are as explained in the subsequent teachings and practices; because these are precisely what can manifest the principle (*tattva*), it is said that "matters possess the function of manifesting the principle.

This is why the skillful means (*upāya*) are praised. Furthermore, it is said: "In reality, how could it be otherwise? Mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these three are nowhere not pervaded by the principle.

Thus, when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reveals and clarifies according to the nature (*dharmatā*), it shows that even the marks of the mundane world are nothing other than the eternally abiding (*nitya*).
The conditioned arising of outflows and other phenomena, whether defiled or pure, all belong to the realm of phenomena (*dharma*).

There is nothing that does not embody principle (*li*) within phenomena, as clarified in the "Gate of the Non-duality of Phenomena and Principle. To speak of phenomena and principle is to encompass those ten gates;

there is nothing that is not the non-dual yet dual, and dual yet non-dual, reality of phenomena and principle. This is just as the current pair of "Phenomena and Principle" serves as the foundation for all ten pairs.
Who would be willing to say this? It means that if one sets aside this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—which reveals and clarifies by discussing the Wondrous (*miao*)—who could possibly expound upon it?

Their understanding is unhindered by spatial boundaries and likewise lacks the distinction of shallow or deep; these words seem to suggest that there are differences not only in their practice, but also in the depth of their comprehension.

However, when judged by the perspective of sentient emotion (*qing*), these are still distinct stages prior to the Grounds, as they are yet considered "contrary cultivation. Therefore, we know that from the very beginning there is no fixed dharma regarding delusion or enlightenment, bondage or liberation;

Regarding the discourse on essence (*tī*) and function (*yòng*), there is both identity and distinction. To speak of "distinction" is to clarify their meaning; to speak of "identity" is to clarify their reality.

How is it that since ancient times, various schools have each maintained their own doctrines, resulting in a chaotic confusion of right and wrong and shallow and deep views?

This teaching serves merely to assist in its manifestation; thus it is said: "Furthermore, by means of diverse skillful means, one assists in manifesting the primary meaning.

It is a constant law of phenomena that a name must have a corresponding essence; how much more so now, when these skillful means constitute a primary function—how could they possibly lack [an essence]?

This term "post-attainment" is used in contrast to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). As for its doctrinal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), they originally derive from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*;

When the essence is defined as "that which is real yet provisional," then expedient means constitutes the essence as it is in itself—this is what is being pointed out.
As for the teaching, it is provisional (*upāya*) while its reality (*tattva*) is the true principle (*satya-artha*) upon which it relies; the provisional must necessarily rely on the real.

this alone captures the correct meaning. If one were to adopt that [other] perspective to explain it, one would have to say that only the long-established [Dharmakāya] is the fundamental, and all others are subsequent.
Regarding the attainment of these two wisdoms, nothing is greater than this; how could others possibly know it?
Although the explanations in the various sutras differ in many ways, they are all subsumed under these two wisdoms.
Now, at the beginning of the True Teaching, as we intend to reveal and clarify these two wisdoms, we must first earnestly praise them in order to inspire the assembly.
The intent of this yearning for the Dharma is that the wondrous essence of the true reality (dharmatā) is inherently and spontaneously present;
thus, even after this praise, the fundamental principle has already been revealed. The commentary explains that the text first expresses admiration and subsequently reaches a state beyond praise.
If one were not to employ words, none could understand it; yet, even with such eulogies, words cannot fully exhaust its meaning—this is spoken according to the underlying intent.

The Tathāgata internally realizes the eternally abiding great samādhi of quiescence, from which he never truly enters or emerges. Even when there are conditioned activities or verbal teachings, they are quiescent yet constantly illuminating.
If even secular teachings say that "when still and unmoving, one is moved and thus attains penetration," how much more so for our Buddha?
In the Great Awakening that transcends the world, how could there be any trace of entering or emerging?

That being so, when it is said that [the Buddha] entered the Samādhi of the Immeasurable Meaning, and now again that he arose from that samādhi, is this not because the Buddhas of the three periods of time follow a constant ritual and manifest traces for the sake of representation, speaking of "entering" and "arising"?
What is meant is that while there is entering and emerging, there has never been any actual entering or emerging.
Unobstructed mastery manifests the great function of liberation that is without fixed direction; thus it is said, "This has that which is shown," and so forth.
If one were merely blank and dull like wood or stone, unable to respond, how could such a state be called the Great Samādhi of unobstructed quiescence and function?
If one understands this principle, there is no need to debate whether phenomena are fixed or principles are fixed; there is simply entry.
There is emerging and entering, yet from the very beginning there is neither emergence nor entry;
even as one enters and dwells within the samādhi of the Dharma-nature like radiance, it does not hinder the teaching of the unspoken through speech, and only after such speaking does one emerge.

Furthermore, it is like the Tathāgata of the Tripiṭaka, who three times a day enters meditative concentration to seek those with the capacity for deliverance—all these are traces of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, each expressing its own specific significance. How could this be...?
Can one perceive the Tathāgata through fixed traces? Thus we know that it need not be discussed. The text is concise;

all four [passages] speak of "compassion" (*karuṇā*) arising from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The commentary interprets this as having the meaning of "pity" (*anukampā*), yet it would be more appropriate to interpret it by using the character "manifestation" (*biao*).
Furthermore, "serene composure" (*ānāpāna*) means settling the mind in the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) and examining it with precision so as not to err.

In the commentary, why does the text address Śāriputra and speak of ten meanings—namely, "relying on" to break small wisdom and reveal great wisdom, and "abolishing" to discard the assembly and open what was concealed—as explained in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text)? Because one is deluded by its smallness regarding the great, and because the faculties serve as a convenient means, he did not instruct others but specifically instructed Śāriputra;

Since that which has already been opened must begin within the context of addressing [the audience], and because from the initial bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) to the final conclusion there is no deviation in principle, the Great Master (Nāgārjuna) gauged this intent to reveal the general framework.

"and so forth. Therefore, by merely opening the provisional (*upāya*), he pre-indicates the opening, refuting, abolishing, and harmonizing [of the teachings].

To take one instance as an illustration of many: throughout the three weeks of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the marvelous skill of "opening the provisional" (*kaiquan*) is singular; thus, the teaching...

Were it not for Tiantai, who profoundly exhausted the Buddha’s intent and skillfully reached the source of transformation, how could one know that at the moment of addressing the interlocutor, such a grand purport was already present?
One should investigate this deeply; one should comprehend this well.
Although the preceding text contains phrases such as "no full-lotus posture" (*paryaṅka*), they do not appear in their proper sequence here;

thus, when these are cited now, they must be understood as being introduced by quoting from a treatise (*śāstra*). For instance, the passage beginning with "binding mindfulness before oneself" also exists in a treatise.

Since it appears that there is almost nothing [of this] that does not originate from textual sources, yet the commentators have missed the essential points, causing readers to hesitate; therefore, [I have corrected this].
This is shown.
Expedient means (*upāya*) constitutes the beginning of the "Trace Gate" (*jijimōn*); the Dharma-exposition (*hōsetsu*) is the commencement of the three cycles (*sanshū*).

At the end of this section, there is a praise of the Buddha’s two types of wisdom (*nijichi*). For the realm of ultimate principle cannot be known, it is therefore expressed by means of ultimate wisdom. If ultimate wisdom...

When there is illumination, its principle is attained; that which is called "ultimate wisdom" (*jñāna*) is the Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*). Buddha-wisdom is signless (*animitta*), possessing both the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*).
The real is the wisdom that illuminates the principle through one’s own practice (*svayaṃcaryā*);

because this wisdom reaches the very bottom of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and exhausts the boundaries of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), being vast horizontally and deep vertically, it is called "profoundly deep and immeasurable. Provisional wisdom is the path prior to one's own practice.
Because it possesses the capacity to lead one into the true wisdom within the Path, it is called a "gate.

This can only be realized and entered through the wisdom of the forty stages of the true cause; since others among the seven stages of expedient means cannot fathom it, it is said to be "difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
The specific mention that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot know it refers to those whose attachments are particularly heavy.

Therefore, speaking in terms of time, throughout the preceding four periods one was entirely unaware [of this]; it is only through the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation and clarification that one comes to know it.
As for the remaining passages concerning the exposition and the resolution of doubts, they can be understood according to the text itself; there is no need to cite them at length again.

The Sūtra says: "Since my attaining Buddhahood... This statement of attaining Buddhahood is, in its general sense, the same as that in the *Honmon* (Original Gate), yet it differs in terms of near and far;
thus, we know this is a passage where Śākyamuni himself expresses self-praise. Furthermore, in the subsequent text, he praises the true wisdom by means of his attaining Buddhahood:
if he were to manifest the original [state] in reality, he should point to the period prior to the kalpa of motes and dust, saying, "It is exceedingly great and remote. Now, however, he praises...
Because he attained the true wisdom of Buddhahood, from the moment he was at the site of enlightenment (Vajrāsana), he spoke of various causes and conditions;
this describes his teaching and transformation throughout the four periods [of the Dharma]. Therefore, following the concealment of the fundamental [truth], we shall for now speak only of the traces.

If the subsequent text states that he came from within the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of True Suchness (*tathatā*) to achieve the Way of Buddhahood, then it pertains to both the fundamental and the trace, as if it were the fundamental itself.
If we speak of the traces [of the Buddha's teaching], they all do not fail to be this Way. Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision refers to his ability to know and see;

"vast, great, profound, and far-reaching" describes the object of what he knows and sees. If we discuss ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), it is fundamentally neither horizontal nor vertical, for its illumination is infinite and boundless;

the terms "horizontal" and "vertical" are used here like saying a chest is large because its lid is large. Now, in discussing the Gate of Traces (*jia-men*), we primarily focus on the Buddha’s capacity to know and see.
Because it speaks of the seeds of wisdom regarding the eye, it says, "that which is called revealing, instructing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," and so forth.
If one includes both the object known and the vision itself, there will be variations in the detail of the expression and shifts between the peripheral and the primary;

this does not mean that the subject (the knower) and the object (the known) are entirely unrelated. Were it otherwise, how could the Buddha’s knowledge and vision not be identical in their entirety to the principle of the Three Truths?

It is further said: "If one discusses ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), it is fundamentally neither horizontal nor vertical. This statement says it is "fundamentally not" [horizontal or vertical] because it is made in contrast to the horizontal and vertical dimensions of conceptual thought (*cintya*).
Now, speaking in terms of the circular fusion of the three truths (*tri-satya*), it is called "horizontal and vertical" because it illuminates the meaning of the infinite and limitless.

If it is horizontal and vertical, it is like a large chest requiring a large lid. Furthermore, the ancients have used this passage to correspond with the preceding section on "discriminating selection" (*liao-kan*).
Subsequently, there are generally three intentions: First, regarding the praise of the Buddhas and their wisdom as a unified whole, this clarifies that their essence (*tattva*) is identical;
whereas the praise of Śākyamuni individually clarifies that his manifestations (*vṛtti*) are distinct. Second, it clarifies the basis for the descent of traces (*traces-manifestation*):

the Buddhas first praised the Real (*satya*), while now [Śākyamuni] clearly manifests the power of the Fundamental; thus, he first praises the Expedient (*upāya*). Third, the Buddhas manifest their own practice (*sva-caryā*), which must first attain the Real; Śākyamuni... [manifests his own practice].

To clarify that the transformation of others should first employ provisional means to manifest alternately through appearance and disappearance, it is intended to show that the essence is perfect and not partial.

However, observing what has been excluded here, it seems both skillful and logical; yet, when interpreting Buddhist scriptures, I fear such interpretations may appear overly clever, and for that reason, I have not adopted them.
Furthermore, although this section and the preceding text both highly extol the two wisdoms, they include both exegesis and summary.

However, one does not yet perceive what makes it wondrous; it is only upon reaching the point where words are cut off and praise is exhausted that one finally perceives the wondrous realm pointed out directly, which constitutes the essence of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*)—the details of which are as stated extensively in the subsequent text.

The *Śāstrasaṃgraha* states: "In definitive sūtras (*nītārtha*), the meaning is determined according to the literal text; in non-definitive sūtras (*neyārtha*), the text is determined according to the underlying meaning.
As it is said here that the teachings on the two vehicles (*dvyāyānika*) and so forth are of definitive meaning, their meaning is self-evident and need only be determined by the text.
However, regarding other passages that record the two vehicles, they are not yet fully decisive and must be determined by means of the underlying meaning. Furthermore, the sūtra says:
"Rely on the meaning, not on the letter; rely on the definitive meaning, not on the non-definitive meaning. This implies that the letter is insufficient to rely upon.

Furthermore, [one might argue] that since the teachings state, "To define the meaning by means of the letter, one will never attain it even once," this would completely contradict the treatise (*śāstra*).
Now, I say that the latter two phrases are not incorrect. Since the treatise itself offers a single explanation, there is no need for reconciliation. Moreover—

The ancient masters interpreted the attainment of enlightenment by all Buddhas through the perspective of equality (*samatā-abhiprāya*) and the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the śrāvakas and others through the perspective of a different time (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*);
thus they revealed that this sūtra is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), as it still requires determination through its underlying intent.
Therefore, it is known that their explanation is particularly not exhaustive of the truth.

When one wishes to cut off speech in order to extol the wondrousness of the Way, it would be perilously abrupt to do so without first proceeding through gradual stages; therefore, one first describes its origins.

Since this proceeds from the preceding extolling of the two wisdoms—the provisional and the real—it is done either by means of "speech that relies on words" to let one know that the ultimate realization of this Dharma resides in the Buddha, or by means of "speech that cuts off words" to let one know that this Dharma can ultimately never be exhausted by words.
I offer these words to those who have ceased speaking; whether one affirms or denies, neither fails to accord with what is appropriate. Thus it is said, "and so forth.
Furthermore, one must know from what dharma the essence of this cessation of praise originates. Therefore, one must clarify its objective realm (*viṣaya*);

once this is known, one will understand that the reason for ceasing praise does not transcend the aforementioned methods of provisional and ultimate truth (*upāya-satya* and *paramārtha-satya*). Thus it is further said: "To speak of the essentials, it is the ultimate; the rest..."

The "phrase" (*pada*) is a provisional means (*upāya*); furthermore, it is a term used to summarize essential points by joining the fingers. The remaining phrases are likewise both provisional and real.

Since the Buddha has fully accomplished them, the ultimate limit of the path of cultivation cannot even be expressed in words; it is simply a matter of following the convenience of each specific meaning.
This is why, in the middle of the praise, the former is called real and the latter provisional: it signifies unfolding the provisional from the real. Now, wishing to cut off all speech, one must—
Because provisional means are subsumed into the ultimate reality, the provisional comes first and the ultimate follows; "stopping, stopping" is precisely the severance of speech.
This is because this Dharma is profound and quiescent, the path of language is cut off, and its essence cannot be expressed; thus it is praised with "stopping, stopping.

Even if one were to employ compassion to preach it, even upon hearing it, one would not understand; therefore, it is stopped. Nevertheless, in all cases, it is because [the truth] is ultimate that it cannot be spoken.
The wondrousness that transcends words should simply be brought to rest right here;
yet even the final point left by the Layman Vimalakīrti still had something remaining to be shown, and when he was praised by Mañjuśrī, it was already quite extensive and not at all slight.
How much more so when one further elaborates upon this the true reality of all dharmas—the ten suchnesses—explaining the reasons for these most profound realms of experience through words?
As for why this is inconceivable, does it not mean that the more words one uses, the further one moves from the Way?

In what sense, then, can it be said that words are transcended? This can only be intuitively realized by those who have attained liberation through detachment; it is not something that those clinging to traces can extinguish.
Nevertheless, since the sutras already contain these words and the Patriarchs have further provided their commentaries, who would say that the wondrousness of transcending words is itself wordless?
The phenomena of all dharmas are the facts, and their true nature (*dharmatā*) is the principle; when these are combined, they constitute the wondrous realm.
When realized to the ultimate degree, it is also called the profoundly deep realm—this is the Way. Among all the perfect teachings, there is none that does not trace its origin back to this.
Therefore, the commentators summarize its purport through ten meanings, stating that the fundamental principle of the *Lotus Sūtra* is the wondrousness of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

It is the ultimate purport of perfect explanation, the primary source of all teachings; it is the essential key for unlocking the interpretation of meanings, consisting of the four modes of explanation;

it is another name for the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), the refuge upon which sentient beings rely; it is the objective realm of the four truths of non-action, the support for the arousal of the bodhicitta;
and it is the single true nature of suchness, the root source of both delusion and enlightenment. It is also...
The "root of non-abiding" refers to the essence of the application of skillful means; "identity" refers to the identity of the provisional and the real.

The "principle of the fruit-virtue" is the fundamental nature of the Dharma-realm; the "thorough completion of a single transformation" refers to the beginning and end of the ripening and liberation of the seeds.
The "finality of the five periods" is the ultimate destination of the three virtues. All of these emerge simultaneously with the present reality.

When different names are understood as having but a single meaning, then the ten meanings are all clarified; thus it is said that "by means of this, all differences are dissolved and everything becomes transparently clear.
The mind contains all phenomena: within the one there is the immeasurable, and within the immeasurable there is the one.

This is so because of the principle (*li*). According to this principle, all is fundamentally equal; were it not for the mind, there would originally be no increase or decrease. Yet, according to emotional attachment (*qing*), one grasps and clings to them.
If the mind does not possess the three thousand [dharmas], then emotion and principle cannot stand together; it would be acceptable to speak of them separately. Why, then, is it not so here?

You say that although ordinary beings possess [the three thousand], they are deluded because they sever principle, and although those of the Two Vehicles possess [them], they seek liberation by abandoning them.
Thus, you seem to present both emotion and principle together. How can this be? I reply: On the surface, they appear different, but in reality, there is no contradiction. It is as always.
It is said that although the phenomenal (qing) and the principle (li) are presented separately, their essence and nature cannot be different.

Precisely because they are not different, both must be clarified together. This is why it is now stated that each of the ten realms is "endowed with" [all others]: this means that the phenomenal is not different from the principle.
Because both are clarified together, their meanings may mutually subsume one another; if the phenomenal subsumes the principle, then only the Perfect [Teaching] can be endowed with all.

The nine realms of mind are not fully present [in the formless realm]. If principle were to override emotion, then regardless of high or low status, all would possess [the Buddha-nature] without exception;
yet when it is said that sentient beings are deluded, this means that principle does not obstruct emotion. Each accords with its own meaning, and there is nothing that cannot be accounted for.
Alas, how can later generations insist on forced and artificial interpretations? Is this not contrary to the underlying principle?
There is nothing in the Dharma more esteemed than principle (*li*), and there is nothing closer to principle than the mind (*citta*).

If one attains its principle, then all the teachings of the Buddha can be harmoniously integrated; if one penetrates the mind, then all principles and natures can be clearly illuminated. Therefore it is said [as follows]:

that which is now elucidated—the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—is the fundamental principle of this single sutra; thus, the parables manifested through the "Dharma-explanation" (the *dharmaparyāya*)...

The teachings regarding past lives, the destinations reached in former times, that which has long been accomplished, and that which is now being accomplished for the sake of circulation and propagation throughout all assemblies—all of these ultimately converge upon this principle.
Once awakened and recognized, it is nothing other than the true aspect (*dharmatā*). The true aspect is without proximity;
nothing is closer than the mind. If one penetrates the various states of the mind, the true aspect is not far off; thus, there is no dharma apart from the mind, and no dharma outside of reality.
Externally, there is no separate mind; what is called the "extensive exposition over eight years" and so forth is none other than this.

Thus, one realizes that the Buddha-activities of the ten directions do not depart from the present dharma-realm, and that the capacities of sentient beings are as clear as pointing at the palm of one's hand. Whether mind or phenomena, there is nothing that is not the treasury of principle.
As it is said, the Buddhadharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges must be recognized upon the tip of a single hair. Is this not so?
How wonderful!
Other sutras have certainly already spoken of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; these "ten suchnesses" are simply the laws of direct cause and effect.
Why, then, do you now single them out as an extremely profound realm and a state of ultimate wonder? What is the underlying intent here?
The opponent says: "Dharmas have no fixed nature; it depends entirely on how the one who realizes them is. Words have no fixed meaning;

it depends entirely on the one who speaks them. Since this sutra states that these are "accomplished by the Buddha," that "only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust [their meaning]," and that "my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable," how could these not be considered the most profound realm?
Is this not a realm beyond the reach of praise? Were it not for Tiantai’s profound realization of the scriptures’ intent, no one else could have employed such a method.
What other sutras describe are merely general principles; therefore, they cannot be used to challenge the present sutra.

Thus, the fourfold interpretation is fully applied here, and by citing the supporting texts, the meaning becomes clear. Therefore, the interpretation based on the ten realms is explained as follows: [The text continues with the specific explanation].
The essence of this Dharma is all-pervasive. To explain it in terms of the Buddha-realm is to demonstrate the ultimate realization of this Dharma;
to explain it in terms of separation and union is to reveal the inconceivability of the Dharma-body; and to explain it in terms of stages is to manifest that it is fully exhausted only by the Buddha.
Furthermore, since there is no pointed indication of the wondrous realm that does not originate from this, one thereby attains the thorough understanding of both the root and its branches.

This is the ultimate purport of [the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue*] and so forth. Therefore, one should know that what is now appended to the scriptural text is specifically a concise summary of the scriptural purport, which has been extended and elucidated.

If one were to lose this profound meaning and treat the *Zhi-guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) as having its own separate discourse, then one would merely be following the specific tenets of that particular section.

As for the current commentary, when compared with that *Zhi-guan*, there is a sense of breadth and narrowness regarding the elucidation of the profound; (as stated), the details are as explained in the text, and shall not be repeated here.
"Xia" means detailed.
First, regarding "the ten suchnesses," when explained according to the ten realms, these ten suchnesses apply universally across all ten realms.
Next, when explained according to the Buddha-realm alone, all ten are the Buddha-realm; this is intended to reveal that the Middle Way is exclusively characterized by neither marks nor non-marks.

This is because it is the Buddha-dharma realm. Furthermore, when explained next by way of "separating and combining," there are distinctions such as "one's own practice" (*svayam-pratipatti*) and "falling into others" (*para-pāta*).
Regarding one's own practice, the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*) are exclusively the Buddha and are all termed the "unsurpassed marks" (*anuttara-lakṣaṇa*).

However, when contrasted with "following others" (*para-anuvidhāna*) and so forth, they extend throughout the nine realms, because they follow the self; thus, through the combination of following others, they are unified, yet through their separation, they are inexhaustible.
Regarding the three truths as measured by this treatise, they are neither conjoined nor dispersed; this precisely reveals the meaning of the inconceivable, and the subtlety lies herein.
Next, when explaining according to the stages, one takes the three—characteristics, nature, and essence—as corresponding to the principle-nature (*li-xing*).

Although they belong to the principle-nature, they actually pervade the ten realms; therefore it is said: "If one investigates these three virtues and so forth, the subsequent seven knowledges follow in sequence."

Regarding the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and so forth, the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*) constitute the horizontal dimension while the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*) constitute the vertical dimension.

However, if one refers to the principle of nature (*dharmatā*), the meaning again becomes horizontal. This is because, when speaking of the principle of nature, it pervades all ten realms and the beginning and end are non-dual;
thus, there are statements such as "though remaining in evil, one does not sink," which serve to manifest the inconceivable and ineffable purport of the teaching.
Thus we know that this single "Ten Suchnesses" (daśatathatā), combined with the various expositions and harmonized with each individual sūtra, can be said to exhaustively capture its subtle essence;
compared to those other theories, it is certainly not of the same order.
"How profound is the phrase 'ultimate equality'! It is the supreme teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Alas, those of old did not understand this;
they sought it only within the beginning and end of the 'Ten Suchnesses. Consequently, they never drew near to the teaching on the wondrous realm of the direct pointer.
How regrettable that their explanations were all不通 (incomprehensible)! Now I say: these very three characters are precisely the ultimate."
The reason why the wondrous revelation opens up the three to manifest the one is precisely because it does not depart from this principle.

Therefore, when explaining [the teaching] by way of the person, the delusion-and-enlightenment, or the teaching itself, there is nothing that is not a concrete manifestation; this is exactly for this reason.

If one were to discuss this purport to its ultimate limit, how could it concern merely the three and the one? Furthermore, what single dharma would not be equal, and what single principle would not be so?
Provided there is speech, there is nothing that is not equal; how much more so for those who have no speech?
Even speech and non-speech both ultimately return to equality. That being so, is there anyone who can transcend this ultimate equality?
If there is, try to tell me so.

Generally speaking, although the commentaries (*śāstra*) and exegeses (*vṛtti*) differ in their respective systems, rules, and structures, it is appropriate to synthesize them because the profundity of what they establish does not admit of divergent interpretations.
Furthermore, it is unnecessary to force every detail into complete alignment, for such artificial accommodation would be improper;
rather, one should simply harmonize their general principles. This is as in the case of the five propositions (*pañca-vākya*) of that treatise.
The intention behind each of these questions is as follows: "What dharma? is a direct inquiry as to which of the ten suchnesses it is.
"How is this dharma? asks for its underlying reason. "What is this dharma like? interrogates it by way of analogy.

"What are its marks and what is its substance? seeks to identify its essential nature and characteristics. If one explains by investigating in this manner, then [one understands] the present ten suchnesses.
This can be clearly understood. Furthermore, if one explains each point by means of the fourfold categories, one will see how the meaning of the Dharma is vast and comprehensive.
This is as clear as the detailed exegesis provided in the *Shu-ji* (Commentary).

However, if one insists on seeking the underlying logic for every single detail—claiming that the school has a specific source from which it returns—I fear the teachings will ultimately become obscured and unintelligible. Each [point]...
When it comes to their principles, it may be acceptable for each to have its own explanation.
That which is inconceivable (*acintya*) does not necessarily transcend words, and that which transcends words is not necessarily inconceivable;
only when both are clarified together as they are now described can it be called ultimate. Yet, how could this differ from verbal expression and written characters? Based on this:
The treatise takes indeterminacy to be the inconceivable; this, too, does not go so far as to indicate a specific characteristic.

If one were to discuss the inconceivable, how could it be merely a matter of indeterminacy? In short, both determinacy and indeterminacy are still within the realm of conceptual thought (*saṃkalpa*), and thus are not the inconceivable.
Furthermore, because it transcends the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) and lies beyond all linguistic expression, it is the inconceivable.

Those who are able to reach [this state] are themselves both conceivable and inconceivable. If one discusses this principle of negation, one must directly cut off all possibilities of reaching or not reaching, and of practicing or not practicing.
One must grasp it with the mind and realize it through silent resonance;
otherwise, even if one fears there may be a portion of correspondence, it will still be difficult.
The treatise uses analogies to demonstrate the inconceivable, and its phrasing is somewhat difficult to understand; I shall now provide a commentary on it.
First, in demonstrating the mark of equality through the identity of form and emptiness, it says "and so forth," meaning that one does not take the destruction of form as the path to emptiness;
rather, observing that form is itself emptiness constitutes the path of equality. As for the phrase "the words are not different," it should also be understood as "not one."
Neither identical nor different is precisely the equality of the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is likened to the coexistence of light and darkness, which are like the identity of form and emptiness.
Those who do not understand claim that light and darkness are different, yet they fail to realize that even as moonlight coincides with darkness, how could they ever be different?
And since moonlight is not darkness, how could they ever be one? It is thus.
They are neither identical nor different, yet they are said to be in conjunction. It is like the rising of the sun and the arising of light:

the light does not coexist with darkness, yet darkness has never departed and the light has never arrived. At the time of darkness, the entirety of the light becomes darkness; at the time of light, the darkness itself becomes light.
In this way, there is neither coming nor going, neither identity nor difference, and yet it is said that the light does not conjoin with the darkness.

It is also like the union of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the Way (*mārga*), which are neither identical nor different; the Way is precisely birth-and-death, yet they are neither identical nor different.

Because the Tathāgata cuts off afflictions (*kleśa*) and emerges from birth-and-death in this same way—neither identical nor different—it is said that "what the Buddha has exhausted, he has already exhausted;
what he has delivered, he has already delivered. This is called the non-elimination of light and darkness, manifesting the Buddha’s *bodhi*.

This is likewise its underlying principle; is it not inconceivable (*acintya*) that it is clarified in this way? The commentary and explanation differ entirely from the present [text], and their respective merits and defects remain undetermined.

"Inconceivable" refers to the ultimate limit of principle (*tattva*). As for the ultimate limit of principle, there is nothing that can be questioned, whether it be mundane or supramundane phenomena (*dharma*).
None of these can be fully grasped through words or the conceptual mind; let us attempt to clarify this by means of worldly matters of karmic retribution.
For instance, the Āgamas clarify the four inconceivable things, and so forth; furthermore, the sūtras clarify that each of the five destinies possesses its own unique inconceivability.
Although these are not the ultimate principle nor the deepest of dharmas, even when seeking their ultimate limit, how could they possibly be conceived or deliberated upon? It is simply this.
Just as in the world, regarding the faculties and their objects in daily life, even at the ultimate level of principle, there are things that even noble wisdom cannot know—
such as why the eye sees and why the ear hears— and as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*,
that these are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously; when investigated in this way, they all emerge from the inconceivable fundamental *tathāgatagarbha*.
That within one there is the immeasurable and within the immeasurable there is one is indeed the perfect explanation of the mutual integration of phenomena and their fruits.
How could the supreme and wondrous function at the stage of fruition arise of itself? There must necessarily be a principle rooted in the inherent nature (*xingju*).
This wondrousness of the inherent nature is not separate from the causal mind; it is called "inherent virtue" (*xingde*), "the root of principle" (*liben*), and "causal principle" (*yinli*).
All of these are its essential purport. It is simply that ordinary, deluded beings are unable to manifest it; yet, even though it is not manifested, it cannot be said that it does not exist.
Since it is fundamentally non-existent as a manifestation, what is there to be manifested? This is precisely the fundamental tenet of our school regarding the inherent nature (xingju).
Those who do not understand this merely engage in redundant talk about the "roundness" of function and use, the "interpenetration" of the Dharma-realm, and its "unimpededness," layer upon layer.
In the inexhaustible mutual integration of each and every phenomenon, one investigates its underlying principle;

yet, as there is ultimately no fixed point of arrival, speaking of it is like [the teaching of] "nature-arising" (*xingqi*) without mentioning "nature-endowment" (*xingju*), which is precisely what our present school points to for refutation. Thus it is said, and again:

"The interpenetration of the environment and the inhabitants on the level of the Buddhas' fruition is entirely due to the fundamental nature of sentient beings; the benefits to self and others, and the gains and losses therein, are mutually [interdependent]."
This is merely to reveal his intent.
*Wenju Geyan*, Volume One;
*Wenju Geyan*, Volume Two.

Those who take the Great [Vehicle] but fall back to the Small and so forth do not share [the same capacity] as those who have fallen back from the Great [Vehicle]. Those whose benefit extends through the upper two cycles do not share [the same capacity] as those who have fallen back from the Great [Vehicle].

Those whose benefit extends through the upper two cycles do not share [the same capacity] as those who possess each of the three faculties (*indriya*). This continues up to the distinction between those who wait for the time and those who do not;
thus, one must examine their similarities and differences one by one. Therefore, it is known that the natures of the faculties across the three cycles are indeed complex and difficult to discern.

What can be distinguished by those of coarse and shallow understanding is detailed in the *Huayuan lun* (Treatise on the Source of Transformation), which distinguishes between the secondary and primary [teachings] regarding the Śrāvakas (*yún yún*).
Speaking from the perspective of the virtue of original nature, all sentient beings are already Buddhas;

how could there be such a thing as a fixed small capacity (*hīna-indriya*) that remains unchanging from beginning to end? It is only because sentient beings have been deluded regarding the Truth and have practiced the Small Vehicle since it was not yet opened.

Since there are indeed those who take themselves to be inferior, the text states at length that, citing the treatise, it clarifies that there are four types of śrāvakas, which do not exceed two categories:
one is real and one is provisional; or, one is neither provisional nor real. The text further states that Tiantai, based on the sūtras and in light of the treatise, sets forth five types;
these four are the same as those in the treatise, though their names and characteristics differ slightly. The fifth is the Mahāyāna śrāvaka, also called...
The Buddha-way, having been opened, speaks for those who have newly entered; yet if one were to judge it in terms of existence or non-existence, it would remain indeterminate.
To say it "exists" refers to what was taught in the past; to say it "does not exist" is spoken for the sake of maturing [the practitioner].

Furthermore, it is said that in the past there was no mention of the Buddha-way’s provisional transformation (*saṃvṛti-nirmāṇa*), whereas now there is no designation of a definitive regression from the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). This is because the discourse integrates both the past and the present.
They are categorized into four types; however, this distinction is clearly evident, so why must one laboriously explain it further?

As for the three cycles of the śrāvakas, their fundamental nature is one and the same, yet they enter [the path] at different times because their delusions vary in thickness, their faculties vary in sharpness or dullness, and their confusion varies in lightness or gravity;
thus, their wisdom varies in clarity or obscurity. Therefore, it is said... and so forth.
Those who possess the capacity for transformation are so called because their root-nature was already determined in the past, yet their sharpness or dullness has not been finalized in the present;
rather, having encountered conditions—both wholesome and unwholesome—in the interim, their sharpness or dullness can be made to transform, and their upper or lower status can be exchanged.

For example, one originally of great capacity but dull nature may, by encountering wholesome conditions, transform from the lower to the upper; or one originally of small capacity but sharp nature may [transform accordingly].

Because encountering adverse conditions causes those of superior capacity to regress to an inferior state, there is what is called "regression from the Great" (*da-tui*); this refers to those of sharp faculties who originally belonged to the first two cycles.

Those of dull faculties should correspond to the third cycle; this is precisely what is meant. It does not concern those whose original status was fixed as being directly addressed by the three cycles.

Once this is understood, the distinction between the primary and secondary aspects of the three cycles becomes clear and can be discerned without the need for further detailed analysis. Furthermore, it must be discussed: [The text continues with a discussion on the nature of the three cycles and their relationship to the various capacities of practitioners.]
The meaning of these passages merely concerns the similarities and differences found in the commentaries (*shuji*), and so forth.

Regarding the question of whether ignorance acts as an obstruction or not—whether the hearing of the Dharma precedes or follows the destruction of delusions—although this is a thesis established by another, it remains a difficulty that cannot be resolved.
Why is this? For instance, consider the capacity of those who attain entry through the three successive assemblies (*san-zhōu*).
Regarding whether the destruction of ignorance occurs first or last: if ignorance were destroyed first, it would imply that hearing the Dharma is ineffective;

if it were destroyed later, it would mean that ignorance is not an obstruction. Now, it is said that for those with the capacity of a Bodhisattva, there is no fixed rule as to whether the destruction of delusion occurs before or after [hearing the Dharma].
However, in the case of Śāriputra and others, it was verified that they only began to destroy their ignorance upon hearing the Dharma; this serves as proof of the merit of the revelation.

However, there are cases where it does not act as an obstruction; this is because the capacity for perfect awakening (*paripūrṇa-yukti*) has already matured and ignorance has been previously subdued, and thus it does not constitute an obstruction.

Furthermore, the Great Master’s understanding of this analogy does not exceed two meanings: namely, that the arising of light and the extinction of darkness cannot be definitively ordered as before or after.

This is because the hearing of the Dharma and the destruction of delusion are like the simultaneous pecking and hatching of a chick and its mother hen; they admit of no temporal sequence, and thus darkness—[though it may seem to exist simultaneously]—does not obstruct.
"Concentration is an obstacle" is stated here with reference to the general nature of the obstacles consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*). This is also said provisionally by way of analogy.

If one were to discuss the hearing of the Dharma, it would not necessarily require that afflictions be eliminated; for if that were so, would it not follow that those at the stage of ordinary beings who are bound by all fetters would all be unable to hear the Dharma?
Thus, hearing the Dharma does not necessarily entail the elimination of afflictions, and the elimination of afflictions does not necessarily entail hearing the Dharma.

To speak directly, if one follows the interpretation of the *Ji* (Commentary), it adopts the perspective of the masters of the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*) to directly address the presence or absence of obstacles through the categories of self and other, and so forth;
it may be said that this represents one particular school of thought.

Regarding the three vehicles of the past, there were those capable of understanding them; however, because they relied on two limited sūtras, they found it difficult to comprehend the passages of the present sūtra that they did not know.
Yet, the textual structure of these passages—advancing and retreating, repeating and reiterating—is somewhat difficult to unravel. Now, one should provide an explanation in two sections.
First, the question is as stated above, which can be understood accordingly. As for the meaning of the answer, it first cites this very sūtra, stating that there are indeed those who...
Regarding the passage on "knowing," although the text initially aligns with the two scriptures as it appears, its meaning remains unclear;
therefore, I shall synthesize three points to demonstrate the significance of knowing and not-knowing, so that each may find its proper place. Thus it is said: first, knowing is clarified;
next, not-knowing is clarified; finally, they are unified in knowing. This is not a state of permanent ignorance, but rather the doctrine of knowing through not-knowing.

Is this not indeed ample? Yet, fearing that those who cling to their views may not yet be quickly subdued, Śāriputra again introduces the passages from the two [scriptures] concerning "not knowing" as a further challenge;
thus, he restates his argument in two parts. First, he cites the teachings to refute the error, saying:
"If one clings to the two texts," and so forth, asserting that both "knowing" and "not knowing" are the Buddha's domain.
The general purport of that sūtra is largely as previously indicated, and so forth. Next, regarding the establishment of the doctrine and its harmonization, it says:
"In the initial stage there are two [aspects]"; if one attains these two meanings, then providing an exposition is not difficult, and so forth.
Furthermore, the text explains this through the provisional and the real, citing the four propositions of former masters; however, I do not adopt those, but shall simply judge them directly.
Thus it is said, and so forth. Although one knows its general outline is thus, there is no harm in consulting the explanatory notes for a detailed understanding;
otherwise, matters would likely become quite confused.

Regarding the theories of this single school concerning the *Avataṃsaka*, there are four: [the theories of] the Place (*Jichang*), the Duration of Time (*Shichang*), the Exhaustion of the Future (*Jinweilai*), and [the theory of] the Ultimate (*Jijing*).
The *Ji* (Commentary) states that "Dharmadhātu" or the "Sixfold" are called the "Ocean of Emptiness" (*hai-kō*) and the "Womb of the Mother" (*bo-tai*).
Regarding the duration of their exposition, their names and characteristics, and their origins, these are all as stated in the text. Although there are six names, in reality there are only four.
