For instance, the "Ocean of Emptiness" in the *Avataṃsaka* may belong either to the duration of time or to the Dharmadhātu, as explained in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text). As for the "Womb of the Mother," it encompasses them all.
Although it is subsumed within the future limit (*anāgata-koṭi*), the teaching as it was spoken at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) also encompasses other times;

thus, its duration is the same as that of its respective class, which concludes with the final section. Since it is identical to this sūtra throughout the future limit and eternally resides on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and elsewhere, it is solely the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is simply the Perfect Principle.
However, regarding the single aspect of "long duration," the term "time" (*kāla*) may be understood either broadly or narrowly.
Regarding the "indeterminate" [attainment], some say it is limited to the stage of *prajñā* (wisdom), based on the text of the present work;

others say it extends to *nirvāṇa*, based on the *Xiangfa jueyi jing* (Sutra for Resolving Doubts during the Semblance Dharma). I now maintain that the latter explanation is correct. Did not our Patriarch say:

"Just as when the sun first rises, it first illuminates the high mountains, and when the sun is about to set, its lingering radiance likewise reaches the steep peaks"? Based on this, the analogy is fundamentally the same.
How can it be that [the text] points to something different by merely stating that "time" extends to later periods and saying "the duration of time is such"?

If, as this current passage says, the teaching after the compilation reaches as far as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this refers to the meaning of giving rise to the ten great minds, which corresponds to the *Prajñāpāramitā*;

it is a specific indication according to the text and is not a general discourse. As for those who claim that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is excluded because it is separated [from the *Prajñāpāramitā*], we say that this too is [not the case].

It is not that one should not hear [the teachings] or that one must necessarily explain them immediately; why insist on universal penetration? As for the specific locations, what treatise would exclude them?
These are all merely the limitations of older treatises. One should simply know that it is thus.
People of that time knew only to explain the *Lotus Sūtra* through such concepts as "opening up" (*kaishō*) and "abolishing" (*fai*), yet they never understood where its true intent lay.
If one does not know the intent of the Patriarch, one does not know the intent of the Buddha; therefore, it is said that he established the provisional for the sake of the real.

The establishment of the provisional for the sake of the real was fundamentally intended to reveal the real; by opening up the provisional, the real is revealed, thereby clarifying the utility of the provisional. If the utility of the provisional were not clarified, [the purpose would remain obscured].

If reality is obscured by the provisional and reality does not manifest, then principle cannot be revealed; thus, "the provisional conceals reality" means it remains latent, while "reality attains manifestation" means it becomes evident.
Whether something is latent or manifest depends solely upon the nature of things.
That which is called the eternally abiding source is the single vehicle’s true aspect, wherein the identity of the provisional and the real has never undergone increase or decrease; therefore, now...

The reason for this demonstration is further stated as "prior to the opening" and so forth; this is a retrospective indication that before the *Lotus Sūtra*, the true intent had not yet been manifested.

Thus, there were no words at all regarding "opening," but only statements concerning what was appropriate for the provisional. This too is merely a matter of taking the underlying meaning; it was never the actual teaching.
Therefore, it is said that the ultimate aim of the *Lotus Sūtra* reaches its zenith here: the teaching of reality (*saddharma*).
The source of all origins is rooted here; the ultimate aim of interpreting the meaning of the teachings converges here;
the treasury where all practices are gathered resides here. What is this? It is nothing other than the true path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
If one can rely upon and embody it, then the teaching will not be in vain and practice will not be a mere exercise; how could one fail to strive for its knowledge?
In the Buddha-dharma, there is fundamentally no distinction between self and other; yet, within this absence of distinction, those who speak of distinctions do so because there exists a "true self.
Within the absence of superiority or inferiority, those who speak of superiority and inferiority do so because there exists the "supremely superior.
What is this supremely superior? It is the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). Therefore, that which is elucidated in the present sutra is the mind.
That which is revealed by the Dharma is the Buddha Vehicle; thus, it is recorded that its distinct characteristics are distinguished by ten pairs, and so forth.
Consequently, all that is taught therein is the realm of the Buddha, not departing from the single mind, which is the natural course of the profound principle.
Nevertheless, although other sutras have indeed once cited this to inspire aspiration among beings, they contain passages of partial praise that, when compared with this sutra, ultimately fall short.
This is not merely a partisan argument; it is simply the nature of things (*dharmatā*).

Regarding the reason why the subtle revelation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* transcends all other teachings of the single lifetime [of the Buddha], let us speak briefly from the perspective of the "Trace Gate" (*jimon*) concerning the teaching of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*).

There are three points that do not go beyond this: first, the essence of the Dharma (*dharmakāya*) is the provisional and the real (*tattva*) of the ten realms. In the case of the Buddha, the provisional...

In reality, these two wisdoms reside within the Dharma; thus, the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) constitutes the root-source for transcending the world and the fundamental basis for establishing transformation.
All functions arise by following and relying upon this path.

Therefore, as briefly opened above, there is the manifestation of the One through the Three—a provisional expression that transcends words—in praise of the two wisdoms, namely, the "true mark of all phenomena" and so forth. Second:
The "transformative intent" (*huà-yì*) refers to the great purport of the Tathāgata’s single transformation. Thus, in terms of time, it spans fifty years of transformative activity;
in terms of teaching, it possesses both the provisional and the real, and functions through the three applications of bestowing, opening, and abolishing.

Therefore, there are passages such as the current text’s "correctly opening the three expedients to reveal the one reality," and "the Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; their underlying intent is difficult to understand," and so forth.

The Commentary refers to it by means of the four meanings of person, principle, teaching, and practice at the beginning of the text because the great essence is further revealed as not exceeding these;

therefore, that which is taught according to what is appropriate as an "opening of expedient means" specifically points to the provisional [teachings] previously bestowed—this is the meaning of "opening the expedient.
Furthermore, the phrase "this Dharma is not of thought or discrimination" is either used as a conclusion regarding the provisional, or as...

To manifest the reality is precisely what is meant in the subsequent chapter by the statement, "All these dharmas are for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. As for manifesting the reality, only a Buddha can fully comprehend it;
whereas as for concluding the provisional, the Buddha's intent is difficult to know. Therefore, those who receive the teachings perceive three vehicles, while the Buddha knows there is but one.
Thus it is said: "Now the three are opened to reveal the one. This serves as an introductory lead, just as when one wishes to take something away, one must first firmly give it.
Regarding its meaning: the three aspects of principle and wisdom have now arrived through the transformative teachings of this sutra;
having already attained Buddhahood, he harbors within his breast this realization and is able to reveal and manifest the wondrousness of the One Vehicle.

Thus, it is said that all Buddhas appear in the world solely for the sake of the great causal condition—namely, to open, show, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—and so forth. However, as for its text:

The meaning is vast and expansive, so profound that it is difficult to comprehend; I have now extracted its major points and presented them in three sections to show [the reader] the source and flow of the scriptures' intent and the general outline of the Buddha’s transformation.
This is intended so that students may understand the origins of the scriptural teachings and the broad scope of the Buddha’s edification.

The Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*) is precisely the single principle revealed by this present sutra. Now, a principle does not manifest of itself; it must be clarified by means of the truths (*satya*).
Furthermore, the truths do not manifest independently; they must be manifested by means of the eyes and wisdom.

Therefore, taking omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) as "knowledge," one takes the perfect illumination of the Buddha-eye as "vision. Although knowledge and vision differ, they both constitute the Middle Way.
The principle of this is one and the same. Where does this principle reside? It resides in the sphere known and seen by the four eyes and two wisdoms;

it is, in its very substance, entirely complete and has never for a moment been deficient. Therefore it is said: "If sentient beings did not possess the knowledge and vision of a Buddha, what would there be to speak of 'opening'?
From this it follows that those very four eyes and two wisdoms, in terms of principle, are none other than the seed of the Buddha-eye and the Buddha-wisdom.
The myriad phenomena in their array are, in this very place, the profound stillness of true emptiness. One should know that these two realms are but a single realm;

yet within this single realm there are two perspectives. Because there are two perspectives within the single realm, they are dual though not two; because there is a single realm within the two perspectives, they are non-dual though dual.
This is why the place where the followers of the Two Vehicles perceive emptiness is now revealed as the perception of the Middle Way.
The principle is that the six realms of ordinary beings are, in their conventional state, immediately the First Noble Truth;
the Bodhisattva establishes the conventional state as being none other than this inconceivable principle. The subtle purport of this revelation lies precisely here; therefore, it is said:
"In order to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Since it says "in order to cause sentient beings," those who are to be opened are the nine realms.
Furthermore, it is said that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (jñāna-darśana) manifest the Buddha-wisdom;

therefore, we know that Buddha-wisdom is not separate from the nine realms, and the nine realms are manifested within Buddha-wisdom. Since delusion and enlightenment share the same source and their opening and manifestation are of one principle, how could this not be wondrous?

Wisdom itself constitutes the obstruction, and the obstruction itself manifests virtue; this is not limited to this particular passage alone. Generally speaking, regarding perfect clarity, there is no delusion that does not function in this same way.

This clarifies that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are fundamentally inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*), yet they must be said to be "opened" because the two types of delusion constitute obstructions in their very essence.
Therefore, they must be broken through in order to be opened, and opened in order to manifest the principle of inherent virtue.
Since the locus itself is entirely restored, it is recorded that the essence of delusion is thus. Why is this? That which is called "delusion" is merely a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*);

when a single thought-moment is deluded, it becomes delusion, and when a single thought-moment is awakened, it becomes wisdom. Fundamentally, there are not two dharmas. Therefore, the substance of thought is precisely this:

it is nothing other than the inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*). Although the three thousand [realms] have not yet been manifested, as long as the essence remains unverified and one is still deluded, [the virtues remain obscured].
This is the substance, but not the principle. That which is "not the principle" cannot be made into the principle by which cultivated virtue is manifested;

it remains merely a matter of deluded defilement and is not what is called the "principle-nature" (li-xing). Although there is right and wrong, there is no distinction between a fixed right and a fixed wrong.
Although it is a single substance, it is divided into the obstacles of the one who is deluded and that which is deluded.
Because the distinctions between the two delusions are not clearly delineated, nor are the virtues and their obstructions distinguished, it is said that they are "difficult to comprehend.
One must know that these few phrases encompass the entire intent of this school regarding the mutual inversion of the principles of phenomena and noumenon, as well as cultivation and nature;
they must be deeply savored. As for the commentary on the critic’s argument concerning the citation of ancient texts, it is not without its merit.
In principle, this merely involves an exegesis following the literal text and is not yet sufficient to reveal the grand framework; this can be understood through careful examination.
This clarifies the intent of the *Avataṃsaka*’s nine and ten periods for the purpose of discerning the numerical categories of causes throughout the three periods of time.
The emergence of two meanings refers to the perfection of number and the fulfillment of principle. Thus, reaching nine [worlds], there are only three periods of time;

the three periods of time are but a single thought-moment; and every moment—past, present, and future—is like a day. In this way, the long and the short mutually encompass one another, manifesting the inconceivable, and so forth.

Furthermore, the *Jì* (Commentary) clarifies that when it is said that the dust motes of the lands of the ten directions throughout the three periods of time all preach [the Dharma], the reader should simply say: "The lands preach, and the assemblies hear."
Regarding the statement on "arising," one does not know who it is intended for. Now, it is difficult to clarify this; according to principle, it should simply be stated thus:
"May those who doubt attain immediate understanding. If there were a point of entry, one would naturally grasp it oneself. Since words have already been spoken, there can be no lack of explanation.
According to the intent of the record, although it generally serves to refute other schools, even if it is said that "every dust mote speaks and every world-system speaks," it is clearly manifest.
One does not know why the meaning of inconceivable perfect interfusion is so called;
moreover, if one were to question this by means of the immediate matters of the speaker and the audience, the intent would not lie therein.
Forced to demonstrate it, one says: it is simply because the natures of sentient beings and lands are equal, and thus their nature is identical.
It reveals that because their principle is the same, their affairs are the same; and because their affairs are the same, their teachings are equal. Thus it is said:

"If one grasps this meaning, then both sides are mutually clarified. Nevertheless, what a fine "speaking of dust and speaking of lands" (dharma-discourse)—yet how regrettable that one dies beneath the words!
It would have been better had he simply said at that time, "Who is it that receives this? This would have left the whole world in a state of doubt. Now, [he] acts...
This explanation must rescue half of the term "opening and revealing" (*kaigeng*), for there are two kinds: first, the "opening" of bestowing (*shikai*);
second, the "opening and revealing" of manifestation (*kaigen*). The present text refers to the former meaning; hence it says, "and so forth.

This means that bestowing is treated as opening, which serves as the basis for the revelation of the reality (*shitsu*). Although these are divided into two meanings, they are in fact one intent. Furthermore:
It is said: "How much more so regarding the provisional as being identical to the real; this is precisely the meaning of the present section.

This means that since it was not previously stated that the three [vehicles] are expedient means, the gate of expedient means was closed; now, by pointing out the provisional as being provisional, the gate of expedient means is opened.

Knowing that they are not ultimate, one must then reveal the real. What is there to reveal about the real? It is simply to demonstrate its provisional nature. What is meant by "demonstrating"? It means to point it out.

This indicates that the place where one perceives reality is precisely this. Furthermore, the subsequent passage states: "Generally speaking, all references to 'the past' possess two meanings," and so forth.

This means that the first meaning is the same as above, as it is explained in relation to what has already been opened up; thus, they are identical, and so on. Now, how then does one perceive that the provisional is entirely real?
It is simply that the benevolent person generates their own discrimination. If discrimination is forgotten, even "reality" is difficult to find.
Having attained skillful means (*upāya*), what doubt could there be? This must simply be understood through personal realization.

While the various manifestations of the Buddhas' transformative traces (*nirmāṇakāya*) differ from their original vows, they certainly cannot be discussed in a single, uniform manner as is done in this present text.
Yet, in terms of principle, there is nothing that is not possible; this is what is meant by "when one Buddha attains enlightenment, all are enlightened."
The perfected Dharma-realm is none other than the Buddha’s reliance and its environment;

furthermore, it is said that all sentient beings possess the very mark of nirvana, which implies there is no lack of reason for them to attain Buddhahood on the same day and enter extinction on the same day.

As for the statement, "What I previously mentioned refers only to those who have obtained a human body, not to the five destinies," if one were to reach the three evil realms, it would necessarily be preceded by [the exhaustion of]...

One must first transform others so that they attain the human state, and only thereafter can one fulfill such wishes as these; thus we know that regarding these matters, there are those for whom it is possible and those for whom it is not.
Nevertheless, even if one shares the same body as a human or a deva, how could everyone necessarily attain Buddhahood on the same day?

For instance, there are those like the Dragon Girl who attained Buddhahood in this very body—how could it be that she did not achieve it at all? Thus, we know that regarding these points in the scriptural teachings:
Regarding the various statements that have been made, how can they be taken as definitive conclusions? For instance, when Bodhisattvas make vows while on the path, they invariably say:
"If there is even a single sentient being who does not attain Buddhahood, I vow not to take perfect enlightenment.

Now, since there is no limit to the number of sentient beings who have not yet attained Buddhahood, would it not follow that no Buddha should ever take perfect enlightenment? It is like the case of [the Buddha] Suśānta...
If many Buddhas attain enlightenment on the same day and enter *parinirvāṇa* on that same day, how could they possibly be described as being of different types?
As for this sutra, it says: "If I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all the Buddha-way," and thus there has never been any difference.
Judging from this, the fact that the Way of each Buddha is the same refers to the intention of equality; their manifested traces (*nirmāṇakāya*) are simply not the same.
This is an intentional teaching regarding a different time; therefore, it is said that "each statement has its specific meaning"—is this not so?
Furthermore, these are the realms of all Buddhas, and they certainly should not be differentiated by means of ordinary conceptual measures.
This sutra states that even minor good deeds of humans and devas, such as bowing the head or raising the hand, all lead to the attainment of Buddhahood;
now, this commentary clarifies this point, stating that its purport generally consists of three parts. First, the essence of goodness is fundamentally integrated:

all phenomena arise from things, things arise from the mind, and the mind arises from principle (*li*); since principle is necessarily fused and undifferentiated, and its essence is Buddha-nature, it exists.
Regarding what is called "this should clarify the meaning of the three Buddha-natures," the commentary states: "The flow of water toward the sea is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that it never ceases;

the flame directed toward the sky is the principle and number by which it must surely be extinguished. This refers to the ultimate limit of principle. Second, regarding that which is permeated by the wisdom of vows, it says:

"For a mountain, it begins with a single basket of earth; for a tree of girth as wide as a man's embrace, it begins with a single hair. This means that one who first resolves their mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*) must necessarily aim for the Great [Vehicle].
The Way is like one whose will is set on building a mountain; it begins with a single basket of earth. If one pursues their original resolve, how could the Buddha-way fail to be accomplished?
This refers to the culmination of the three [aspects]. Regarding the third, "merit arises from revelation":
whether dharmas are great or small, subtle or manifest, if one exhausts their principle and accords with their nature, there is none that is not wondrous—this is due solely to revelation.
To manifest this essence, it need not exceed the two meanings mentioned above; because there is no dharma that is not wondrous, nothing is more wondrous than this.
All that can be known by analogy requires no further separate explanation.
Generally speaking, there is no teaching among those revealed that is not subtle; yet when discussing mental conduct, there is certainly a process of selection and exclusion.

How could one speak of the Subtle Dharma with such indiscriminate uniformity? Therefore, the Treatise clarifies that even the mundane minor virtue of a child playing with sand—if the mind is free from discrimination—then what practice would not be accomplished?
This is a general inclusion. However, if one considers the coarse-minded ordinary person and the person of small wisdom, these two...

Since one must distinguish between these when practicing while confronting and counteracting attachments, it is said, "and so forth. This also serves to manifest the sense of refutation within the treatise;
however, as for distinguishing from ordinary sentiments, there is nothing that is not excellent, so there is truly no need for further discussion.

Furthermore, regarding whether [the capacity] has been opened or not yet opened, or whether [the response] has been granted or not yet granted—if one were to scrutinize each of these minutely, I fear one would lose the Great Dharma. As the record also says: "Even if there is past goodness..."
To say that [the nature of things] is like the sands of the Ganges seems somewhat too extreme;

however, as explained below, since the essence of goodness is fundamentally wondrous and conforms to the minds of those who grasp it, there is nothing that cannot be so. Now, I shall resolve this: the sutras speak of "infants not knowing infants.
It is precisely because the sutras speak of them in this way that they are called "wondrous"; it is precisely because they do not know [in this manner] that they are so named.
Because the union with the Way is too clearly defined, beings each follow their own preferences.
The distinction between mind and object is not easy to clarify; how can terms such as "coarse" and "subtle" serve as definitive criteria?

Nevertheless, since the relationship between mind and object is quite pervasive, let us first illustrate it through a single instance: if one takes the ten realms as the object, one must necessarily take the three types of wisdom as the mind.

Based on this, one may discuss the coarse and the subtle, the opening and the non-opening, and so forth. In short, although there are four permutations, when the mind is open, there is no coarse object that does not transform;
if the object is coarse while the mind is subtle, then the object follows along with the transformation—the principle of this can be understood.

Furthermore, these meanings may be applied to the four permutations of "not depriving the person" and "not depriving the object. For instance, if the object is coarse while the mind is subtle, then the object is deprived [of its power].
The remaining phrases regarding the "seizing" of others may be understood by analogy. Furthermore, as for the mutual discussion of "person" and "object" in terms of their reciprocal seizing:

if one is turned by objects, then the object seizes the person; if one can turn objects, then the person seizes the object. The meaning is assigned in this manner, though it is not necessarily exhaustive.
As for the opening, the turning, and the seizing, these must be realized by the person themselves; they have nothing to do with external phenomena.

How comprehensive and profound is the teaching of the One Vehicle! There is nothing that does not take nature (*xing*) as its root, begin with seeds (*zhong*), arise from conditions (*yuan*), and be perfected through teaching (*jiao*).
All of this is fully exhausted within these verses; hence it is said, "and so forth. Now, as for nature, it is the nature of no-nature.
If one speaks of nature in terms of its original extinction and dissolution, then it is the nature of detachment; it is the absolute oneness that transcends all relativity.
Speaking of its nature, it is the nature of the Middle Way; speaking of it comprehensively, it is the foundation of the rational nature (*dharmatā*).
One who illuminates this principle possesses the seed of Buddhahood—that is, the seed capable of producing the fruit of Buddhahood.

Since arising does not arise of itself, but must necessarily depend on conditions, if one takes teaching and practice as conditions, then supramundane perfect enlightenment arises thereby. It is also because of this.
Because of the two causes—the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) and the completing cause (*paripūri-hetu*)—the true causal Buddha-seed (*tathāgata-bīja*) is able to arise.

Once the true cause is manifested, the fruit of Buddhahood is thereby accomplished. It is precisely through the accomplishment of this fruit that one is able to expound this teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

This is why it is said that future fruit-Buddhas manifest the reality; this applies to all [categories] such as the rational nature-seed (*dharmatā-bīja*), yet the text specifically singles out this point.

Because the faculties of sentient beings were sharp or dull during the Buddha’s lifetime after his parinirvāṇa, the texts and teachings vary in their detail and brevity regarding the meaning of the words, as is the case with this present passage.
During the Buddha’s lifetime, those with sharp faculties were told directly that there is "no nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) alone.

When their capacities and conditions led them to realize that "no-nature" is the immediate absence of all natures, and that even "no-nature" is non-existent, they were able to awaken to and enter the fundamental nature within the single principle of ultimate reality.

Emptiness has nothing else besides it. Since those of dull faculties cannot achieve this after [the cessation of] extinction, they must rely upon the four reliances to investigate and clarify this principle;

thus, they enter into cultivation through the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). As it is said: "The first is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)," and "possessing the second, the absence of intrinsic nature," and so forth.
Regarding these two types of emptiness, although there is a sequence in their verbal expression, their function is simultaneous: when one is empty, all are empty.
"Since there is nothing that is not empty, and this very emptiness is also empty, it is called the 'inconceivable two emptinesses.

Furthermore, it is said that 'if one does not understand these [principles],' etc.; this shows that our school establishes these two emptinesses to trace back to the fundamental, thereby manifesting the merit of the contemplative method.
Moreover, it is said that 'therefore, regarding the true path, one must be proficient in the cultivation of nature,' etc., which further perfects the gate of the true contemplation."
One must cultivate both nature and practice simultaneously for the qualities of nature (*xingde*) to be manifested through the clarity of cultivation; hence it is said, "and so forth.

Furthermore, statements such as "pushing forward but not entering" are based on those of the most dull faculties. Therefore, one must combine the investigation of the threefold falsity with the cultivation of the myriad practices—practicing both the primary and auxiliary methods together—and only cease once entry is achieved.
Only then can one be called "opened" (*kai*); otherwise, how could one receive this name based on mere superficial talk?
Kai-xie asks:

The intent of the question and answer is to show that the four propositions fundamentally investigate the rational nature (*dharmatā*) of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which is inherently pure; why, then, is this [fourfold analysis] still employed?
The answer is: because the nature is fundamentally non-arising. Why then ask about dependent origination? If one conceives of arising, it is not a question of the rational nature regarding phenomena.

Regarding principle, one merely calculates that all things are real, yet these must all be refuted through investigation. Once their inherent nature is eliminated, both phenomenon and principle vanish together;

why then refute cultivation alone while failing to refute nature? If one grasps this intent, the purport of the three objects of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) can subsequently be clarified.
Therefore, when investigating dependent origination, one still encompasses continuity and dependence; how could it be limited merely to the formation of causes? Thus we know.

This meaning has not been clarified since ancient times; were it not for the combined study of both the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra*, how could one know the teachings on the threefold provisional nature of essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)?
Furthermore, the subsequent selection and clarification is for the sake of those of sharp faculties, meaning that it is an opening and revelation.
Therefore, there is no need for this so-called "fourfold contemplation method" of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, which is intended only for those of dull faculties in the final age.
The commentary on the passage concerning the *Tathāgatagarbha-pratītyasamutpāda* now extracts the essential points as follows:

"Regarding the necessity of recognizing the nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) within the context of correct conditions (*pratyaya*), this means that while the seeds are categorized according to their nature and the conditions apply to both the defiled and the pure, the underlying principle is neither defiled nor pure," and so forth.

Next, regarding the explanation of the Middle Way as being without self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the subsequent text states: "Establishing original non-self-nature as the virtue of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*)," and so it says.
The statement that "the present seeds are precisely the seeds of the nature" is made in order to clarify the dependent origination of the nature; thus, it is spoken of in terms of "seeds.
Consequently, although it is called "dependent origination," it is not identical to dependent origination, and although it is called "nature-virtue," it carries the meaning of "seeds.

To speak with ease, this must refer to the interval between the nature and its categories; therefore, there is the aforementioned case where the ten realms and the rational nature are both nature and exist simultaneously.

In this section following the preceding discussion, the defiled and pure dependent origination is elucidated. Regarding the defiled aspect: due to ignorance, the nine realms arise as the dependent origination of the dharma-nature;
that is, the aforementioned nature-seed arises within sentient beings, which is the meaning of True Suchness (Tathatā) following defiled conditions.
Next, the pure conditions are explained: by hearing the teaching of the One Vehicle, one gives rise to the practice of the One Vehicle and thereby achieves Perfect Enlightenment. Its...

The meaning can be understood as follows: furthermore, below the section on "lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*), the three causes are explained by correlating the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*) and the "perceiving cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*) with the "direct cause" (*hetu-hetu*).
This is an explanation based on the mutual accomplishment of their functional characteristics. If one discusses the substance of practice, however, each of the three causes contains three aspects;

these are the three causes of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*). Once the fruit of the seeds has been accomplished, then "one arises and all arise. When the fruit of the ordinary person is accomplished, it relies upon the direct cause, the primary cause, and the accompanying conditions.

There is nothing that does not arise; arising is itself the fulfillment of the fruit. When the vehicle of fruition reaches its ultimate limit, cultivation and nature merge as one, no longer remaining separate.
This is entirely the rational nature (*li-xing*), wherein the three causes are developed without alteration from beginning to end; therefore, they are collectively termed "nature" (*xing*).

Thus, both cultivation and nature, cause and fruit, are fully contained within this text, and its general principles may be understood. To explain the specific characteristics of cultivation in detail, one must refer to [the following].

Regarding the passage on "stopping and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) and so forth, it subsequently provides a retrospective explanation of the meaning of cultivating both nature and characteristics (*xing-xiang*) while simultaneously encompassing self and other, as detailed in the chapter on the "Three Objects of Nature and Characteristics.

In summary, this establishes the principle of the Buddha-seed of dependent origination and so forth, ultimately converging upon the single truth of beginningless and endless suchness (*yīrú*). (And so forth.)
There are cases where the words share the same principle but differ in meaning. For instance, when one speaks of the "true mark of all dharmas," no doubt arises;

yet when one speaks of the "eternal abiding of worldly marks," doubt does arise. This is likely because [the listener] is too familiar with the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) and takes only that which is subject to birth, destruction, and transformation to be the characteristic of the world.
Thus, upon suddenly hearing the term "eternal abiding," they become doubtful. How could they know that two fives make ten? (That is, they fail to recognize the obvious.)
Regarding these obscurations and erroneous causes, the Sūtra reverses two phrases to state: "The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding;
this is the dharma abiding in its own position. This either negates several manifest [views] or serves as a response to the question:

"If it is truly the case that the characteristics of the world are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, and thus obscured by the notion of eternal abiding, then this is merely an emotional view (*qing-jian*); what does it have to do with the intent of the Sūtra? Thus, it reveals and clarifies [the truth].

Is it not perverse that the wondrous response of the single principle is met with such opposition? As the ancients did not say: "The ultimate discourse and wondrous understanding run contrary to common sentiment"?

If one observes from the perspective of principle, this is precisely what is attained. However, if one understands the texts of the commentaries and records in this manner, they will be resolved as easily as a blade meeting the edge of a whetstone.

If it were otherwise, one would follow the teachings while harboring doubts for a lifetime. That the Sūtra specifically mentions first that "the Dharma abides in its own station" is for this very reason.

To "show its basis" means that the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding; to "converge upon its ultimate" means that the true awakening of sentient beings is inherently present within the dharma-position.
Since all phenomena are entirely the principle manifested as events, they do not transcend this suchness, and thus there is no duality.
That the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding is precisely the supramundane true awakening; both sentient beings and the world are the world. Once [this is understood],...

If one takes *tathatā* (suchness) as the locus, there is no distinct characteristic outside of that locus; if one takes *tathatā* as the characteristic, there is no distinct locus outside of that characteristic.
Therefore, whether they be ordinary beings or Buddhas, all converge upon the ultimate of the single suchness; this is why it is called the "Unity of Principle.

However, while converging in this way, it does not preclude their being differentiated; thus, there are the distinctions between the principle of "afflictions already severed" and "already purified," and the principle of "realization" and "proof."
Furthermore, his arguments state that while defilement and purity, delusion and enlightenment, are fixed and limited with distinct characteristics, their nature is one;

that one uses awakening to reveal delusion and cultivation to verify the nature, employing metaphors to substantiate the principle. Though such explanations are repeated with great detail, one has never heard a word of direct pointing.
This seems like a mind full of doubt and words that branch out. Now, I shall interpret this by means of a single passage from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, explaining it as he does for the "one."

All phenomena are said to be constantly characterized by the arising of appearances while being unborn in nature; because this nature is eternally constant, is it not the case that appearance is itself dependent origination?
To realize that within the very place of dependent origination there is fundamentally no birth is precisely the mark of eternal constancy; there is no other principle.

Only then can one speak of the "identity of the state of appearance," where sentient beings and Buddhas are non-dual across the two times, and both the phenomenal and the noumenal are eternally abiding. Is this not wondrous?
However, it is not that the Master of the Doctrine was unaware of this; it is as if he said: "By mutual agreement, following conditions, there is defilement and purity within conditions;

though the conditions are either defiled or pure, they are equally termed 'dependent origination' (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This passage is currently suspected of being incomplete and lacking text. Now, one should supplement it by taking the remaining text, which says:
"The nature of the momentary is constant, and the principle of dependent origination is one. Furthermore, the phenomena of dependent origination are fundamentally unarisen, and only then do they..."
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* also speaks of the wondrous oneness of appearance and essence (*lakṣaṇa-lakṣya-ekatva-nityatā*), yet its meaning cannot be fully exhausted in words;
its intent lies in the student’s own contemplation and self-realization. Since that meaning has already been expressed therein, it may now be stated briefly.
Now, as I wish to perfectly manifest this teaching, I must explain it by means of that [text]. This is for those who investigate the ultimate school.
As for the meaning of the question:
it is simply because while their *status* (位) may be the same, their *characteristics* (相) cannot be the same; thus, he further distinguishes them with these words.

The intent of the answer is likewise to first follow the question by stating that although conditions (*pratyaya*) are either defiled or pure, they are both equally termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

This single phrase is profoundly significant. Based on what was said previously, if one realizes that at the very locus of dependent origination there is fundamentally no arising, then its principle is naturally and eternally abiding;
thus it is equal [to the ultimate]. Therefore, the metaphors of waves and moisture are adduced, and so forth.

Since the entirety of moisture constitutes the waves, the entirety of the principle constitutes phenomena. When the characteristics of phenomena are non-arising, their essence is itself eternally abiding; hence it is said, "The characteristics and... (the principle).
The names "Constantly Abiding" (changzhu) are the same, meaning that the names for both sentient beings and perfect enlightenment are identical in both locations;

yet, since defilement and purity are already distinguished, it follows by analogy that their respective stages must also have the distinction between delusion and awakening—not only in their characteristics (xiang). Therefore, one knows that the identity and difference of waves and moisture must coexist;
as the Fourth Patriarch (Sima Guang) said: "When water is clear and then becomes turbid again, its movement and function [are evident]."

If one were to follow the same pattern for defilement and purity, the worldly names would likewise differ; yet now, we take up their common meaning to use the manifest to awaken the deluded and the pure to reveal the defiled.
In the case of the constant phenomenon and the constant principle, their ultimate aim is one; therefore, it is said that "the principle is one.

However, when this is further examined through the lens of opening and revealing, and when one is interrogated regarding the transformation of delusion through faith in the teachings—if one indeed transforms that delusion, how could [it not be so]?
This is to ensure that those who have not yet attained faith will cause students to forget the words and grasp the essential meaning.

Previously, it was established that the characteristics of sentient beings and their states are all "constant" (nitya) because they are like [empty] illusions; now, by correlating the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas) with the three causes—whether in conjunction or separation—they are likewise shown to be "constant.

Although the provisional and the real differ, both belong to the mundane world; although there are differences in how these characteristics arise through causes, their underlying principle is one and the same.

To speak merely of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana) brings one somewhat closer to the principle and its objects; yet, by stating that they are neither identical nor distinct, the meaning becomes further integrated and clarified.

Moreover, this accounts for the three causes while simultaneously conforming to the gate of cultivation and accords with the meaning of the aforementioned lineage (gotra); therefore, it is explained again on this basis.
As for the mention of "six dharmas," this text from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* serves as an auxiliary explanation here: it is simply the five aggregates with the addition of a self (ātman).

You should state that the three causes are not identical to the six dharmas, yet they are not separate from the six dharmas. Now, regarding the partial statements in the text, one must observe their underlying intent:
because the true cause (*zhengyin*) is logically identical to the six dharmas, it simply says "not mutually [identical]";

thus, "not separate" can be understood. However, as for the conditional cause (*yinyin*) and the contributory cause (*liaoyin*), since their cultivation is not identical to their nature in relation to the six dharmas, it simply says "not separate"; thus, "not identical" can be understood.

Thus one may know that if one understands that the six dharmas are neither identical with nor separate from [the self], it reveals that the three categories of aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) are all devoid of intrinsic nature.
Because they lack intrinsic nature, their essence is unborn; because they are unborn, they are suchness (tathatā); and because they are suchness, they are eternally abiding.
To know that the characteristics of the five aggregates are eternal makes the purport even more clear, and it also demonstrates that the previous explanations are all rendered brilliantly manifest.

In the fifth section on the text, it is inherently difficult to clarify whether the Buddha’s physical body or his manifested form (*nirmāṇakāya*) preached the Dharma, as well as the chronological sequence of these events.

Furthermore, since the sūtras and śāstras were produced at different times, their respective tenets—whether refuting or establishing positions—are likewise hard to comprehend. As the commentary cites the Master Xiaoyun’s explanation, taking the twenty-one days as the period during which the Dharma had already been preached.

Master Hua cites the "Flower King" chapter of the present sutra as evidence, asserting that from a contemporary perspective, it may be said that the Buddha’s wisdom was taught in the *Avataṃsaka*, though this does not necessarily mean the three-week period refers specifically to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

His record follows that commentary by identifying the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* with the *Avataṃsaka* and further using the second seven-day period to symbolize the response-body Buddha’s teaching and so forth. Thus, whether one advances or retreats from this position, both are incorrect.

If one holds that the *Avataṃsaka* should not represent the teachings of the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha, yet considers the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to be identical to the *Avataṃsaka*, then why is it said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* represents the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha?
Both of these views contain errors regarding the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). Therefore, citing the *Yun* commentary, [the author] refutes them both;

the meaning is clear: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is also taught by the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha. However, what is now being distinguished here is the superior within the inferior; it is not merely the *Avataṃsaka-śiṅguṇa-sūtra*.

Because [the opponent] adorns their body with [their own views] and cites the *Mūla-śāstra* as proof, and further claims that "ancient masters have said so," it becomes evident that both positions are incorrect;
thus, they establish that this is indeed the teaching of the Dharma-Buddha of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Therefore, concluding with a definitive judgment based on principle, he says:
"[...]". From this perspective, the distance between our current judgment and those who, in their petty manner, engage in such groundless refutations and establishments is vast indeed.

The analogy of requesting the chariots has long been discussed in the treatises on the gates of the teaching. Its difficulty does not exceed the distinction between requesting the Great [Vehicle] and the Small [Vehicle] when speaking of "requesting.
While the text records three earnest requests for the Great [Vehicle], according to the primary analogy, it says that those who "seek the Buddha-way" [request it];
yet according to the literal text, it says, "We pray that you grant us the three kinds of precious chariots."
This is why one holds to both ends with doubt and is unable to resolve it. I believe that while this passage is clear in its wording, commentators have been unable to apply its meaning.
Now, when the text is already explicit, there are three ways of seeking its significance: first, seeking through the mechanism of emotion (*jìqíng*), which is great;

second, seeking through the mouth (*kǒusó*), which is small; yet the time for the mechanism of emotion does not necessarily coincide with the seeking by the mouth, though seeking by the mouth serves to fully manifest the mechanism of emotion.

Therefore, since the mental disposition (*citta*) of the seeker was present in the past, while the verbal seeking (*vāk-śodhana*) occurs only now, and since the verbal seeking necessarily encompasses both the mental disposition and the verbal expression, the present question asks:
"In the past, you departed from the house seeking the three grades. This means that at the time of verbal seeking, the mental disposition must necessarily have been present;

thus, the text reiterates this. However, one may raise an objection based on the literal text: "If it is as previously granted, this is merely seeking the three [grades]; what does it have to do with seeking [the Buddha]?"

The first is to use verbal inquiry to probe the underlying intent (*jīngíng*). When answering, one says, "I did not see [the vehicle] when I went outside," thereby responding to the verbal inquiry with the underlying intent.
This means that at the time he granted permission for the carriage within the gate, he originally intended to grant three vehicles;
yet because he mounted the carriage and went outside the gate, he did not see the vehicle he had intended to grant. Thus, one must know [the distinction].
There is a different path; one who follows this different path already knows that he will be granted a great carriage.

Thus, although his mental disposition already possesses the grand intent, he cannot simply request it from the Great One by verbal seeking alone; he must instead rely on what was previously promised to secure his distinct purpose.
Therefore, although his verbal seeking is small, the actual mental disposition lies in the Great; hence it is said, "He also obtains it."
These "solicitations" (so) are one and the same; therefore it is said that the three solicitations all reach toward the Ultimate Sage.

Furthermore, the distinctions between "responding" (fu) in terms of the manifest and the esoteric, or between the "real" (qing) and the "provisional" (jia), are all intended to convey this same meaning. One need only rely on this text to directly address the former difficulties, and the matter will become clear of itself;
why must one seek elsewhere? If you wish to know the details, there is the *Suoche Yizhang* (Treatise on the Meaning of Soliciting the Chariots), which says [as follows]. (etc.)
Birth and death are the realm of saṃsāra; nirvāṇa is the dharma of peace and bliss.
Furthermore, birth and death are the side of existence, while nirvāṇa is the side of emptiness. Now, is nirvāṇa within birth and death, or is it outside of birth and death?
Unless one has personally realized it through direct experience, it remains either internal or external.
All are "not as such. When one attains awakening, then both "as such" and "separate from such" are simply "only this.
Because they are all "not as such," one cannot avoid doubt; only by attaining awakening is this doubt dispelled. What is called "attaining awakening" refers to the realization of accord with reality.
Furthermore, because birth-and-death and nirvana are viewed as distinct, both are considered "night"; because birth-and-death and nirvana are seen as one, this is [the day].

Whether the sun is one or many cannot avoid engendering doubt; only by attaining awakening can one transcend this duality of oneness and difference, for it is only when the sun has risen that such doubt is dispelled.
What is called "attaining awakening" is truly not easy to describe; it must necessarily be realized through practice before it can be harmonized with the truth.
Yet, the compilers of the records explain it in terms of the various stages of the teachings (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*), and scholars likewise treat it as such.
The reason why the systems of teaching have converged yet people ultimately fail to know their subtle points is that they have missed the mark;
how could this not be known? Among those in the world who study the Buddha-dharma, there are two types.

Although each has its own preferences according to their individual capacities, when comparing their relative merits, those who enter gradually are superior to those who practice the Great [Vehicle] from the outset. This is because those who enter abruptly...

Regarding those who may not yet have fully understood this Dharma-gate, if they enter the Great Vehicle from the Small, proceeding from the subtle to the manifest, then there is no Dharma-gate, whether Great or Small, that they do not thoroughly study; thus, every aspect is fully prepared.

While it is true that entering the Great Vehicle as a Śrāvaka differs from entering it as a Bodhisattva, if one compares their respective capacities—whether sharp or dull, circuitous or direct, shallow or deep—it is further [not the case that they are identical].
Having already discussed this general framework, the remaining details are as explained in other commentaries, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the unsurpassed path," who would not know it without being told? Its meaning is not merely elucidated at length in the sūtras and śāstras;
rather, the Patriarchs have cited and expounded upon it. Of what dharma-gate could it be said that its vastness and inclusiveness are not such? Upon hearing this, one ought simply to...
Having thus received and taken it up for use, there will eventually come a time when one attains resonance and efficacy;

at that time, it is not difficult to discern between the partial and the perfect, or to discuss their relative depths. However, for a beginner to suddenly attempt such discussions is like making an overly premature calculation.
For instance, if one attempts to choose the partial in favor of the perfect without understanding them, both the partial and the perfect are lost—this too is a sickness of the student, and so on.
As it is recorded in the *Shiyao* (Essentials of Explanation), those who wish to know may select from this at will;

there is no leisure for a detailed exposition [and so forth]. The ten titles of the Tathāgata manifest that every Buddha is endowed with these ten virtues. For this reason, it is said: "The ten titles of the Tathāgata apply to every Buddha;
their names are not displayed in vain. Thus, when the ten virtues are complete, all myriad virtues are likewise perfected.
Should one not contemplate the name "Admiring Virtue" (Mude) as the perfect cause? Is it merely a matter of knowing it, or is it a hollow admiration? Who is the Buddha? He is simply within oneself.
It requires only that one reflect upon oneself without the slightest deficiency; the essential point lies in the individual aspiring toward this.
This is precisely the model for contemplating the mind—what more could be added? If one does not act thus, one will naturally give rise to despondency.
Alas! These were all the Patriarchs’ urgent efforts to resolve the delusions of others and inspire faith in them.

They feared that if worldly people encountered these many varied and obstructive doubts within the scriptures and teachings, they might fail to offer admonitions and warnings, potentially leading to slander—a harm that is by no means trivial.
Therefore, I have not spared the trouble of prolixity and have set these forth once more; do not reproach me for such repetitive and earnest speech.
This is indeed so.

The Sūtras state that there is "only one gate," and they further say, "by means of the Buddhist gate. Thus, principle is that which is elucidated by the teaching, and the teaching is the gate through which one approaches that principle.
Therefore, we know that it is not permitted for principle alone or the teaching alone to constitute the gate; if one were to treat them as separate, then...

The meaning of "gate" (*mukha*) is not established as a literal text; regarding the two gates of the chariot and the house, it means that because one obtains the chariot at the location of the gate, the house is also called the "chariot-gate.

However, there is a difference in their function of exiting and entering, and they differ in size, as explained in the commentary where it first clarifies the distinction between the two gates, and subsequently investigates their similarities and differences.
Therefore, it says: "If the house-gate were different from the chariot-gate, etc., it would also not [be so]."
To speak of their identity and difference is to recognize that one cannot determine their reality solely through identity or difference.

If this is so, what is the intended meaning? The text of the record itself clearly states it: "The paths of the Great and the Small are different; therefore, they are distinguished separately. Because the Small is immediately the Great, they are identical when [the distinction] is discarded;
thus, the chariot and the house are eternally distinct, yet when opened, the two gates are not different," and so on, as explained in detail therein. (etc.)
The meaning of the doctrine that "what was originally non-existent now exists" is not easily clarified, nor is there a definitive consensus;
the records differ according to the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and even when explained through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the interpretations vary.

The ancient critiques and difficulties cited therein are all visible in the present record, as it says: "The phrase 'originally non-existent' is a common saying among people, yet it is the most difficult [to explain]."
Furthermore, it is said that if one’s interpretation does not accord with principle, the chamber of Nirvana will collapse; therefore, this matter cannot be discussed lightly.

Zhiwen first cites the teaching of Zhang’an, stating that "that which was originally non-existent now exists" means that the eternal is itself the impermanent, claiming that the literary meaning thus accords perfectly.
However, when the *Ji* (the Record) presents its own formal explanation, it states: "One should say that afflictions are beginningless," referring to the relationship between afflictions and bodhi.

If one grasps their essence and characteristics as identical, both are devoid of beginning or end; yet if one considers their functions and characteristics as alternating, they are originally non-existent and now existent.
Each of these perspectives encompasses two meanings. Thus, Bodhi may be called the "beginning of the beginningless," and afflictions may be called the "end of the endless.
While the whole substance gives rise to function, it is without beginning or end, yet it possesses beginning and end; if the whole function returns to [the substance], [it likewise transcends them].
In its essence, although there is a beginning and an end, it is devoid of beginning and end;

though this is the meaning when discussed in terms of perfect penetration, the scriptural passage concerning the four ways of exiting *nirvāṇa* follows a different path and cannot be restricted by the present context.
As for the teaching that ignorance is without beginning, its meaning is as discussed in a separate treatise (etc.).

The "house" is used as a metaphor for the triple world (*tridhātu*), so it is appropriate to say it is "burning. The "gate" is used as a metaphor for the teaching, meaning that one exits by means of it.
Why, then, is it also said to be "within the gate that is being burned"? The text provides an analysis to address this, citing ancient interpretations and refuting objections, and so forth.
Our current explanation states: "The gate has both a bolt and an opening," and so on. This means that while the bolt can be burned, the empty space cannot; this serves as a metaphor.

If it were in accordance with conventional rules, the teaching would follow the expressive words and thus possess the sense of being subject to abolition; therefore, it would not be the eternal principle.

Since its fundamental nature is without marks, it cannot be destroyed and is not, consequently, impermanent. Now, because it emerges from the opening of the gate, it is said to emerge "from the gate that was burned.
This is merely stated according to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teaching. If one relies on the Mahāyāna, the teaching of liberation through letters is itself eternal.

If one abides [in this realization], one penetrates that there is neither burning nor non-burning; only then can it be said that one has attained peace and emerged from [suffering]. Yet the record states: "Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings on form are all eternal.
The intention here is that although the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ, the essence of form is one. Speaking from the perspective of this unity, it may indeed be called eternal;

however, when analyzed according to the principles of identity and non-identity, it is described as both burning and non-burning. In reality, the Buddha-dharma is fundamentally not [subject to these dualities].
How could that which is destructible, like Māra, possibly burn the Buddha’s body?

Since the body is fundamentally composed of the aggregates (*skandha*)—both physical form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*)—it is here described solely as form (*rūpa*) because it is being discussed in relation to the mind.

As for the textual explanation of the body by means of the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), this is done below in order to provide a detailed commentary on the scriptural analogy of the body being tormented by fire; thus, it is consistent with other texts.
It is not that there is no identity or difference; for what reason? Because the meaning of "pressing upon the body" also encompasses consciousness.
Furthermore, this consciousness, together with the five sensory consciousnesses, may be termed "simultaneous mental consciousness.

Yet, when it is said that they "together experience painful objects" rather than referring to the first moment, it is because that consciousness fundamentally extends through both the initial and subsequent moments; thus, this statement regarding the simultaneous experience of painful objects does not refer to the first moment.
Regarding the statement that even when not yet discriminating, one is only able to discriminate the formation of the three types of sensation (*vedanā*):

this is a re-explanation of the aforementioned meaning of experiencing the objects of suffering simultaneously. It means that it lasts for only the subsequent moment, and one cannot thereby establish contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) with this mental consciousness;

furthermore, it takes up the sense that the mind does not yet feel weary or distressed. Once suffering gives rise to weariness and distress, one will certainly be able to cultivate contemplation, as stated in the subsequent text.
This means that when one first applies the mind to cultivate contemplation, one takes the sixth consciousness as the starting point for observing phenomena;

this is the reason why [the capacities of] these [beings] differ in their ability or inability [to attain realization]. Siming stated: "It is because this mind can give rise to longing and aversion, thereby acting as the cause for good and evil.
Thus, we know that the meaning of such textual passages is truly not easy to clarify; how can one wish to rely on explanations based on stubborn delusion?
To explain this essential point of the text, one sees many who offer convoluted interpretations.

The gate is but one; that which emerges from it is called the "Gate of Dwelling" (*zhaimén*), for its gate is inherently small. That which enters through it is named the "Gate of the Chariot" (*chemén*);
though its gate is originally large, because it lacks the [discriminating] mechanism (*jī*), it is termed narrow and small. This is based on the great...

To speak of "small" does not mean it is actually small; opening up the small reveals that it is none other than the Great Principle. Therefore, the reasons for explaining the general and the specific in a concise manner are as follows:

"General" refers to one gate encompassing all three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle; "Specific" refers to each of the three—teaching, practice, and principle—individually clarifying one gate.

Although there are both general and specific aspects, they both refer to the Great while speaking of the Small. Regarding those who "know" or "do not know," this refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
People not only do not know how to enter that [state], they also do not know how to exit this one.

Not knowing how to exit this is not knowing the provisional (upāya); not knowing how to enter that is not knowing the real (tattva). Is it not the case that, within a single gate, one distinguishes the "great" and "small" based on entering and exiting?

The gate is a metaphor for the principle of emptiness, which is one and the same. From the perspective of the Two Vehicles, exiting the boundaries of the triple world is called the ultimate; from the perspective of the Bodhisattvas...

Entering the limit of reality is called expedient means (*upāya*). If one opens the small, it is immediately the great; thus, there is nothing here that is not expedient means within the essence of the body.

This expedient means is itself reality; they are no different. Therefore, while those of the Two Vehicles know how to exit [the world] but do not know how to enter, even Bodhisattvas who are dull-witted like the Two Vehicles likewise do not know how to enter.
Those who are sharp-witted may know it, yet if they are still bound by the path of teaching, even when it is stripped away, they still do not know it.
This treatise not only clarifies the meaning of the "narrowness" of the single gate, but also distinguishes between the Great and Small Vehicles through the two gates of the chariot and the house;
thus, its meanings are all made manifest.

Regarding the doctrine of the "regression of the six minds," which originates from the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), the difficulties in its interpretation are already fully detailed within the Japanese *Da-mon* (Questions and Answers).

The established teaching is sufficient in its own right; it merely states that both knowledge-vision (*jñāna-darśana*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed, and that this is not a permanent liberation. Thus, there is no room for doubt.
Even if other explanations exist, there is no need to force artificial interpretations, which would only serve to increase the proliferation of terminology and conceptual constructs.

The three provisional [teachings] and one real [teaching] constitute the great numerical principle of the provisional and the real (*upāya* and *bhūta-artha*). To speak generally, the provisional may also be considered as one;
for example, the "transformed city" (*nirmita-nagara*) is only one, yet it can also be considered two or three, just as if there were only two chariots, there would be three.
Other examples follow this pattern, such as being both three and two, as stated in the text. However, one must not say that the real is universal.
If one considers two truths, three truths, and so forth, what destination could there be that is not accessible? Nevertheless, to say that "three are provisional and one is real" is the permanent;
to say that all are equally pervasive across the three and the one is the transformative. Since the transformative is inherently and constantly pervasive, it cannot be considered permanent.

Thus, we know that names and characteristics are opened or closed according to what is appropriate; how could there be any fixed theory at the outset? Those who hold rigidly to such views are surely deluded.

The perfect realization that object and contemplation are non-dual, as well as the afflictions to be severed—which are fundamentally ignorance—when spoken of from their origin, should properly belong to the eighth consciousness-mind.
