The various textual records and commentaries are detailed;

indeed, regarding all the dharmalakṣaṇas, names, and meanings of the teachings of the past that have been transmitted to the present day, none fail to encompass both the sense of identity and difference, for only after establishing these two meanings can one be said to have attained [the truth].
As it is said in the *Śāstra*: "Regarding ministers, subjects, and servants, there are two gates: identity and difference," and so forth. The commentary states: "To transcend..."

The "sections" (*jie*) constitute the same [category], while the "divisions" (*fen*) constitute the different [categories]. Regarding the reasons for this sameness and difference, there are generally three meanings:

First, as for the divisions within a section and those that span across sections, this has already been indicated at length in the previous *Xuanshan* (Profound Commentary), etc. Second, there are the "same essence" (*tongti*) and "different essences" (*yiti*), also termed "within the essence" (*tishen*) and "outside the essence" (*waishen*).

This refers solely to the two dharmas of the provisional (*quan*) and the real (*shi*). Because of the differences between the present and the past [teachings], there arises the distinction between sameness and difference.
This is because they are distinct. If one discusses their essence (*tattva*), they should not even be considered the same; how much less could they be said to be different?

What is now called "essence" is merely a provisional designation of two essences—distinguished as "opened" and "unopened" based on the present and the past, respectively. Thirdly, regarding the bestowal of skillful means (*upāya*) and the opening of those skillful means:

because the bestowal of skillful means occurred in the past, it is considered "different"; because the opening and manifestation occurs in the present, it is considered "the same. Therefore, there is no difference.

To bestow upon what is different that which is the same, yet in that sameness there is no differentiation; to open up what is the same so as to reveal its differences, yet in those differences there has never been any divergence.
To bestow upon what is the same that which is the same, yet in that sameness there has never been any identity. To investigate this thoroughly, it is fundamentally neither the same nor different.

Depending on how one bestows or opens it, it may appear as the same or as different—so what is there to say about "sameness" or "difference"? This is merely a discourse on the single nature (*ekaprakṛti*).
Therefore it is said: "The official and the commoner are by right subject to two authorities; the present three explanations can unify all matters.
Thus, the divergent opinions of antiquity may be settled. If one grasps the essential point, there is no need for prolixity.
In the middle section, using the parable of the four elements, the teaching for the śrāvakas, headed by Kāśyapa, was fully revealed.

Having thus completed this, the parable of the deluded son comprehensively encompasses the five periods of the Buddha’s one transformation; there are both the uniform and the profound. The uniform comprehension refers to the events of today’s *nirmāṇakāya*, which are also uniform.
The partial comprehension and the exploratory comprehension refer to those on the stages of the *dharmakāya*, who reflect upon today’s events and are also termed "appropriating."
The "intentional guidance" (*yìlǐng*) refers to this: seeing that the Tathāgata’s establishment of transformation for me did not begin only today, his grace is profound.

However, it was previously unmanifest; it was only at the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*) that he detailed the opening of the two [vehicles]. Thus, "guidance" begins from the Deer Park where he led and attracted [beings] to the stage of equality (*qi*).

It may also be understood as including the preceding *Avataṃsaka* [period]. Furthermore, the section beginning with "on another day" constitutes the "exploratory guidance" (*tàn lǐng*), which likewise includes [the previous stages].
Subsequently, extending this reasoning, it is understood that all five periods encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles due to their differences; thus it is said: "Furthermore, on another day...

This passage takes the underlying intent to show that while the Dharma-body has long been illuminated through skillful means (*upāya*), although this [teaching] is currently restricted to the Small Vehicle, its general discourse is not exclusively for the Small.
Therefore, there follows below the explanation of merging the two beginnings and ends into a single beginning and end. As for the reason for this merger:
The intention is that each [school] clarifies five periods; thus, their investigation and comprehension also extend to the Mahāyāna.
Speaking from this perspective, the texts concerning the "comprehensive" (Qi) and "investigative" (Tan) schools do not merely rely on [the distinction of] "again" (*you*) and "other days" (*tadi*).

Since the intent of the "comprehensive" and "investigative" schools encompasses both the upper and lower [vehicles], each school discusses two types of comprehension. If one intends to indicate the meaning by combining the texts, then the investigative comprehension must necessarily include the comprehensive.

The two "comprehensions" (*ling*) also involve the investigation of principle; they must necessarily coexist. However, the scriptural text is concise, and since the detailed exegesis was divided beginning from the Deer Park, it has been treated as if separate.
By grasping the general principles of their progression and regression across both earlier and later periods, the long-standing and confusing debates can finally be resolved.
Once this is achieved, one will have already understood more than half of the two comprehensions. This is explained in detail in other treatises.

(As stated above). The reason the old treatise finds it difficult to grasp [the meaning] is that, because the words have long illuminated the skillful means, what is grasped is only the Small [Vehicle].

However, [Master] Cha said: "Since he has long known the capacities for both the Great and the Small, and since he bestows transformation through the 'one' and the 'three,' what is grasped thus extends to both the Great and the Small."
This has been the subject of discussion since antiquity. Now, I maintain that this is not difficult; one may simply resolve it with two statements.

To say that "probing and grasping" (*tanting*) refers exclusively to the Small Vehicle is based on the literal words used at the Deer Park. To say that it also encompasses both the Great and Small Vehicles is an explanation made by way of the topical headings (*biaozhang*).
Therefore, when the text indicates the underlying intent—that the Dharma-body has long been illuminating—it cannot help but encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles.
As for the meaning of this, what further explanation is needed? However, my commentary on the subsequent passage is somewhat difficult to follow due to its cross-referential structure;
it can be understood through careful and detailed examination.
At first glance, the commentary on the subsequent passage contains references to "two selves" and "three others," which may seem circuitous in expression.
Whether broad or detailed, if one seeks its underlying intent, everything has a point of convergence; it is no empty talk. What the ancients called "the fragmented and the simple" is precisely this.
When the *Wenyan* speaks of "the other," it means taking the expedient means of the Two Vehicles as "self," while regarding that which is not the dharma of the Two Vehicles as "other.
This "other" refers to the Dharmakāya. The "sun" is used as a metaphor for wisdom, meaning that wisdom functions in accordance with the Dharmakāya at all times.

The wisdom that illuminates the capacities is what is called "real wisdom" (substantial wisdom) illuminating reality for oneself, while "expedient wisdom" (provisional wisdom) illuminates skillful means for others;

however, since both are explained in terms of the dharma-body aspect, taking reality as "self" and expedience as "other" does not refer to the distinction between self and other in relation to the two vehicles.
Next, explaining "other" in terms of the dharma-aspect: the character "day" (日) signifies the simultaneous reception [of light], referring to the activities of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya).
This does not exceed the allocation of two sections to the three pairs of self and other, provisional and real.

Although this fundamental exposition primarily clarifies "exploring" (探) while simultaneously employing the term "alignment" (齊), it must necessarily discuss exploration in relation to alignment, for it clarifies oneself by contrasting with others.
If one correlates these with the three pairs according to the text: first corresponds to self-cultivation; next, to both self and other; and next, to transforming others, as the text states.

The *Keshi* (Explanatory Commentary) states at length that the reason one must speak in terms of the three pairs is precisely because the essential import encompasses the entirety of the Buddha’s teaching (*ekābhisamaya*).
Thus, the provisional means for converting others are attributed to the Deer Park [the first turning], while the realization of both self and others belongs to the subsequent flavors;

only then does the meaning find its proper destination, proving that the teaching was not established in vain. Although this is recorded, the reader should not fail to provide such a point of interpretation.
I understand this.

Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*’s refutation of the provisional [teachings], there was originally no difficulty; it was only that people of the past were deluded and took it to be difficult. Now I shall rectify this directly:
even the *Āgamas* clarify that there are bodhisattvas who do not sever their fetters (*asaṃprayukta-kleśa*), yet the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refutes this.

For example, regarding things such as poisoned vessels, it is as if one says they do not exist; yet the Master of the Commentary reconciles this by stating that the *Śāstra* refutes the provisional (expedient) teachings when it speaks of "non-existence," and this does not mean absolute non-existence.

Just as the treatises composed by Kātyāyanīputra and the calculations of ancient thinkers all claim that these [Bodhisattvas] are provisionally non-existent, the Master of the Commentary refutes this, saying:
"How could the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* merely bring together the two vehicles [to show them they are Bodhisattvas] and then cause..."

The Bodhisattva’s return is likewise consistent with the Āgamas; furthermore, according to the traditional interpretation, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*’s unification of the three vehicles occurs twelve years prior [to the Nirvāṇa].
These views are merely provisional assertions of inclusion and exclusion; how could they be taken as literal truth?
In the previous analysis, *cīvara* (the formal robe) was categorized by dividing it according to the preceding and succeeding moments of another day;

thus, *cīvara* possesses both a beginning and an end, while *paryeṣaṇā* (the seeking) possesses an end but no beginning. Furthermore, when discussing the two types of possession regarding the beginning and end, both ends do not involve subsequent flavors (*rasa*).
These are all points difficult to clarify regarding *cīvara* and *paryeṣaṇā*; therefore, the previous explanation established that each—*cīvara* and *paryeṣaṇā*—has its own distinct beginning.

In the end, they merely merge into one; the initial principle likewise applies to the subsequent four flavors, which are also opened up as two, as both are pervasive throughout the beginning and the end, each having its own point of convergence.
Therefore it is said: "Now, the two types of convergence. This refers to the two types of convergence: that of the beginning and that of the end.
The two terms "convergence" (*tan*) and "convergence" (*ling*) manifest this briefly; in reality, all five flavors converge and are simultaneously equal. Spoken of in this way, those that merge—

This is precisely for the purpose of opening up the way for later [texts] to explore [the meaning]. That which "opens" is intended to penetrate the subsequent four flavors (*rasa*) in its exposition. Thus, the *Record* says:
"The 'leaving the residence' and the 'exhaustion of thought' share the same meaning as the two ends. It also says: "The 'releasing' and the 'giving' together constitute one beginning and end;
these are mutually identical with the five flavors. The profound reason lies right here. People who do not perceive this merely engage in superficial debate.
Though [the teachings] have been opened and closed, people have ultimately never known their essential intent; now that I have set them forth, they are already made clear.

Nevertheless, when discussing the similarities and differences among the various sūtras, one cannot do so by a single path; I shall therefore explain them according to four principles: First, speaking in terms of their essence (*tattva*), the various sūtras have never been different.
Second, speaking in terms of their dharmas (*dharma*), the various sūtras have never not been different. Third, speaking in terms of what has been established...
In their underlying intent, they may differ or coincide; yet, according to their *siddhānta*, they each respond differently to specific conditions—this is the general rule.
As for their respective categories, when the principle of perfect permanence reaches its ultimate limit, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* are the closest to one another.

This is why they share the same flavor within a single division, representing the final consummation of a single period of teaching. Nevertheless, regarding their distinct characteristics, there still remains [the following]:

If such are the distinctions among the sixteen meanings, how much more so regarding the similarities and differences among other sūtras? Thus, we know that the critical analysis and interpretation of the scriptural teachings is truly no easy task.

Therefore, it is well said: "To lose sight of these similarities and differences makes it extremely difficult to provide a coherent exposition and support for one's arguments"—this indeed possesses profound significance.
The analogy of "entrusting the family business" refers, in terms of the Dharma, to the manifestation of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
While such a teaching and its analogy are not easily explained in words, according to the present text—since it speaks of "entrusting the family business"—one must certainly know the reason for this.
From the time when father and son were separated until the present day, throughout that intervening period...

It may be said that protecting [the Dharma] through skillful means was indeed difficult; yet, having arrived at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he was finally able to realize his original intention and establish the nature of his destiny.
The meeting of father and son and the entrustment of the family business reached its ultimate point here. But what, after all, is the matter being entrusted?
If one considers the "all Mahāyāna teachings"—both extensive and abbreviated *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, as well as common and uncommon dharmas—spoken of in the present text, by means of these...
If the "entrustment of karma" were the object of this transmission, it would pertain solely to the *Prajñāpāramitā* and have no relation to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Furthermore, these various Dharma-gates are teachings that were sought through diligent effort over many kalpas and realized at the site of enlightenment; there is certainly no principle whereby the Tathāgata bestows upon me a samādhi.
If the Buddha’s knowledge and vision were the object of this entrustment, they are inherently present as the original nature and virtue of all sentient beings.

How could it wait for entrustment before existing? Moreover, since you have now been entrusted with the family business, you have immediately received the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Having received the prediction, one attains Buddhahood;
is this not as the *Prajñāpāramitā* says—that in reality there is not a single dharma that attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Why then do you now act contrary to this? This concerns the ultimate intent and cannot be spoken of hastily; to speak of it hastily is to grasp it superficially. For now, let us set it aside.
It is simply as stated below: "For now, we shall merely punctuate the text according to its meaning and no longer provide detailed, word-by-word commentaries;

the priority lies in grasping the essential meaning rather than waiting for prolixity of words. Yet, alas, it is a pity that many within the scholarly community do not understand this, remaining trapped by their own attachments and prejudices. How regrettable!
I, Śākyamuni, declare that the great kindness [of the Buddhas] is difficult to repay; together we shall establish ten points of intent.

From the time each of you received the Great [Vehicle] in previous lives, there were intervening periods of decline and loss. Through compassion, I have provided rescue and stabilization in various places until reaching this realm where I attained Buddhahood.

There, I first employed gradual teaching, followed by the threefold samādhi, and finally reached the Lotus Sūtra, whereby you have at last obtained wondrous benefit and the prediction of your own enlightenment to benefit all beings—from beginning to end.
This grace may be said to be difficult to repay; it is comprised, in sum, of three things: clothing, seat, and chamber. What is called the "chamber" is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);

the "seat" is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*); and the "clothing" is gentleness and patience (*kṣānti*). Each of these possesses several aspects, which are collectively enumerated as ten types within the *Upadeśa*.
Furthermore, they are presented there with the sense that they mutually support and manifest one another, and so forth. It is through these that Kāśyapa has received and borne this grace.
Because it is so great, it cannot be repaid by the karma of any other expedient means.

One must say that if one does not preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, there is ultimately no way to repay this debt of gratitude. This is like the general teaching; indeed, this is the ultimate repayment according to this sutra.
The commentators [cite] the saying that "a thing does not answer a gift from Heaven and Earth," and "a son does not thank his father for giving him life."
The Mother Śrī’s record states that when one encounters the difficulty of explaining retribution correctly, how can one resolve it by claiming there is no retribution?

I now maintain that the commentators’ arguments do not mean there is no retribution; rather, they mean that the retribution has vanished. This is because such an ultimate kindness transcends the reach of verbal discussion;
thus, they borrow that expression to convey the point. The intended meaning is that "retribution through non-retribution" is the very pinnacle of retribution. Otherwise, [it would be untenable].

There may be one theory that perhaps approaches the truth: since there is no favor greater than providing clothing, shelter, and seats—these three essentials—it would not be fitting to now propagate the sutras through these same three means so that they may circulate in the末代 (final age)? Apart from this, I know of nothing else that could achieve it.

In the seventh section on phrases, what is not encompassed by the term "all"? Now, speaking in terms of skillful means (*upāya*), this refers to the three types of grass and two types of trees mentioned in the subsequent passage, which correspond to the single real ground;
these represent the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). Yet it must be through the wisdom of skillful means that one is able to expound them.
Only by attaining its reality can one then illuminate its provisional means; because one is able to illuminate it, one is able to explain its Dharma. Illuminating reality is called wisdom (*prajñā*);
illuminating the provisional means is called the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*). In essence, these two are originally one body.
Speaking of them in this way is to describe their essential grasp and to open up the three [vehicles]. The Dharma he expounds is fundamentally based on this sameness.
By embodying the illumination of both the provisional and the ultimate, this explains why [the teaching] is said to accord with the capacities of beings and also to accord with the principle.
"Accordance with their capacities" refers to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*), spoken of because of following the provisional;

"accordance with the principle" refers to the fact that all dharmas are established upon the ground of the single ultimate reality, and when speaking from the perspective of the final consummation, they all likewise reach this ground of the single ultimate reality.
This refers to the statement that "all dharmas are established from the root of non-abiding," which is the meaning of the phrase "ground of wisdom" (*jñāna-bhūmi*).

This term is also derived from analogy, as explained in detail in the *Ji* (Commentary), and so forth. Because these are spoken [in this manner], they are collectively termed "teachings according to the doctrine" (*yuejiao*). This, then, describes the manifestation of reality (*shixian*) by means of the teachings;
the text is as clear as the sun, yet other followers merely steal its interpretation. Previously, it was through "speaking" that one knew this to be the teaching; now, by this—
Observing that it is known as wisdom (*jñāna*), one cites wisdom to explain the teaching.

If one considers that the ultimate destination of all phenomena (*dharmas*) and the practices of the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*) are fundamentally and originally most profound—such as the "ultimate end of the beginning and the end"—are these not the destination?
And are such things as "purity" not the practices of the profound mind? Now, this is contrasted with the subsequent reality.

Because the meaning is elucidated through provisional means, one knows that the purport of the text cannot be discussed in a general manner; it is explained solely by way of medicine and illness, and thus everything resides within the provisional.
Being provisional, there are both near and far aspects. The "near" refers to the various destinations of humans, devas, and the three vehicles—namely, precepts, wholesome deeds, and so forth.
The "far" refers to even such acts as bowing the head or raising the hands leading to the Buddha-way; thus, they reach the profound awakening of Bodhi from afar.
The mental activities (*cittasamudācāra*) also have two meanings: first, attachment to the primary and secondary elements (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) gives rise to profound and heavy obstacles;

second, attachment to the phenomena grasped as real gives rise to the obstacle of dharmas (*dharmāvaraṇa*), such as the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*). Since all of these can obstruct the fruit and retribution (*vipāka-phala*), it is known that the deep mind itself is the manifestation of illness.
All of these are what the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is able to penetrate and transcend, and they are ultimately [resolved] within all phenomena.
Because those who possess clear understanding know that this is what is illuminated by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

Since true wisdom accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), there is no phenomenon that does not enter into reality, just as the hundred rivers flow toward the sea. If one does not understand the specific medicine for a particular illness, one cannot be considered ultimately clear;
while such partial illumination may occur through provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), true wisdom must necessarily illuminate the ultimate source.
Because it can demonstrate such wisdom to sentient beings, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Knowing the mind of desire and so forth through knowledge as-it-is (yathābhūta-jñāna) is called knowing the profound mind; penetrating according to principle is [the meaning].

However, when it speaks of "unimpeded penetration" regarding expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), it discusses the real based on the expedient; when it speaks of "all dharmas" regarding ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*), it discusses the expedient based on the real. These are two textual passages.

They are seen in this mutual relation; by inferring from this, it follows that in the ultimate sense, they are neither provisional nor real, neither differentiated nor non-differentiated, yet one may also say they are both differentiated and non-differentiated—just as the earth has no differentiation, yet grasses and trees appear in their various forms.
Furthermore, when discussing the mind in terms of dharmas and discussing dharmas in terms of the mind, the mind is not separate from dharmas, and dharmas are not separate from the mind.
"Mind-derivatives (caitta) are not derivatives, yet they are merely derivatives; the rest is as explained in the commentary, etc.

One earth and one rain serve as a metaphor for non-differentiation; yet each is mutually complete within the other. It is not that there is no differentiation, as it is said that "each receives its own portion.
When it rains from a single cloud, then differentiation is itself non-differentiation. Now, it is clarified that even within non-differentiation, there is [differentiation].
Because they are differentiated, although the text initially speaks of them as "though," it reveals the difference within non-difference; this is the purport of this passage.
As for the statement that "there are three," the wording is somewhat abbreviated; one should add the word "like" (*pí*) to each, such as saying:

"The first is like that which is produced from the earth," referring to the stages prior to the mind-ground and so forth; thus the text would become clear. This refers to what is called the stage prior to the mind-ground.

The first meaning is this: "those who are born" is a metaphor for ordinary beings from the stage of the ground up to the five kinds of sentient beings, all of whom grow and develop by relying upon the single Buddha-nature.
Although their mental grounds are the same, the merit of their growth and development actually issues forth from the stage of wisdom attained after fruition (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
The second meaning is this: "the rain showered by a single cloud" is a metaphor for that which is proclaimed and expounded by a single voice—the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Its...

Although the development [of sentient beings] differs according to their respective capacities and grows with distinctions, from the perspective of what is appropriate for them, it is ultimately a single voice, a teaching of equality.

Third, the analogy of the three types of grass and two types of trees illustrates that while the benefits received differ, there are none that do not rely upon the growth of the same earth and the moisture of the same rain;
in the end, they all return to equality. Furthermore, each of these points is said to be "not of itself."
The Awakened One also takes the ground of grasses and trees as a metaphor; it is just like the meaning of what is called "sentient beings using themselves [as they will] without knowing.

From the section on the five kinds of roots of goodness (*pañca-kuśalamūla*) downward, each point is reversed and applied to clarify the preceding meaning, though there is a slight lack of sequential order.
The statement that the teachings of the five vehicles are all Mahāyāna is also made by way of "leaping over the stages" (*kua-jie*) within the single Buddha-vehicle (*eka-buddhayāna*).
Because they explain the meaning of the three [vehicles] through differentiation, all are in fact the Mahāyāna, converging toward the Buddha-wisdom, yet they do not know it themselves.
Only the Tathāgata is able to know this; this too is the knowledge of non-knowing within the equal and great wisdom.
The rest is as explained in the commentary.
Previously, a single earth and a single rain were cited to establish the analogy; now, a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and a single flavor (*ekarasa*) are used to correspond to the Dharma.

Thus, the earth is used as an analogy for principle (*tattva*), and the rain is used as an analogy for teaching (*deśanā*). The three types of grass and two types of trees are used as analogies for the capacities of sentient beings (*indriya*);

because there are differences in these capacities, there are various distinct characteristics. However, since there is no difference between principle and teaching, they constitute only a single characteristic and a single flavor. This is "the single characteristic."

All sentient beings possess the same single characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*). What is called the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation do not lose their nature as the characteristic of True Suchness.
To speak of these characteristics means that the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is likewise of a single flavor;

yet because "one" does not exist in isolation, when viewed through the lens of capacities and provisional means, there appear the distinctions of the five vehicles and the seven stages of expedient means.
There is nothing that does not rely on the distinctions made within the One Vehicle; thus, they converge at the ultimate point, which is simply the ground of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
Now, "nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to principle (*li*), while "explanation" refers to teaching (*śāsana*). To cultivate based upon conditions refers to practice (*caryā*).
Since practice must have its fruit, it leads ultimately to the wisdom of fruition. When these are distinguished separately, they constitute the three aspects of nature, teaching, and practice.

Regarding the three wisdoms, there are three [aspects]. If one correlates them with the cultivated nature (*bhāvanā-svabhāva*), there are further meanings of separation and integration, such as the three being identical and so forth;

these cannot be clarified by anyone who has not deeply mastered the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) of this specific school. The rest is as explained in the commentary (*yù rú jì shì*). (And so forth.)

The passage concerning "one characteristic and one flavor" is the same [in both versions], yet now there are two explanations, each exhausting its own principle; therefore, they are recorded together.
The "one characteristic and one flavor" combined with the preceding teaching and principle are entirely without distinction, but the explanation of the meaning is more detailed here.

The "characteristics of liberation" and so forth are annotated and explained by way of the meaning of the "true characteristic" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). "One characteristic" is precisely the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), which fundamentally establishes all dharmas.
Therefore, that which is non-abiding and signless establishes the principle of differentiation among all phenomena through the principle of non-differentiation.
For example, the single element of earth is without distinction, yet it can produce grasses, trees, peaches, and plums; though these are different, they share the same characteristic of solidity.

If one knows that the earth possesses peaches and plums, one recognizes the provisional within the real; if one knows the solid nature of peaches and plums, one recognizes the real within the provisional.

There is a real distinction between the meanings of differentiation and non-differentiation; the principle is as follows. Furthermore, "one flavor" refers to the true teaching (*saddharma*) being pure and unmixed, which may be understood by analogy with the "one characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
The "characteristics of liberation" and so forth are all explained in terms of the Middle Way in contrast to the two extremes, and so on.
Ultimately, even when reaching the stage of "all-knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is likewise manifested by way of extinguishing the characteristics of delusions regarding the two extremes.

The Middle Way and the Knowledge of All Modes are described in this way; entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the initial arousal of the mind, and its ultimate clarity is the wisdom of the Buddha.

Next, to clarify the meaning of differentiation, the passage beginning with "There being sentient beings" and following refers to all sentient beings—likened to the three types of grass and two types of trees—who hear the rain of the Tathāgata’s One Vehicle Dharma, accept and practice it, and receive its nourishment.
This refers precisely to the meaning of the "differentiation of growth. Although each receives benefit, they do not know the reason why;

therefore, it is said that "none can know it. Examining this present commentary, one sees that the wondrous principles of the "Dharma-realm of non-abiding" unique to this school—the doctrines of cultivation and nature, the inherent presence of all phenomena, the identity of essence and attributes, and the non-duality of the provisional and the real—are all contained herein.
Wen has grasped this; the theory of the fundamental path is clarified without needing further debate. Will not scholars consider this the ultimate discourse?

Wen explains that while there is one aspect (*lakṣaṇa*), the three aspects are fundamentally the three dharmas of intrinsic virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*); these three natures are themselves the three paths, which are the three virtues (*guṇa*).

What is called the "nature-seed" (prakṛti-gotra) is precisely this: it simply takes the dharmas as the dharma-nature itself; since its very substance is entirely true, how could there be such things as birth and death to be rejected?

When it is said that there are no characteristics of birth and death and so forth, this is merely an explanation based on cultivation and a provisional description regarding the transcendence of deluded emotions—it is what is meant by "removing the illness but not removing the dharma.
Furthermore, this is explained by turning back to the fundamental dharma of non-abiding.

Regarding the "Single Character," four propositions are established here to explain it. Those of the old school must surely trace it back to its origin; however, what is now called the "origin" has no other basis than that which is stated in the *Sì míng*: "If one were to discuss exhaustively the 'Dharma of Non-abiding' and so forth, the single character 'complete' (jù) therein possesses a profound purport. This does not depart from the general principle; I shall provide an explanation for all such passages as these. [The text continues: ...In this regard, there are those who say: "The Dharma-nature is originally quiescent and eternally still; it neither arises nor perishes, and it is not subject to birth or death. It is like empty space, which is not produced by causes and conditions. Because it is not produced by causes and conditions, it is called the 'Unconditioned. Since it is unconditioned, it is eternal. Because it is eternal, it is called 'Nirvana. Nirvana is the ultimate reality. Because it is the ultimate reality, it is called the 'Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is the Buddha. Because he is the Buddha, he is called the 'World-Honored One. Furthermore, there are those who say: "The Dharma-nature is originally quiescent and eternally still; it neither arises nor perishes, and it is not subject to birth or death. It is like empty space, which is not produced by causes and conditions. Because it is not produced by causes and conditions, it is called the 'Unconditioned. Since it is unconditioned, it is eternal. Because he is the Buddha, he is called the 'World-Honored One. Finally, there are those who say: "The Dharma-nature is originally quiescent and eternally still; it neither arises nor perishes, and it is not subject to birth or death. It is like empty space, which is not produced by causes and conditions. Because it is not produced by causes and conditions, it is called the 'Unconditioned. Since it is unconditioned, it is eternal. Because it is eternal, it is called 'Nirvana. Nirvana is the ultimate reality. Because it is the ultimate reality, it is called the 'Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is the Buddha. Because he is the Buddha, he is called the 'World-Honored One. All of these various assertions are merely the proliferation of conceptual views. They do not accord with the true meaning of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Why? Because they take what is not the Way to be the Way, and they take what is not the Buddha to be the Buddha. They are like those who, having never seen an elephant, rely on hearsay to describe its form. Their words are all empty and false; they are nothing more than the idle talk of those who have not yet awakened to the truth. How could they possibly fathom the profound mystery of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? Therefore, one must realize that the Dharma-nature is fundamentally devoid of characteristics. It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing, and it transcends all categories of being and non-being. Only when one realizes this can one be said to have entered the gate of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. This is what is meant by the "Single Character. It is not something that can be grasped through intellectual speculation; it must be realized within oneself. If one relies on words and letters, one will only increase one's delusions and wander further from the truth. Therefore, the ancients said: "The Way is not in words; it is found in the silence between words. One must transcend all traces of thought and return to the source. Only then will one see the true face of the Buddha. This is the meaning of the "Single Character. Do not seek it elsewhere; look within your own mind. If you can see your own nature, you will immediately attain liberation. This is the essential point of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. One must not allow oneself to be led astray by the various interpretations of others. If one can maintain this single character in one's heart, then one will be able to respond to all things without obstruction. This is what is called "the power of the Single Character. It is not something that can be described in detail; it must be experienced directly. Therefore, the ancients said: "The Way is not far; it is right before our eyes. One must simply cease all seeking and rest in the natural state. This is the true meaning of the "Single Character. Do not let it become a mere object of intellectual play. Regarding the meaning of principle and phenomena, delusion and awakening, I have thus extracted the essentials and presented them through four propositions to demonstrate their underlying rationale.

This serves as a general guide to various texts, such as those in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning), and so forth. Is this not indeed a thorough synthesis and explanation that successfully establishes the doctrine?
As for the detailed meanings concerning the combination and separation of dharmas, as well as their categorization and pervasion, these are fully explained in other chapters (and so forth).

The text states: "Suddenly hearing for the first time the name of 'inherent evil' (*xing-è*) and so forth" refers precisely to the fact that the practice of the One Vehicle must necessarily arise from inherent virtue (*xing-dé*).
This inherent virtue is fundamentally rooted in inherent evil and is manifested through it.

If one can thoroughly understand that every phenomenon accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), being free from marks and quiescent, then even seeking liberation is unattainable—how much more so the bonds of karma? If even evil dharmas are thus, how much more so [the case for good ones]?
If one thus thoroughly understands the essence of wholesome dharmas, then the practice of inherent virtue exists right here; this unconditioned cultivation is not obtained from without.
Only when one attains awakening to this difficult-to-attain principle does one truly know it.
Regarding this statement that they "do not know," there is a further meaning to be considered: if we speak from the outset of these five types of people, they are inherently ignorant in two ways.
First, they do not know that the Tathāgata originally transforms and guides all beings through a teaching of a single flavor (*ekarasa*).

Second, according to what each has received, they each cling to their own interpretation as being the absolute truth, unaware that their respective understandings are like grasses and trees [lacking sentience].
They know their own superior, middling, and inferior natures, yet they do not know either the provisional or the real.

Speaking of it from the present perspective, since they have heard the teaching of the single characteristic and the single flavor, how could they be entirely ignorant? It is simply that because the Tathāgata’s ultimate and clear realization surpasses verbal expression, he says they do not know;
this is also said because the wondrous state is beyond the reach of mental activity and thus cannot be known.
If one seeks to know through words what is beyond knowing, then the Tathāgata is "able to know"; yet if one forgets that which is known by relying on such knowing, then the Tathāgata is "not knowing.
To have something known is not the knowledge of the Tathāgata; the knowledge of the Tathāgata cannot be expressed in words. Initially, this was explained by means of four dharmas:
lineage (*gotra*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), essence (*svabhāva*), and nature (*dharmatā*). Regarding "lineage," it refers to the Buddha-lineage (*buddha-gotra*), which exists.
The nature of existence possesses a category-nature; this refers to its origin. All sentient beings originate from the three paths.
These three paths are the kin of afflictions (*kleśa*). Because of afflictions, there is *prajñā*; because of karmic fetters, there is liberation;
because of the path, there is the *dharmakāya*. This is like ice being the seed of water: apart from the ice, there is no separate water. It is entirely these three.
The obstacles are the absence of these three virtues; there are no distinct virtues apart from the removal of the obstacles. This is spoken of in terms of their mutual opposition and inversion.

As for their "categories," this refers to the fact that the three causes are of the same category as the virtues found on the level of the fruit, for if the three causes were absent, the fruit could not be manifested.
Thus, the distinctions within the lineage (*gotra*) are themselves non-distinctions, and non-distinctions are themselves distinctions; the Tathāgata knows them all completely.

Thus, one reaches the ultimate source and bottom; regarding the three aspects of appearance, nature, and substance (*lakṣaṇa*, *svabhāva*, *bhāva*), each is discussed differently according to the ten dharma-realms—this is their differentiation.
Yet, when one realizes that the nature and characteristics of the ten realms are identical within the single Buddha-dharma realm, then difference is non-difference and non-difference is difference;
there is nothing that is not clearly illuminated. Nevertheless, there are various appearances, substances, and natures from which one must know them so that they do not become non-existent.
If the nature of seeds and characteristics is such that no phenomena exist at all, by what means could they be known?
Furthermore, if the very essence of seeds and characteristics were itself the knowing subject, how could there be anything to be known?
Thus, since nothing can be known, when one reaches the ultimate limit of neither knowing nor not knowing, what can be said? How then could I possibly know it? Let this matter rest.
Since the ten categories, such as the "seed-characteristic" (*bīja-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, exhaustively encompass all phenomena, they are now employed to demonstrate the objects of knowledge.

Thus, the four dharmas are the objects apprehended by the three types of wisdom, while the one true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) is that upon which cause and effect depend. Therefore, these ten are none other than the spheres of objects known by the Buddha-wisdom.
To speak of "seeds" is to include their essential natures (*prakṛti*); they do not transcend either the innate (*prakṛti-stha*) or the cultivated (*samudānīta*). All [phenomena] are thus subsumed.

Because it serves as the seed for producing the fruit of Buddhahood, it is said that there is a "nature of arising"; thus, it is called a "seed. Although it is initially divided into two, they are in fact a single entity;
therefore, when speaking in terms of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), all Abhidharma principles are one from beginning to end.
Now, using waves and water as a metaphor, you previously asked: "If ice is the seed of water, does this not contradict [the principle]? This is indeed so if one discusses the substance (*svabhāva*).

Ice-water and wave-water are fundamentally no different; it is only when speaking of "wave-water" that one still includes a portion of clear waves, which may lead to confusion regarding the categories.
If one takes opposing characteristics as counterparts, ice-water should be used as the analogy.
Yet, if one intends to express the deeper meaning, using ice and charcoal as the "seed" (the primary cause) best reveals its subtlety. As it has been said: "Waves are the seed of water."
That fire can produce ice is truly marvelous; this can only be spoken to those who understand. The text says:
"Sentient beings have, from time immemorial, constantly dwelt within the three realms of existence; this is precisely the three causes of the rational nature (*li-xing*).

Among them, who lacks even a single hair’s breadth of a seed of goodness? How could it be merely the *dharmakāya*? What is now called the 'seed of the *dharmakāya*' refers to its cultivated nature (*xiu-xing*)."

This is because of the meaning of their relative separation and union; therefore it is said that those three natures are united as one *dharmakāya*, and so forth—one should distinguish between their separation and union to understand this point.
If they were neither separate nor united, these three would not be distinct from one another.

In that case, what would differentiate the *jāti-dharmakāya* (the *dharmakāya* of the lineage) from the *prakṛti-gotra* (the nature-lineage)? Therefore, [the text] selects [this point] and answers: "The principle is one, but the meanings differ."

The "different principles" (li) refer to those whose meanings can be known as distinct; because that which they oppose is not the same, taking fundamental purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and phenomenal purity (*vaimalya-viśuddhi*) as categories constitutes the category of "analogy" (*jāti*).
If one considers them in terms of the opposition between defilement and purity, or delusion and awakening, this constitutes the category of "opposition" (*pratipakṣa*).
Only a Tathāgata can know their ultimate limit; although ordinary beings do not know it, they should realize that its very substance is itself perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna*).
Its manifestation in accordance with the nature [of reality] is such that nothing else can surpass it; the rest is as explained in the *Yìzhāng* (Chapter on Meaning).

The "transformed city" (*huàchéng*) and the "jeweled destination" (*bǎosuō*) are designations for the provisional (*quán*) and the real (*shí*). To speak of the "transformed" and the "real" is merely to employ alternative names.
Thus, by knowing the transformed, one knows the real. The explanatory text of the *Jì* (Commentary) makes this even more evident, which is why it says: "speaking of the transformed."

This refers to "opening the provisional" (*kaishen*) and so forth; however, when compared with the superior [teachings] of the Dharma and Parable [sections], the phrasing for "opening the provisional to reveal the real" (*kaishen xianshi*) differs slightly.

Furthermore, it says: "Therefore, regarding the previous discussion on the 'Teaching' (*jiao*), the phrase 'this is the Perfect Teaching' (*yuanjiao*) and so forth must be understood as encompassing both the meaning of the [specific] section and the general teaching.

Thus, one may interpret the preceding text. Although this present sutra is of the Perfect [Teaching], there is still a need for "opening and revealing" (*kaixian*); the difference lies merely in the detail or brevity. This is what the student must know.
This is something one must not fail to understand.

The Sūtra states: "Though he sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him. According to the commentary on the present text, this merely means that his conditions for conversion were remote.
However, the commentators state: "Therefore, his attainment of Buddhahood cannot be entirely equated with that of the Tripitaka masters and others in this land."
All of these are interpretations derived from the orthodox explanations of the sūtras and śāstras; that their principles should be understood in this way is certainly beyond doubt.

However, when the Chan school employs "picking up and pointing out" (niantie), or uses events to clarify principles, or selects passages to capture the essential meaning, it differs once again from this. As it is said:
"When one engages in such contemplation, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear, constantly dwelling therein as they walk, stand, sit, and lie down. I always [contemplate] during the day...
Reflecting on such matters as these during the night, and regarding the present passage which says "and so forth," if one wishes to clarify this according to other traditions, one should ask:
"Why did he sit at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him? To which he would simply reply:

"Because there was still Buddha-dharma remaining. Furthermore, the text says: "Regarding the events prior to becoming a Buddha, there are two [aspects]," and so forth; one may also ask about the matter of attaining Buddhahood.
The Buddha later asked: "What is the matter prior to attaining Buddhahood? Let students try to answer. The Sūtra says:
"How is it that within this [Dharmadhātu], which is fundamentally pure, sentient beings suddenly arise? This is identical to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s question:
"How is it that within the fundamentally pure [nature], mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? What a fine koan! Yet it was already exposed by Tiantai, even so.
When did the Great Master ever say that this very "head-word" (hua-tou) was still being tested? He merely provided a substitute turn of phrase for the sake of students, saying simply:
"From where have you just come?

If one wishes to know the beginning, middle, and end of the long-term transformative influence of the Tathāgata’s teaching in the *Ji-men* (Trace Gate)—namely, the stages of planting the seeds, ripening them, and liberating them—one must look here.

Regarding these signs, none are as detailed as this text. What is called "attaining liberation through three cycles in the present life" refers to a class of beings who, at the very moment they first encounter the Dharma, plant the seeds of the One Vehicle.
From that time onward, there are those who regress and those who do not.
Those who regress may later encounter [the teaching] again, whether it be through maturing them with the Great Vehicle or receiving them with the Small Vehicle, occurring throughout the four seasons.

Through skillful means and harmonization, one reaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, where the beginning and end of a single transformation finally become the conditions for full maturation and liberation.

Thus one knows that the path of the One Vehicle is not easily entered, and that the source and flow of the Tathāgata’s long-term compassionate transformation—both its fundamental and its manifested aspects—can now be said to have reached their ultimate fulfillment.
I have once summarized this in my *Huayuan lun* (Treatise on the Source of Transformation), which was produced for the sake of students.
If one does not wish to know the source of transformation, then that is that; but can one truly fail to devote one's whole heart to this?
Within the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle, it would not be difficult to attain this.
The Buddha-way is one, and the karmic conditions are also one; yet why do the scriptures and teachings speak of attaining the Buddha-way as if they were different? What scripture [says this]?
Is it that the kalpas differ in length due to the varying speed of time’s passage?

According to the current commentary (*shu-wen*), it states directly that the four *siddhāntas* respond to capacities, being sometimes long and sometimes short, possessing both provisional and ultimate aspects, as detailed in the text. However, the record (*ji-wen*) states:

"Although the four *siddhāntas* respond to capacities according to the [Buddha’s] marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*), whether long or short, if one discusses his own practice (*svayaṃ-caryā*), in the end there is no such thing as merely sitting with folded hands [in passive inaction]. Thus, the four *siddhāntas* respond to all capacities.

The "capacity" (ji) refers to the limits of established transformation; ultimately, there is no one who can remain with hands folded [in leisure], as this is discussed from the standpoint of relying upon the Treasure [of the Dharma].
This is what is meant in the *Awakening of Faith* when it says: "There are no Bodhisattvas who do not pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

If one judges according to the gate of the provisional teaching (*upāya-śāsana*), it should be known that the teaching and practice of the provisional teaching exclusively speak of long periods and cannot be shortened; such is the case for the teaching of reality (*yathābhūta-śāsana*).
Among these, there are those with long [paths] and those with short [paths], or those who suddenly achieve Buddhahood, such as the woman Ti-p'o (Dīpaṃkarā) and others.

Furthermore, it is said that within the Perfect and Real Teaching (Yuan-shih-chiao), those of the six faculties and five grades may expect fulfillment within a single lifetime; although other texts do not specifically cite this, it is further stated:
"Long and short depend on the person; how could the principle be otherwise? This means that when speaking in terms of principle, one should not become negligent because the path is long.
If one who seeks only the Way is neither sincere nor diligent, what need is there to discuss whether the time is long or short?

This may be called an argument that exhausts the principle. Nevertheless, one must further understand why the partial and small [teachings] necessarily require length while the Perfect and Sudden alone is brief;
this, moreover, should be discussed in terms of the vehicle, the lineage, and the ripeness of the faculties. As for the practice of the Perfect and Sudden today:
How could this be in vain? It must be because their seeds from past lives were already deep that their entry into the Way was easy;
whereas for ordinary people who are biased toward the small [vehicle] and whose seeds from past lives are shallow, the time required is long. This is an immutable principle.
Knowing this, one can remain free from distress.

Regarding the two meanings of horizontal and vertical as applied to the lands, one should consult the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan) and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* (Jingming shu), as stated in the present record (*ji*) and elsewhere.
According to the text of the *Zhiguan*, these meanings are clearly revealed. As for the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*, it originally contains no explicit text on this matter;

however, the record states: "Yet, discussing horizontally, the Land of Common Dwelling possesses all four [spheres], while the other three gradually decrease," and so forth. This is the analogy for the horizontal and vertical.

Although the administration differs from that of the present day, this particular assembly is an ancient difficulty regarding the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the four lands within the gates of teaching.
I have once resolved this through two principles, stating: "The horizontal and vertical dimensions of the lands in relation to the teachings are exactly as in the current text;
however, the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the lands in relation to the lands themselves are the opposite," and so forth. I shall now apply this here.
Regarding the assembly of Vimalakīrti: one meets his application of the teaching, but does not meet his [description of] the corresponding land.

It is simply that the textual passages on Vimalakīrti’s application of the teaching are implicit, while the textual passages on the corresponding land are explicit; thus, they are somewhat difficult to perceive.

However, as for what is called "the four [realms] being fully present in the Land of Common Dwelling," this is merely a matter of comparing lands with lands—how could it be considered difficult? Former scholars were not adept at distinguishing between these two locations.
The differences between the various systems of interpretation arise merely from the difficulty of reconciling horizontal and vertical texts, which conflict like arrows and stones;
thus, they could not be harmonized. Now that these have been clearly distinguished, there should be no further confusion.
From the time we first formed this karmic connection in the past, throughout our encounters and pursuits, we have experienced all four seasons and undergone many detailed stages and episodes.
Coming down to the present moment, as he is about to preach the Lotus Sutra, one might wonder what kind of Dharma he will speak;
yet it is simply said that in this world there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction, but only the Single Buddha Vehicle.
Nirvana is merely the fruit; why is it described as being so wondrous, and why is its explanation so difficult?
It is because one has never heard that this wondrous path of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) originates from the same source as the Buddha and that delusion and awakening are non-dual.

Beings are thus deluded and turned away from it, failing to realize it themselves; they are what is called the naturally true treasury of awakening, submerged in the long night of ignorance. Thus they are born.
In the ocean of the suffering of death, sentient beings are not only deluded and unaware, but they further become attached and flow along with the current, forgetting their way home.
Their resolve is narrow and inferior; though they wish to forcefully pursue and return, it cannot be achieved. Because transforming them is not easy, it is all the more difficult to teach them.
Because teaching them is already difficult, praising them becomes even more so. This is why the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*...

That the Single Vehicle alone is wondrous and transcends the five periods, surpassing both past and future, is precisely because the direct transmission of the path of the One Vehicle is so exceedingly difficult.

Now that it has been transmitted, the fundamental basis for transcending the world is fully realized. Therefore, the Way says: "Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Dharma of the One Vehicle;
the other two are not the truth. To speak of its ultimate limit, it is said: "All [beings] by means of..."
The Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa and brings all beings to parinirvāṇa; not a single sentient being fails to attain Buddhahood, for the Great Matter is thus completed.
This is like the nine-fold elixir of the immortals that transforms iron into gold by a single application: the wondrous fruit of a single word does not depend on much;
who could obtain it so easily?

Regarding the meaning of the "one, three, movement, and stillness" in the context of the old selection concerning the city and the chariot—observing the questions and answers at first glance, they are indeed ingenious.
Even if considered from a single perspective, this principle is not without its validity; thus the Record states, "The Dharma is summarized through metaphors," and so forth.
This is also consistent with the theory of returning to the city by means of the chariot, though when viewed from the standpoint of the present essence, it remains distinct.
Thus, that [position] is partial, as correctly identified in the *Jipíng* (Commentary and Critique).

The fundamental clarification regarding the existence or non-existence of the chariot-city states that the primary intent of the "transformed city" (*pariṇāmika-nagara*) is for the purpose of withdrawing from the Great Vehicle;

this is explained above in terms of the Buddha’s wisdom (*buddha-jñāna*) as being both existent and non-existent, while that which is clarified by expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is taken as existent, such as the city itself.
That which is clarified by wisdom is "non-as-such" (wu-ru);

because the "phantom city" (huacheng) is used to contrast with the objects of the [first] two *zhous*, this text was composed to further discuss their similarities and differences, as stated in the *Ji*: "It must be explained by reversing [the order]," which is precisely what this means.
If one relies on the three *zhous* in terms of their primary application, it is not yet necessary to point to the past regarding the first two *zhous*.

The "original small vehicle" (yuán xiǎokě) refers to those who previously emerged from the third [vehicle], meaning they were originally those of the great vehicle who had regressed. Therefore, the Record says: "This is for the time being a one-way [path];
it may also involve regression. As for those of the great vehicle whose capacity is sharp enough to penetrate the upper two stages (the second and first), they were originally of the great vehicle;

however, because their faculties became dull, they were made sharp through the upper stage to attain entry. As for the original small vehicle practitioners, their dullness would correspond to the third stage according to the standard explanation.
If this can be understood, then the principles regarding the explanations of the similarities and differences—and the reversals—of the three cycles are clear.

Why, then, do you insist that the chariot and the city definitely exist or do not exist? Although the purport of the constant text has been briefly clarified, the correct meaning regarding the śrāvakas as secondary [to the bodhisattvas] is still not yet detailed.
As stated in the *Huayuan lun* (Treatise on the Source of Transformation) and other such works, the text generally employs multiple meanings to clarify the chariot and the city.
The principle of existence and non-existence, unity and plurality, movement and stillness has never been confined to a single extreme;
by this standard, when compared with previous interpretations, the difference is as vast as that between heaven and earth. The rest is as explained in the Record (and so forth).
To silently contemplate a single matter is not inherently what is known; however, because it exists within the sutras, one forms this thought.

Furthermore, the statement "Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One," and so forth, indicates that he attained realization through silent contemplation. Therefore, it is said that "realization through silent contemplation" constitutes a great realization.
The intention behind citing Vimalakīrti’s silence as an example is based on [the fact that] Vimalakīrti’s...

Since Zimo had already demonstrated the ultimate entry into the Gate of Non-duality, he was already possessed of what might be called "words"; thus, his present silence may be taken as a primary instance of such understanding.

Furthermore, when it is said that "the provisional and the real are inconceivable, being neither speech nor thought," this refers to the aforementioned "speech that is not speech" through which understanding is verbally expressed;
by verifying this against the present "thought that is not thought," can it not be understood that he has attained realization through silence?
This is also like the single "Yes" (vī) in the gate of Confucius, which can be used as a brief precedent for understanding [the matter] (and so forth).

Now, as for what is called "protecting, upholding, assisting, and proclaiming," how could it necessarily require being the foremost among those who preach the Dharma before one is capable of doing so?
Furthermore, regarding the traces of the *śrāvaka* and *bodhisattva* teachings (*miàn-mǎn fǎ*) applied throughout the five periods of transformation until the present day...
There is nothing that does not assist in proclaiming [the Dharma].

Extending this principle, if one can thoroughly understand the true reality (*dharmatā*) in all places and skillfully penetrate the core of the sutras, then every person, in every situation—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—and at all times, will be none other than assisting in the proclamation of the Buddha-Dharma.
Thus, one enters the chamber of compassion in every place and dons the robe of tranquil patience.
What distinction, then, can there be between the ancient and the modern?
Is it not so that the wind-swept branches, the moon over the marsh, all clarify the school of self-nature, while the misty islands and forested clouds fully accord with the principle of non-arising?
If there were no women, there would necessarily be no evil realms; thus, women are the root that brings about the evil realms.

Yet, there may be women where there are no evil realms, which means that the specific conditions for them do not exist. Therefore, one cites the transformative events of the land of Akṣobhya Buddha as proof.
How so? Because the state where both [women and evil realms] are absent is purity. Thus, the presence of women without the occurrence of such [evil] matters indicates...
"One who possesses a compassionate mind is what the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra refers to as 'female. The Great Sūtras frequently employ the female as a metaphor for the compassionate mind;
there is indeed a profound reason for this.
*Wenju Geyan*, Middle Volume."
The "Wenju Gege" (Verses on Phrases and Maxims), Volume Lower, is contained herein.
To summarize, the essential point is that one must truly accord with reality as it is revealed;

although the explanations from ancient times are not without merit, because they focus exclusively on names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), the underlying principle is ultimately not perceived—this is why scholars of the North remain obscured.
Now, if it is demonstrated in this way, one perceives that within each and every phenomenon there is a subtle marvel. Furthermore, tell me:
how is it that being neither identical nor separate constitutes the true mark? This must be understood with subtle insight before it can be attained.
The ancient masters condensed the provisional and the real across the three periods into three chapters;

although our own school does not adopt this, even their discursive explanations are not without merit, as they succeed in encompassing the textual meanings and doctrinal characteristics so that they find their proper place. However, if one errs, the meaning becomes overly fragmented and the principle fails to reach its simplicity;

thus, the choice of what to accept or reject rests with the individual. It is merely said that within their respective contexts, these [teachings] must not be confused such that one serves as the provisional while the other serves as the real.

If one were to treat the gates as mutually being provisional or real, it would be impossible; yet, if they are explained in relation to one another and discussed in terms of their sequence, even our own school may admit such a principle.
However, when examined through the lenses of the "opening" and "not-yet-opening" of the present and the past, or "within the essence" and "outside the essence," it may still not be entirely clear.
Therefore, I have now presented these arguments from both sides to demonstrate that my selection and rejection are not undertaken lightly. The rest [is as follows].

As stated in my own *Weishi jiexi* (Exegesis on the Consciousness-Only) and elsewhere (*etc.*), the present clarification of the principle of the three-in-one has already refuted the attachments of [false] views without contradicting the essence of the Dharma. As the aspects of cultivation and nature become mutually manifest, it may be said that the source and root are exhaustively and wondrously realized;
this stands far removed from the old chapters. I shall now proceed to elucidate this further. Regarding the "three": [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates a break in the original text.*
The essence of the One is one, yet there are differences according to how it is applied and revealed. The "three-in-one" of the past followed the specific applications;

therefore, it was neither identical nor non-identical, and thus it was insufficient to manifest [the truth] to one another. If one were to dogmatically cling to it, it would become a sickness of views.

The "three-in-one" of the present is discussed in terms of the fundamental and its manifestations. Because it is based on manifestation, the essence is identical; thus, within the One Buddha Vehicle, distinctions are made.

Regarding the testimony of the three [teachings], the reason these three are mutually constitutive is that the three established outside the One in the past have become the three within the One in the present;
thus, one may manifest the three by means of the three, and manifest the one by means of the one—a principle that can be seen through such analogies, and so forth.

Furthermore, it is said: "To manifest the three of self-nature (svabhāva) by means of the three of causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya) refers to the fact that causes and conditions constitute the provisional manifestations of the teaching."

The self-nature of these matters is termed "intrinsic virtue" (xingde); these two aspects complement one another and are called the "discrimination of the cultivated and the intrinsic" (xiuxing hebian).
What is referred to as the "latent" and the "manifested" is beneficial to the conditions of sentient beings; this is precisely what is meant by "present causes and conditions.

That which is the eternally abiding source, never increasing or decreasing, is precisely what is meant by "present self-nature. Nevertheless, although their names and characteristics differ, there is both oneness and threefoldness.

This is because their distinct forms are fundamentally non-dual. What is called "marvelously exhausting the source" means that throughout the dispensation of a single lifetime, there is nothing that does not manifest from this self-nature;
it is something never before spoken of in other texts. Therefore, it is said:
"If one is deluded regarding this principle, one merely wastes mental energy. How could these words be false?

Explaining the sutra is indeed difficult, and clarifying its essential tenets is no less so. As the ancient commentators understood the intent of the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa," they employed the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) from the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* to clarify the nature of that vision.
Thus it is said: "The great assembly saw the stūpa"—regarding this as a sense organ (*indriya*), it is one's own seeing;
regarding it as the object (*viṣaya*), it is the seeing of another; regarding it as consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is common seeing. Extensively employing these analogies and categories...
Regarding the refutation of the notions of self and other, our school now rejects this, asserting that at the time of beholding the stupa, one’s state is no longer that of ordinary sentiment;
how could it be permitted for the faculties and consciousnesses to suddenly become identical to those of common vision, such that one must refute the distinction between self and other?

Furthermore, since that method of contemplation was originally intended for the final age when the capacities of sentient beings are dull, it is entirely inappropriate for the present. Thus, even when the previous commentary employs it, it does so as a means of interpreting the sutra’s description of the visualization.
The principle of practice ought to be thus; since they do not understand this, how can they recklessly employ it?
Therefore, in interpreting the sutras, one must know what is permissible and what is not—is it not the case that "universal vision" (pāṭaliputra) is exactly like this?
Formerly, some used this passage to determine that the teacher of the *Lotus Sūtra* was not the "Venerable Special Form" (zūn tè), based on the evidence of his entering a stupa;

yet they were unaware that this was intended to refute the Daśabhūmika masters—who did not understand what was being expressed and instead interpreted it as the Dharma-body—and thus they refuted it superficially, claiming that such a "lofty and majestic" being should not be within a stupa, and so forth.
This is merely a general objection for the duration of one teaching period.
As described by Nanyue regarding the supreme characteristics of the three bodies (*trikāya*), how could they ever be definitively inferior?

Moreover, since what is clarified here is said to be "distinguishing excellence through the inferior" and "the three as one," what hindrance is there to entering the stupa being simultaneously narrow and vast?

How could this compare to the limited, fixed realm of ordinary beings? Furthermore, it has been said that "vastness and narrowness, excellence and inferiority are difficult to conceive," yet within this...

Because one should understand that the "equalizing of characteristics" (應相) actually refers to the "meeting through contemplation" (思議會), it is known that the former explanation of the "equalizing of characteristics" regarding the lifespan of the One Family (一家) was merely an interpretation based on personal views following the literal text; how could such an explanation have known what is called the realm of the Buddhas?
Once a student grasps this single point, they can apply it to all other cases.
If one discusses ultimate reality (*tattva*), it fundamentally cannot be reached by the conventional designations of "extensive" or "concise";

rather, it is merely attained by being free from the four modes of existence (*catuskoṭi*) and transcending the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*). Nevertheless, without conventional designations there would be no way to perceive ultimate reality, and without the extensive and concise [teachings] there would be no way to demonstrate ultimate reality.
Therefore, it is said that ultimate reality has three aspects; briefly stated, ultimate reality can be summarized in a single word.

This means that the true mark (*dharmatā*) is signless (*animitta*), transcending the paths of speech and thought; it can only be realized through resonance (*yoga*) and cannot be grasped through deliberation.
An ancient master said: "It can only be understood in this way; it cannot be demonstrated in this way. This is perhaps close to the mark.

When expanded, the hundred negations are thoroughly dispelled and all conceptual attachments to a self-nature (*svabhāva*) perish. For whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory; even if one were to negate it a thousand or ten thousand times, it would still be so.

This is insufficient to reveal the point of the true reality; what is spoken here as "the Middle" refers merely to the general outline of the meaning of the "Eight Negations" as set forth in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
However, the records state that although there are many things that can be negated, that which is capable of negating them is but one.
Furthermore, what is this very "One" that serves as the Way?
To understand the treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, one sees it in the four characters "profound, firm, remote, and far-reaching" (*shengu youyuan*).

If we discuss this principle when it has not yet been revealed, it is profound, firm, remote, and far-reaching; once it is revealed, it is likewise profound, firm, remote, and far-reaching, for no one can reach it.
Thus, even when it is fully realized, it remains profound, firm, remote, and far-reaching. However, one must not [cling to] it as being merely profound, firm, and remote.

Because it is distant, it is difficult to see and difficult to reach; yet, it is only because the Buddha, for the sake of teaching and transforming those with the appropriate karmic conditions, has manifested this within that which is devoid of names and marks.
One must know that this principle pervades all phenomena, its majestic and manifest whole body contained within them.
Though one spends an entire day, one cannot know it; precisely because one does not know it within the very substance of reality, nothing is more distant than this.
Since its essence is this very thing, there is nothing more proximate than this; how could there be any difficulty in seeing it or reaching it?
It depends solely on the individual to set aside words and grasp it through intuitive realization.

Regarding the cultivation of contemplation based on the sutras, there are two explanations: the first is that which the sutras themselves clearly elucidate as the practice of contemplation, such as that found in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

Regarding "Practicing Cultivation to Gather the Mind" in the *Zhongguan* (Exhortation to Practice): whether walking or sitting and so forth, these constitute the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) of this single sutra.

If one truly desires to cultivate them, one must rely on the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), which is specifically intended to demonstrate the methods of cultivation for practitioners;
this is what is meant by "contemplation according to practice. Second is "contemplation according to the text"; thus, the Great Master [Zhiyi] [applied this to] various passages.

The following clarifies the two types of contemplative gates—relying on phenomena (*sho-ji*) and attaching to the Dharma (*fu-hō*)—which involve subsuming phenomena into principle (*ji-sō-jū-ri*) to cultivate the methods of contemplation.
This [latter method] does not depend on a specific object of contemplation; rather, at any time, in any place, whenever one encounters or hears [the teachings], it can be practiced.
Yet, the masters of the commentaries (*shō-so*) do not mention this at all, lagging behind even in their practice of contemplation (*kan-gyō), and instead go so far as to disparage Tiantai for it.
To cite texts that merely share names while manifesting different meanings, and to falsely fabricate such citations, may be called a failure to understand what is essential.
