Regarding this, the Master of the Record (Jizang) earnestly exhorted and lamented his own shortcomings, saying: "I have suddenly neglected this profound meaning; I regret that I have not yet been moistened by it.
I possess only a heart full of devotion and infinite sighs of reverence—how much more so for others, and how much more so for those of future generations!"

The transformative activities of the Buddhas are indeed not easily subject to a single, uniform standard of judgment; yet there are also those matters that can be discerned through careful consideration.
There are instances where, finding no other recourse, one must resort to the principle of following conditions (*pratyaya*).

As the *Śāstra* clarifies, because the Buddha Prabhūtaratna did not preach the *Lotus Sūtra* before entering parinirvāṇa, there is the teaching regarding the making of vows and sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). Master Nanyue said: "That Buddha..."
Since there is already the statement addressed to the bhikṣus, how could it be that he did not speak at all?

Judging by the underlying intent, it must be that while Many Treasures (Prabhūtaratna) was able to open the three vehicles, he was unable to manifest the ultimate truth; such is the case. Nevertheless, how could one dare not believe the judgment of the holy masters?
Now, I shall briefly discuss this: the opening of the three and the manifestation of the one is an inevitable principle. That [Buddha] was able to open the three...

Those who cannot manifest the reality are shown that dharmas have no fixed characteristics; or, because they hold that *nirvāṇa* itself is the ultimate manifestation of reality, [the Buddha] did not speak of it.
Although he did not speak of reality, how could the constant Way of all Buddhas ever permit contradiction?
Therefore, he again made a vow to verify the sutras so as to preserve them. Furthermore, although various points were used to examine [the matter], in the end...
Providing answers according to conditions and thus establishing various traces that differ from one another is likewise done by reflecting upon the capacities of those present;
these are all arguments of "helplessness" (wu ke nai he) rather than matters where one dares to make a hasty judgment. One should consider it to be thus, and not assume it to be literally so.
That a dragon girl, with a body that is not a fit vessel, was able to come to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and receive the Buddha’s prediction of attaining Buddhahood in an instant—this is what is suspicious.
Therefore, Zhijixian took this as a basis for his departure and raised objections, while Śāriputra harbored doubts within his breast, and so forth.
Consequently, there exists the "Explanation Clarifying and Resolving Doubts," which provides a definitive interpretation to eliminate those doubts; its words state:
It is said: that which constitutes the Buddha’s attainment of Buddhahood lies in profoundly penetrating that sin and merit fundamentally arise from the one mind.
Since the nature of the one mind is empty and devoid of sin or merit, by realizing and penetrating this, one enters the single true reality (*ekasatyalakṣaṇa*).

Thereby, one gives rise to the light of *prajñā*-wisdom, which can then penetrate and illuminate the ten directions—the objective realms of the ten dharma-realms, including both the environments and the beings therein.
Because one realizes this seal through wisdom, the Dharma-body of innate virtue is manifested in a single thought-moment; this is why the cultivated and the innate mutually manifest one another.

Thus it is said: "The subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body is endowed with the thirty-two marks," and so forth. This also provides profound proof that the physical characteristics and marks of the Dharma-body are manifested in accordance with its nature.
Therefore, the general description of being "venerated and looked up to by devas and humans" ultimately points back to this.
The Buddha is precisely thus; moreover, is it not by means of this that I have attained Buddhahood?

Therefore, the reason the Dragon Girl used the fruit to clarify the cause and demonstrated the swiftness of attaining Buddhahood was to resolve the doubts of Śāriputra—this is all now clearly illuminated.
Furthermore, her offering of a perfect pearl to the Buddha refers to the "pearl of the mind"; the pearl of the mind is inherently perfect, and furthermore—
Receiving the teaching signifies that she has attained liberation through her cultivation of virtue; presenting it to the Buddha signifies that she will rely on this cause to achieve the fruit;

and the Buddha’s immediate acceptance signifies the swiftness with which she attains the fruit. These are all the subtle mechanisms by which the Dragon Girl resolves doubts, and their subtlety lies precisely here;
were it not for Tiantai, no one else could have explained them.

Observing the present dialogue, one can perceive therein the subtle exhaustion of all Buddhas’ transformative functions (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) and the phenomena of the shifting and coming-and-going of the essence of their lands (*kṣetra*).
This dialogue occurs because Mañjuśrī has come from the ocean to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; such is the meaning of the passage. The first point is clear.
As for the second point—that the Dragon Palace remains unmoved while its dwelling has already been transformed—it means that transformation and non-transformation [coexist].

The element of transformation resides in a single locus and has never begun to differ; therefore, when it comes from the place of non-transformation while undergoing transformation, its coming is a non-coming.
It should likewise be said that when there is transformation within non-transformation, there is no coming and yet there is coming.

These three points are explained according to the inconceivable spiritual power of the Tathāgata; thus, although there are traces of being followed by those who have come as disciples, the mountains and seas remain distinct and clear.
However, although some in the assembly see [the land] while others do not, the substance of the land has never changed. Thus we know that this principle is beyond the reach of ordinary sentiment;
the passage concerning Mañjuśrī’s “going without arising” and so forth is simply an extension of this same intent.
Furthermore, as for the question of “going without arising,” one must again rely on the power of the sūtra to know its source. Now, as for that—

This repeated elucidation is intended to demonstrate the subtle mystery of neither coming nor going; instances such as Vimalakīrti pressing the earth with his toe are all illustrations of this principle.
Indeed, there is no fundamental teaching that does not conform to this pattern. By means of this, one may attain that [realization].
As for the fact that Benming used the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* to challenge the notion of a dragon girl attaining Buddhahood, his intention was to provide an alternative interpretation.
Although there are obstacles, in the end, their attainment of realization is one and the same. The reason for the apparent difference is this:

whereas the former undergoes transformation and the latter lacks the sensation of relinquishment—this is one way they differ—they both state that the *dharmatā* is like the great ocean; thus, regarding the swiftness of attaining realization, there is no distinction between them.
As for the resolution of these objections, the meaning is found in this very text; therefore, it is said: "In the South, the conditions have matured."
"Equal" means that because the conditions were ripe in that region, it was appropriate to transform them through the eight manifestations of a Buddha; thus, there were traces of such transformations.

In this land [Jambudvīpa], because she was transformed by means of a dragon girl, there was likewise no matter of "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" sensation (*upekṣā*). All of these are the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). The *Ji* (Commentary) explains and discriminates this, saying:

"Is it for the sake of not abandoning the body, etc., that the *Xiejaiting* (Sūtra on Entering the Womb) poses the question? Or is it for the sake of not remaining in the body, etc.? [The former refers to the case of the dragon girl.]

Since the current text poses a question, it concludes the objection with the phrase "and so forth. The response judges both through the dual perspective of the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*), stating regarding these two passages:

"The present passage [speaks of] the Dragon Girl from the perspective of the provisional, while the *Tāizàng jīng* (Womb Sutra) speaks from the perspective of the real; both are merely 'one-way' interpretations.

From a 'two-way' perspective, it is said that the current text is not without the real, and thus: 'If the practice of the real is not unreal,' etc.; likewise, that *Tāizàng jīng* is not without the provisional."

It is then said: "If one has truly attained [the fruit], since you have already stated that they may manifest spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), is it not the case that there is also transformation, as in the case of the Dragon Girl?

Furthermore, it is said: "When one realizes the Perfect Sūtra, is it not the case that even the Dragon Girl knows that, like the *T'ai-ching* (Womb Sūtra), there is originally no abandoning or receiving?
Therefore, it is said: "In all such cases, one must resolve doubts and obstacles by means of the non-duality of the provisional and the real. Moreover—
It is said that the intention behind terms such as "expedient skill" (*upāya-kauśalya*) is not necessarily that the present manifestation of the Dragon Girl constitutes expedient skill;

rather, it is because she simultaneously embodies both essence and function through expedient skill. Thus we know that those who grasp the essential meaning find the textual expressions fundamentally straightforward, whereas those who lose sight of the intent engage in forced interpretation to seek out differences, thereby making things difficult for themselves. Why is this so?
I have often observed those who study our teaching reading such textual passages merely as ordinary prose, failing to pay close attention;
they do not realize that these very words concern matters of vital importance for practice and personal cultivation.

Not only do they lead to one's own progress on the Way, but they also serve to navigate the world and interact with others, providing total protection against harm, allowing one to examine one's own heart and conscience, and inspiring a longing for the sages.

O worthy ones, all such undertakings were originally those for which the Buddhas and Patriarchs offered exhortations and entrustments; yet in later generations, these have been treated as mere common parlance—is this not to be called a reversal of priorities?

Thus, the commentary on this chapter frequently cites sutras and śāstras to admonish those in the末代 (final age) that they should not merely conform to the outward form of bhikṣus, but should instead practice the Way by donning the armor of patience and employing the five methods to contemplate evil persons and the like.
All this is the merit of those who study; those in need should examine it, for it serves as a clear mirror by which one may gain insight.

Recently, I have observed that among the monastic community, there are those who, having completed the reception of the full precepts (*upasampadā*), subsequently receive the Mahāyāna precepts, calling them the "augmenting precepts" (*zengjie*).

This is merely a matter of taking the so-called "pavilion precepts" (*louge jie*) from the Hinayana teachings and receiving them in successive stages. As stated in the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary): [text follows].

It is said that if one first practices the minor precepts and later the major ones, the uncreated body of the precepts (*asamskrta-śīla-sarīra*) is entirely transformed into the inexhaustible treasury of precepts (*akṣaya-śīla-kośa*).

This is also a clear textual proof for the "increasing of the precepts" (*vṛddha-śīla*). In that school, there is mention of "perfect precepts" (*pariṇata-śīla*), which intends to refer to the essential precepts of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-zong*).
However, I have never heard of any explicit scriptural evidence for the "increasing of the precepts. Speaking from the present perspective, the *Shuji* (Commentary) contains the following:
This passage serves precisely as proof for the doctrine of "augmenting the precepts" (*adhiśīla*).

It means that by receiving the threefold pure precepts (*tri-saṃvara-śīla*) on the basis of the Hīnayāna precepts, one is now said to be "endowed with the augmented three trainings," which is what constitutes "augmenting the precepts. Thus, both the name and its meaning are fully realized.

Otherwise, those who cling to a single set of rules while remaining ignorant of others are merely deficient in their observance of the precepts; how could they be said to have augmented them? Where, then, would such a person stand?
Is it not possible that one may attain the fivefold Dharma-body through concentration and wisdom? Therefore, is it not appropriate to take this as a testimony now?
The worldly teachings have a saying: "It is man who can propagate the Way, not the Way that propagates man," and again: "If it is not the right person, the Way will not flourish."
The Wondrous Dharma is indeed wondrous, yet the Dharma does not propagate itself; it is propagated by people.
It is not that people necessarily believe, but rather that belief arises from practice. Therefore it is said: "If one does not practice oneself, one cannot cause others to believe.

Thus, to be unable to transmit and propagate [the teaching] due to a lack of faith is like having an illness and offering medicine for sale—these words are well-founded. As for practice, it serves as the standard for the present age.
To speak of it, the three practices of clothing, sitting, and the chamber arise precisely because the essential purport of the sutra is rooted in the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*);

the practice that can propagate [the teaching] must necessarily correspond to them. Therefore, it is said that the "three cycles" (*tri-parivarta*) reveal and manifest [the truth], for the three virtues do not transcend the cultivated nature (*bhāvanā-dharmatā* and *prakṛti*).

Thus, when speaking from the perspective of the nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), the hidden and the manifest are of equal import; there is no distinction between what is opened and what is not, for this applies to the cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) as well.
Thus, designations shift according to the times and names follow the objects; although there may be differences, the essence is but the One Vehicle.

This One Vehicle is precisely the central tenet and ultimate convergence of this sutra. To speak of the robe, the seat, and the chamber as three distinct things, rather than as the One Vehicle, would not be the method for propagating the Way according to this sutra.
Now, there are those who possess peace and happiness yet cannot advance, and those who can advance yet cannot abide in peace while practicing;
neither of these constitutes what is meant here by "peaceful and happy practice" (*anraku-gyō*). Indeed, that which is called "peaceful and happy" here must mean:

peace is the mind abiding in the true reality (*shinjitsu-sō*), and happiness is the body necessarily being in non-action (*mu-i*). To proceed by means of this is to be without fabrication and without striving.

Because this is the practice [of the Bodhisattva], it is said: "Abiding on the ground of patience, one does not act with sudden violence. Generally speaking, there are three meanings for explaining this chapter:

first, regarding the actual facts, such as distancing oneself from the ten kinds of disturbances; by doing so, one attains the "Peaceful Practice" (*sukhavihāra*) within the context of those activities.

Second, regarding the attachment to the text, which clarifies that the "Peaceful Practices"—both in terms of conduct and principle—are shown to have a basis. Third, regarding the Dharma... [text fragment].

Regarding the gatekeeper: generally speaking, those who provide explanations today do so because they have attained their realization through a fundamental source; thus, they encounter the origin from every direction, and there is no dharma-gate that does not accord with it.
Although there are three types of interpretation, they essentially do not exceed the categories of phenomena and principle, calming and medicine, or practice and conduct.

Having already established this for one's own cultivation, one further employs it to propagate the sutra—what could surpass this as the perfect and sudden sublime practice? These words are indeed sufficient.
This means it is ultimate.

People merely see that four modes of peaceful conduct are enumerated, yet they do not realize that these are rooted in three practices and brought to fulfillment through the guidance of compassion and vows;
only then does this gateway of practice become fully perfected. Therefore, compassion and vows—
One must necessarily proceed by means of the three karmas; yet, even with the practice of the three karmas, one cannot reach this state without compassion and the vow.

Therefore it is said: because there is cessation in bodily karma, one is detached from the coarseness of the body; because there is contemplation in bodily karma, one does not apprehend the characteristics of the body.
Because no characteristics of the body are apprehended, one does not fall into the stage of ordinary beings; because there is compassion, one does not fall into the stage of the two vehicles.
This means that one cultivates compassion within bodily action; by means of this compassion, one extensively benefits sentient beings until they all reach the ultimate state.

Through the three types of action (*karma*), the three practices (*caryā*) are accomplished; with the three practices, there then arise the three norms (*vidhi*); and with the three norms, the three virtues (*guṇa*) are perfected.
These three virtues arise in mutual succession, pervading both wisdom (*prajñā*) and cessation (*nirodha*), and are manifested without departing from the three types of action.
When the Dharma-body is manifested, its purposeful activity is fulfilled; this is how the superior and inferior aspects mutually complete one another, remaining consistent from beginning to end.
The Sūtra speaks of "the place of practice" and "the place of proximity," yet the commentaries do not go beyond explaining "practice" as non-practice and [proximity] as non-intimacy.
If one explains what is near by means of what is near, its meaning will be correctly grasped. Why?

Because if one explains "practice" (*caryā*) by means of "non-practice," it is fundamentally based on abiding in the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*) and observing all phenomena as having the mark of jewels; this non-practice is precisely the perfection of the place of practice.
It should be understood as follows in the subsequent text: neither practicing nor not practicing, neither non-practicing nor non-non-practicing—such are the three modes of practice.

This is because they both rely upon the same principle of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). By not being intimate with what is called "intimacy," one simply knows how to distance oneself from the ten kinds of disturbances;
thus, that which one is intimate with can be known. Furthermore, as stated in the text below: "Although that which is abandoned is near, the ability to abandon it is truly far.
If one knows the distance of this ability to abandon, then one attains the proximity of that which is near. To comprehend the essence of these two is [the practice].
If one practices in this way, then the practice of peace and bliss is fully realized; what further matter remains?

The scriptural text is one and the same, yet it is explained by increasing the count to approximately three dharmas. This is indeed because the Buddha’s intention is manifold, and our Patriarch’s wisdom is unimpeded;
furthermore, there is a deeper purpose here. In response, the scripture states that "ground" (*bhūmi*) should be explained as a single dharma. The scripture says:

The practice of patience (*kṣānti*) should be explained through two dharmas; where the sutra speaks of "contemplating the true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it should be explained through the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*).
Thus we know that each meaning has its proper application and is not arbitrary. To explain by means of a single dharma refers to directly taking one truth as the object;
thus, all things find their ultimate resort, and all dharmas serve as the basis without discrimination—this is the meaning of the "ground" (*bhūmi*). This is according to principle.
Because it is the Middle Way, it is that to which all phenomena return and where all practices find their rest; thus it is called the Stage of Forbearance (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
It is the practice of non-practice. Furthermore, the Middle is the root of principle;

just as the myriad things grow by obtaining the earth, so too does one obtain the capacity to be supple within the rigid, to be compliant within the contrary, to govern the violent, and to bring peace to the startled—all of which are attained thereby.
This is the efficacy of principle; therefore it is said that immeasurable merit arises from the Middle Way.
To arise from non-arising is precisely the practice of non-practice. Its essence is pervasive and without discrimination; this is the principle of the reality of the Middle.
It is not only the foundation of practice, but also the foundation of non-practice—just as the earth makes no distinction between walking and not walking.
Therefore it is said: "Neither practicing nor discriminating is precisely the practice that is neither practicing nor non-practicing.
This is also the meaning of what is called in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng): "In the absence of cognitive awareness, one does not distinguish between the real and the unreal.
Next, the explanation based on two or three dharmas can be seen in the text (*yúnyún*).

The two emptinesses of persons and phenomena fundamentally apply to both the partial (Hīnayāna) and the universal (Mahāyāna); however, as we are now discussing the Perfect Teaching, they are elucidated through the perspective of the True and the Conventional.

Specifically, the inconceivable True and Conventional are such that the True Truth corresponds to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the Conventional Truth corresponds to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

This is because it is expedient to explain the ultimate reality by way of the conventional. Furthermore, according to the *Xuanyan wen* (Profound Meaning), when analyzed from the standpoint of what is being refuted, the meaning is the reverse of this.

The conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) refutes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and thus intrinsic nature is real; the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) refutes the provisional (*prajñapti*), and thus the provisional is empty.

Furthermore, it is said that when the provisional is refuted, characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are empty, and so forth; this is spoken from the perspective of what is revealed. Therefore, on one hand, characteristics correspond to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), while intrinsic nature corresponds to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Although these differ according to their respective contextual applications, they are identical in that they both reveal the principle of non-duality.
Therefore it is said that the refutations of opposing views and so forth are detailed as explained elsewhere (*etc.*).
When the Dharma contradicts common worldly sentiment and reaches the ultimate limit of the mind's capacity, it becomes extremely difficult to believe and accept.

As for what is being discussed here now, were it not for those who have previously cultivated the seeds of the Path, how could they hear it and remain at peace? Few would not be startled and terrified, instead of undergoing a transformation of their perspective.
During the Buddha’s lifetime, there were still those who feared his teachings, refused to hear them, and gave rise to slander;

by this we know that the Perfect and Sudden Great Dharma is not easily accepted. Yet nowadays in the Age of Dharma-Decline, there are often those who hear it and do not consider it strange—not because they are able to believe and accept it, but simply because they treat it with contempt. This, moreover, is something that cannot be overlooked.

Although this is so, in these present degenerate times, there are those who, with ordinary minds and limited capacities, have been able to hear the ultimate teaching without being startled or doubtful;
even this is sufficient to attest to the benefit of their perfumed seeds, yet such individuals are not easily found.
Furthermore, to be able to advance one step further—how could that be easily measured? How can one not exert oneself?
"All sentient beings are the very mark of bodhi; the five acts of immediate retribution are all the mark of liberation. Furthermore, it says:

"To walk upon non-paths and yet penetrate the Buddha-way"—if this is so, what is near and what is far? Thus we know that while dharmas have neither near nor far, the Way has its orientations and aversions.
It is precisely because one turns away from it that it is not far yet becomes distant, which is called the non-path; it is by turning toward it that one approaches.

Therefore, that which is not near yet is designated as "near" is what is called the Way (*dharma*). This is why there is: discussing the near by means of the distant; discussing the near by means of the near;

and discussing the near by means of that which is neither distant nor near. Discussing the near by means of the distant is, for example, like distancing oneself from the ten kinds of afflictions and disturbances;

this is to rely on the gate of precepts (*śīla*) to assist in contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), wherein contemplation itself is the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukhavihāra*). This is discussing the near by means of the distant. Discussing the near by means of the near refers to... [the rest of the text follows].
Regarding the "near," such as the practice of collecting the mind and so forth, these are attached to the gate of concentration (*samādhi*) to serve as an aid.
Regarding the "neither far nor near," such as the contemplation that all phenomena are empty (*śūnyatā*), these are attached to the gate of wisdom (*prajñā*) to support them.

Not only do they assist in the accomplishment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), but they also serve to assist in the propagation and universal dissemination [of the Dharma]. Furthermore, this is explained by way of contemplating the mind.

Regarding the ten kinds of distancing (*daśa-viveka*), the commentary states: "If it were not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), what would there be to distance oneself from? It continues until it says:

"Although the initial mind realizes that all things are fundamentally non-existent, one must repeatedly draw near to distancing and so forth. All of these are explained through reverse interpretation;
the underlying intent regarding contrariety and conformity is, when examined thoroughly, that each instance takes that which is to be distanced as its object, by means of the three [aspects].
Contemplation is "near" and the three delusions are "far"; thus, the meaning of near and far is established.

In the ninth fascicle of the *Wenju*, the statement "neither far nor near" is made in contrast to the preceding discussion on "distancing" and so forth; therefore, this should be understood as a double negation.
To contemplate all phenomena is to possess the objects of the ten dharma realms—is this not far? Yet it is but the single mind—is this not near?
Although there is neither far nor near, among these contemplations, none is nearer than the Middle Way; therefore, the Middle Way is taken as the proximate locus.
To base one's contemplation on the Middle Way and say that "all phenomena are empty" means that this emptiness is itself the Middle, which is ultimate.
Because it is emptiness, when spoken of in terms of its true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is not a partial emptiness.
Terms such as "non-inverted" all manifest the meaning of the essence, characteristics, virtues, and functions of the Middle Way; one should seek these details herein.

If one wishes to understand the purport of the Middle Way, one need only seek it here. However, that which exists by way of causes and conditions is also termed "empty" in contrast to the general heading mentioned above.
Because it exists by way of causes and conditions, it is what is called "dharmas produced from causes and conditions.

This demonstrates that what has been explained in the interim is none other than the Middle Way; thus, its principle is clear. Furthermore, it is said: "Above, the essence of the Middle Way's contemplative wisdom was directly clarified;
now, the function of simultaneously illuminating both extremes is clarified. The passage beginning with "The rational nature is ultimately pure" is a re-explanation of the meaning of this essence.

The phrase "as explained above" refers to [the previous discussion], while the subsequent passage beginning with "arising from the causes and conditions of delusion and awakening" is a re-explanation of the functional meaning (*vṛtty-artha*), as seen in the following text.

Therefore, it says: "One should always joyfully contemplate such dharmas as these. This means that one who now propagates this sutra through the "Practice of Peaceful Bliss" (*sukhavihāra*) should always joyfully contemplate the dharmas of these three truths (*trisatya*).
Furthermore, the section beginning with "but merely... again focuses on the object (*viṣaya*), the teaching (*śāsana*), and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
The third section explains the text: that which arises from causes and conditions and from perversion does not go beyond the ten realms of phenomena;
it is none other than the wondrous realm of the three truths. To speak thus is the wondrous teaching; to contemplate thus is the wondrous contemplation.
By explaining the text directly in this manner, its meaning is already manifest. Now, it may also be said that the initial passage refers directly to—

The contemplation of the essential nature (*tixing*) primarily reveals the ultimate excellence of the inherent qualities (*xingde*); what follows merely provides a further explanation by means of the concealment and revelation through delusion and awakening, thereby further clarifying the sequence of the merits of cultivation and manifestation.

Reflecting upon this, it becomes clear. As for the application of the eighteen phrases to the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*) and so forth, there is no hindrance to such explanations of simultaneous correspondence;
however, one who has grasped the underlying meaning may subsume [all of them] within a single phrase.
Regarding the eighteen kinds of emptiness, there is no reason why each individual emptiness could not be endowed with eighteen phrases; please examine this further.

The four practices are the essential core of the propagation of the sutra, and the ten vehicles constitute the fundamental principle of contemplative practice. Although they differ in breadth and brevity, their true nature (*dharmatā*) corresponds as exterior and interior.
Therefore, by means of this, the general purport is brought into alignment with that [text], so that those who cultivate the practice of peace and bliss may take it as their mental object.

There are those who, by means of this, penetrate that; there is no benefit greater than this. Therefore, the preceding text diligently points this out precisely because it fears that students might lose their fundamental principle, because it establishes the great foundation, and because it exhorts them toward reflection and cultivation—how could one not bear this in mind?

Within this, the mention of the "eighteen factors of the path" (aṣṭādaśa-mārga-varga) refers to the fact that, as the text corresponds to the eighteen emptinesses (aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā), these are likewise a category of the factors of the path. It is also...
"Not discriminating between the open and the obstructed" means that one discriminates the obstructed but does not discriminate the open.
As for "arising obstruction within non-discrimination," this obstruction must also be破除 (shattered/destroyed); the rest may be understood and need not trouble the text with further elaboration.

I have previously presented the teaching that the perfect severance of delusions within one family involves the essence of delusion being eternally present, which—being partial yet predominant—is given its name;

this precisely accords with the present text. Since all obstacles are already eliminated from the stage of the Ten Faiths onward, we know that the mention of the "three poisons" refers merely to the coarse delusions of the desire realm.
Therefore, it is said: "Because the ten faiths fully eliminate the delusions of the three realms, one is only then able to be called 'One'."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "all obstacles," it is said that below this level there still remain the three afflictions of views, thought, and so forth;

thus, one knows that the ignorance (*avidyā*) destroyed at the stage of Truth (*bhūmi*) also encompasses these three delusions, though it is referred to as "ignorance" alone because of its predominance. Therefore, this serves as proof.
Dreams are inherently among the inconceivable phenomena within the realm of reality; as in *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, a dream is used as a metaphor for the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment.
In the present text, this is used to represent how within a single instance of the wondrous Dharma there are infinite manifestations.

How much more so, then, regarding a dream brought about by the power of propagating the sutra through the "Peaceful Practices" (*anrakugyō*)—how could this not be a precursor to the attainment of the fruit? Therefore, the Record states: "The merit of transformation returns to oneself."
The signs of the fruition manifest beforehand; this means that one can, by means of a dream lasting but a single *kṣaṇa*, surpass the duration of billions of *kalpas*.

This serves to illustrate that the merit of one lifetime’s propagation of the teachings far exceeds that of accumulated eons. Yet, it may be that the merit and practice of propagating the sutras have not yet reached their full consummation.

How could the sincere words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs deceive us? Formerly, it was said that there are two types of dreams: those caused by external factors (*hetu*) and those arising from mental ideation (*saṃjñā*). Furthermore, Liezi enumerates six kinds of dreams.
It is said that only the Buddha does not dream, because he is free from doubt and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and furthermore, because of two specific factors, he has no dreams.

It is also said that dreams arise from five factors or seven factors; although there are various enumerations—whether expanded or condensed—they do not exceed the fact that they are caused by mental conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
Furthermore, it is said that when the present mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not see form, it simply does not perceive forms that are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That which is perceived by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within a dream is an object known through inference (*anumāna*).

Furthermore, when one perceives future events within a dream, this too is an inferential conceptualization (*saṃjñā-darśana*), not the power of knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*). Although a Buddha has no dreams, he may still lie down to demonstrate that he shares the human condition;
thus, he may also experience sleep for the sake of disciplining his body. This [explanation] was omitted from the text due to its being a secondary matter.
One need only know whether [the work] advances or falters; this marks the beginning of the "Original Gate" (Honmon), intended to cause the assembly of that time to listen with rapt attention.
Thus, he composed it and said: "... One can well imagine how those who heard it at that time must have felt, and what their response would have been.
Alas! Had my ancestors' writings possessed literary brilliance, they would surely have been worthy of admiration; it is a pity that they were not produced.

In this regard, one may briefly observe a portion of its character. When it says, "At the single command of the Tathāgata, those from the four quarters rushed forward," one can see that his teacher was stern and his Way was honored.
Again, when it says, "The moon is one, yet there are ten thousand reflections; who could fathom them?
then how could the abundance of the Tathāgata’s manifested traces be surpassed? Furthermore, when it says, "Empty space is serene and still, with neither early nor late," this again...
That which cannot be reached by words or deliberation—yet to call it the "Dharma-assembly of the young father and the old son of Quiescent Light" is indeed a discourse unprecedented in the past.
Does not the tradition say, "He who possesses virtue will surely have words"?
This may be called one who possesses virtue and speaks accordingly.
The Land of Quiescent Light (*Jigō*) is the fundamental essence of the body. Although it is identical to the body and the land, it transcends the realm of body and land.
As for its substance, it is neither spatial location, nor numerical quantity, nor physical form; it cannot be seen or heard.
Since its principle cannot be demonstrated through traces, it is symbolized by emptiness (*kū*), yet even emptiness is not it. If so, how can one speak of its ultimate nature? Please explain.
To discuss it by way of its name: the essence (*tǐ*) is eternally quiescent yet ever-luminous, and its function (*yòng*) is ever-luminous yet eternally quiescent;
this is what constitutes the subtlety of the body and the land (*shēn-tǔ*). It is also that from which all bodies and lands emerge. Therefore, it is said:

"The eternal is precisely the virtue of permanence," and so forth. The records concerning Japan mention the four virtues (*sìdé*), and so on; these are all such that they cannot be pointed out and cannot be [fully] expressed.

To summon [the reader], I have for the time being indicated this through names and words; it is not meant that one should stop here. It is further said: "When below, it does not belong [to the lower];

such things are neither this nor that, neither above nor below, and thus ultimately returns to the Middle Way alone. When there is the Middle, there is reality; when there is reality, there is constancy;

when there is constancy, there is perfection; when there is perfection, there is wondrousness; when there is wondrousness, there is the ultimate; and when there is the ultimate, one has reached the pinnacle.

To say, however, that "this arises from neither above nor below" is likely an error; even if the commentator provides a convoluted interpretation, it ultimately does not conform to the style of the text.
It should rather state, "It is not that [the principle] is not below," for only then would its meaning become clear.

Furthermore, when the record uses a specific instance to clarify a principle, the statement that "one [principle] encompasses all" may be called a comprehensive theory. Within this passage, the textual meaning is profound and subtle; let students not [be confused].

If one reads this with a superficial mind, one might attempt to argue that within the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, it is clarified that each of the six perfections must necessarily contain all six, and that each of the ten wholesome acts likewise contains them all.
This is indeed stated in terms of mutual inclusion and mutual adornment, and their characteristics can be understood as such; yet, even down to the present day...

The text states that by means of a single *pāramitā* (perfection), the ten realms (*dhātu*) and so forth are fully contained, eventually reaching ten thousand; then, by traversing the six *pāramitās*, sixty thousand dharma-gates are established.
The record notes: "In reality, there are no ten thousand *pāramitās*. This seems somewhat difficult to understand.

Now, I say it is simply a matter of taking the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*) and so forth as representative of the ten realms, and applying them to the six *pāramitās*—hence the figure of sixty thousand. It is not that the six *pāramitās* themselves possess ten thousand dharmas.
In truth, there are no separate entities; it is simply that each is established through the winding interconnection of provisional names.
Therefore, it is said that every practice of the perfections (pāramitās) is none other than the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and the Dharma-realm is itself the contemplation of the wondrous object.

Regarding the statement that sixty *kṣudra-kalpas* are like the duration of a meal: previously, it was clarified that forgetting fatigue while listening to the Dharma pertains primarily to the capacity (*tāyin*) of the listener;
now, it is clarified that the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata pertains primarily to the response (*yìng*) of the Buddha. Nevertheless, were there no capacity, how could there be seeing?
Is a mirror ever dependent on beauty [to reflect]? This still refers to the "response. It is so because of form; thus, it also pertains to the capacity.
This is what is meant by "there being such a person. Some say that this statement combines the previous arguments to reveal the characteristics of their similarities and differences.

The commentary evaluates this by stating that while there is a failure in the response despite the attainment of the stimulus, it is as if there were a fault in the Tathāgata’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*).

Ultimately, however, this is fundamentally due to the inconceivable nature of temporal conditions; thus, when viewed with the Buddha-eye, length and brevity are non-dual. Regarding the four eyes, there are certainly no differing conditions.
Therefore, according to their delusion or awakening, some may see the short as long or the long as short;

it is just as the myriad phenomena of the phenomenal world appear diverse to ordinary people. Furthermore, it is like a blind person who cannot see despite being in the light, while a bat can see in the night.
Thus we know that even the retributive dharmas of the outflows are like this; when the principle is revealed through such facts, its meaning becomes clear.
Thus, it can be known that what is long is also short.
While observing the commentaries of various masters, their phrasing is entirely excellent; yet, when these interpretations are compared with one another, there are inevitably differences in quality.

Although the Great Master [Jizang] was lenient and did not refute them, he engaged in debate specifically with Guangzhai regarding the permanence and impermanence [of the Buddha-body]. Even according to Guangzhai’s view...
It is said that [others] claim to possess its excellence alone; yet when they interpret the present *āyus-pramāṇa* (lifespan) as being impermanent, they conversely fall short of the various masters.
This is particularly a point that must be refuted. Therefore, I shall now establish and refute [the views] by means of the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

When compared to those various masters, our own school may be called one that has synthesized the great achievement and attained the essential substance; thus, the *Records* contain both affirmations and negations.

If one rejects these [interpretations] and grants them [to others], then the various masters would not be without the intent to reject; yet if one seizes upon their words alone, then nothing at all could be preserved.
Therefore, it is said that "eliminating" the literal text is not without its own significance; this statement may also be considered appropriate.
Examining various texts that explain the lifespan, there are none that do not take the three bodies (*trikāya*) as their foundation;

yet some present them as six capacities and two functions, while others discuss them according to the four propositions of name and reality. This is because each follows its own specific meaning. Although these texts may be partial in their approach, their meanings must necessarily complement one another.
As in the present text, which addresses the divergent interpretations mentioned above, it does not go beyond the two meanings of "measurable" and "immeasurable."
This vehicle refutes the defects of antiquity by examining names and realities through a fourfold analysis. Although there are four phrases, their essence ultimately converges into three;
specifically, the first two phrases refer to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), meaning that all so-called response Buddhas are comprised within these two measures.
The second phrase refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body), and the third phrase refers to the *dharmakāya* (dharma body). Even if one examines the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, although...
This reward body (saṃbhogakāya) is titled "Immeasurable" (*amita*) and thus belongs to the third phrase; however, it may also be considered the true dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
If these are correlated with the six capacities, the first and last phrases correspond to the latter three capacities, while the second phrase corresponds to the former three capacities.
This is because they are not discussed here in terms of the correspondence between name and reality, and thus the third phrase is omitted; nevertheless, since the third phrase...

This Dharmakāya is the very substance that is capable of responding through the six modes of manifestation; thus we know that while names and characteristics may differ at first glance, their essence is fundamentally not distinct.

Because people of the past did not understand this, they fell into numerous divergent views. Those who grasp its essential meaning find that a thousand chariots follow the same track—this can be known from the commentaries and exegeses.

In answering questions, there are generally four methods; here we see two of them. By this, one can know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other scriptures share both similarities and differences.

As for their differences, they consist of distinctions between the extensive and the concise, as well as between those that bring about a great assembly (*saṃnipāta*) and those that do not. As for their similarities, they are no different:
thus the One Vehicle is simply the eternally abiding (*nitya*), and the eternally abiding is precisely the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). All dharmas return to this single source.
And that is all; what further difference could there be? To insist on generating further conceptual distinctions is to know that the ancients were falsely creating superfluous excrescences.
The Patriarch has clear warnings, yet how can students remain ignorant and blindly cling to the mere words? What is meant by "seeking the expression to meet the source"?
This is the true intent of this teaching; it may be called a discourse for revealing the fundamental. People today do not understand this.
For the disciples of the Buddha to seek only the literal words is like eating dregs and husks without recognizing the true flavor;

to inquire about the bridge while remaining ignorant of where it leads—is this not a cause for lamentation? Furthermore, it is said that the teaching is fundamentally based on conditions (*pratyaya*); because conditions differ, the explanations vary.

There are the doctrines of the *siddhāntas* (established tenets) and the four methods of accommodation (*anupravṛtti*). Pushing this to its ultimate limit, it is simply the realization of the principle. If one does not...
To realize the principle yet remain stuck in explanations that merely accommodate circumstances is like lingering on the road without ever reaching home;
it is what is called "losing the goat at the many forks. Spending one's whole day outside the gate—how could one know the true Dharma-treasure of Nirvana?

In the mastery of the scriptures and the establishment of the teachings, what is prized is knowing the fundamental principle (*mūla*). If one knows the fundamental principle, the extent of the text is certainly irrelevant;

whether it be much or little. For instance, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* takes "eternal abiding" as its fundamental principle, while the *Lotus Sūtra* takes "long-term fulfillment" as its fundamental principle;

thus, their texts are extensive because they contain everything other than that which is not the fundamental principle, yet they are concise because they contain nothing other than that which is the fundamental principle. Nevertheless, a single phrase may be the fundamental principle, and many phrases may also be the fundamental principle—just like a single drop [of water].
"Milk is milk; the milk in a single vessel is also milk. Why take up or reject it based on its quantity?
The principle of many phrases is like milk with water added, while the principle of a single phrase is like pure milk. I know that one would surely abandon the much and follow the little;
how could one follow the much and discard the little? It is only right that this be called a demonic teaching, for it is not so."
The Buddha’s teachings are like the commands of a Son of Heaven: a single word is a command, and many words are likewise commands.
How could one disregard them simply because a single word is few? Moreover, the passages in this sutra stating that the eternal principle of the future is identical to Nirvana are no less numerous;
such as the saying "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding," and the frequent designation of it as the *dharmakāya*, all refer to this.
How can one not clarify the doctrine of eternal abiding by means of this sutra? If one were to claim that the *dharmakāya* is impermanent, that would be truly terrifying.
The words of the Tathāgata are not easily spoken; they should not be taken even once, much less twice or thrice, and certainly not in measureless ways.
The Tathāgata does not come; that which comes is not the Tathāgata. If this is so, why then is the fruit called the "Tathāgata"?
Within that which is devoid of name and mark, one provisionally employs names and marks; once the name has been manifested, what harm is there in [the distinctions of] two or three?
Thus the Treatise says: "Riding upon the path of suchness, he comes to achieve perfect enlightenment. It also says: "That which comes comes from nowhere. Does this "coming" then constitute a coming?
Does the fruit come? Because it comes precisely by not coming, it is called the Tathāgata. The Great Master summarized this to clarify the two or three [aspects];

the Tathāgata is discussed solely through the middle two phrases, which already contain the four meanings of object, wisdom, cause, and fruit—namely, "Tathā" (Thus) is wisdom, "Āgata" (Come) is the real object, "Tathā" is the path-cause, and "Āgata" is the awakening-fruit.
If one speaks of "Tathatā" (Suchness) alone, there is no suchness; if one speaks of "Āgata" alone...
To speak of reality: reality is truly incapable of being "like" [an object], yet because cognition has already conformed to the object, it can be "like" that which is like;
and that which is like conforms to that which can be like. This is the Dharma of the vehicle, and the one who rides it is the person.

Because the person rides upon this Dharma, proceeding from cause to fruit, the path of awakening is thereby perfected. This is why those who come riding upon the path of suchness and achieve perfect enlightenment are truly so called.

The Body-Tathāgata (*kāya-tathāgata*) also comes to be born within the triple world by riding this path; he who manifests as one who has attained perfect enlightenment is the Response-Tathāgata (*nirmāṇa-kāya-tathāgata*).
Speaking from the perspective of its opening, that which arrives without moving from the realm of the Dharma-suchness (*dharmatā-tathatā*) is the Dharma-Tathāgata (*dharma-tathāgata*);

that which arrives in accordance with principle through the wisdom of Dharma-suchness is the Reward-Tathāgata (*saṃbhoga-kāya-tathāgata*). When these are unified, they are able to respond through the eight aspects of manifestation.

One who has attained the Way should be like the Tathāgata; as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this means understanding according to the characteristics of reality (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and teaching according to the characteristics of reality.
The present text employs this principle to open up and correspond to the three bodies (*trikāya*), perfectly capturing its essential purport. This is merely a general outline;
for the rest, refer to the explanations in the commentaries (etc.).
Now, various sutras clarify the principle that the three bodies (trikāya) are neither identical nor distinct, as this text states:
"These three Tathāgatas cannot be grasped individually, nor should they be grasped collectively; whether taken horizontally, vertically, or separately, none can be grasped.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "The Dharma-body is also not [the Buddha]," and so forth. Why is this? Because their principle is one and their meanings are harmoniously integrated.
Therefore, although there are three names, they are in reality a single entity; and although it is a single entity, there are distinctions such as the three marks and three functions.
Thus, one cannot seek it through unity, nor can one seek it through difference; only by manifesting a comprehensive vision do the three dharmas appear as the provisional name "Tathāgata.
Furthermore, as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which treats them as distinct conditions to clarify how the flower pedestal and the flower petals are discussed in relation to their mutual origins.

The traces (the manifested forms) cannot be separated from one another; that they are not separate means they are identical. Furthermore, it is said: "One may only speak of their mutual relation, but not of their identity.

This is also clear proof that the Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Response-body are neither identical nor different. Nevertheless, while the Buddha is eternally identical [to them], when he appears before sentient beings (the capacities), he may appear either as the same or as different.
Moreover, the *Xiàngfǎ juéyí jīng* (Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Regarding the Semblance Dharma), in its concluding chapter on the final assembly of the *Nirvāṇa*, states:
Since the phrase "or [one may see]" (*vā*) is used, we know that the Buddha is fundamentally without three bodies; rather, they appear as distinct due to conditions.
Furthermore, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* concludes its discussion of the *Lotus Sūtra* by stating that these are different names but not separate entities.
These textual passages clearly demonstrate that the three bodies are neither identical nor distinct, ultimately converging upon the subtle, profound, mysterious, and inconceivable.
In recent times, it has been claimed that the new translations of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* are incorrect in identifying Vairocana as Śākyamuni;

this is why the Dharma-body and the Reward-body have become indistinguishable, with no means to discern between the two. However, judging by the ancient translations of the sūtras and śāstras, the essence of the Dharma is eternally pervasive and its name must not be confused.
Because its name must not be confused, one must distinguish between the Dharma-body and the Reward-body, for the sake of that Dharma.

Because the essence is eternally pervasive, there is neither "acceptable" nor "unacceptable. Although there is nothing unacceptable, one must still distinguish between delusion and enlightenment, and between cultivation and nature;
these cannot be conflated as one. If they were identical, then even ordinary beings and Buddhas would be the same—how much more so the Dharma-body and Reward-body?

Therefore it is said that "ordinary beings and Buddhas are non-dual. This is not merely a matter of the three bodies; below, the text specifically addresses the teaching of non-explanation, instructing one to make such distinctions.
The meaning of this consists of four points: first, the distinction between what is taught and what is not; second, mutual identity; third, following principle;
and fourth, the correspondence between phenomenon and principle, and so forth. Only through these four points can their purport be fully exhausted.

That which is called "the resonance of sentiment and the wondrous accord, wherein all pure attachments are lost"—is this not a statement free from falsehood? As for the discourse on crossing the "Wojiao" (the Abyss of Water), its principles are indeed ultimate.
What has been said regarding this matter may not yet be exhaustive; we only know that the water does not increase, yet we have never heard it said that the tide fails its appointed time.
What is the reason for this? Therefore, one should know that even a Buddha might keep such a principle secret and refrain from discussing it.
Now, one must understand that the meanings contained within the sutra’s definitive exposition of the three bodies (trikāya) are not to be ignored.
For instance, when the Buddha perceives the triple world as neither identical to nor different from [reality], this is precisely the Middle Way; and the Middle Way is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Furthermore, one who knows and sees the triple world as it truly is possesses the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) through that very capacity for knowing and seeing—how could this not be the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*)? Moreover, it is said: "Or..."

The manifestation of one’s own body, the bodies of others, and so forth, refers to the meaning of the *saṃbhogakāya*. Thus, when these three bodies are distinguished according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), they differ;
whether considered sequentially or simultaneously, they are each distinct, and thus they are called the "three bodies.

As for the passage stating, "If it were merely the three Tathāgatas of the nature-merit (*xingde*)," this further distinguishes the provisional traces (*ji*) to reveal the fundamental reality (*ben*), citing treatises to harmonize them, as explained extensively in the text; the meaning is clear.

Furthermore, regarding the distinct teaching known as the "vertical and horizontal" (zōnghéng) discourse on cultivation and nature (*xiùxìng*), which somewhat involves the doctrinal gateways, the Record states:

"The vertical and horizontal aspects of cultivation and nature are not the Perfect and Wondrous [Teaching]. This means that although the distinct teaching contains expressions concerning the nature-endowment (*xingdé*), all three [aspects] reside within nature alone and do not mutually integrate.
Why is this? Because according to the ultimate reality of principle (*lǐshí*), each one must necessarily possess the other three; however, in the provisional teachings, these are superseded.
For this reason, it is not said that cultivation arises from the complete nature; rather, it is so arranged that the three horizontal aspects of the nature all reside within the nature itself.
Just as three kings each occupy their own domains and are not a single sovereign with two ministers, they possess a relationship of mutual containment;

thus it is said that they do not interpenetrate, which constitutes their distinctness. As for the statement that the three Tathāgatas of cultivated virtue are "vertical" and so forth, these are precisely the three dharmas within the aforementioned nature.
Since one does not yet realize that cultivation arises from the entirety of nature, the three aspects of nature are merely designated as the Dharma-body alone;

therefore, it is necessary to cultivate the conditions and the understanding separately as the means of manifestation. That which manifests the manifested is called the Reward-body (Sambhogakāya) based on the means of manifestation.

Because the Reward-body must necessarily have the Response-body (Nirmāṇakāya), the three bodies are discussed in terms of vertical progression, thereby establishing the sense of "lengthwise" (sequential) meaning. Thus, that which is manifested by the conditions and the understanding—
There are some versions that speak only of the Dharma-body, yet claim that the three bodies are manifested horizontally at the stage of fruition;

this is also spoken in terms of provisional teaching versus ultimate principle and of affirmation and negation, because they fail to realize that the three are identical to the one and the one is identical to the three.

This meaning is extremely difficult to grasp; none but those who have deeply penetrated the principles of the vertical and horizontal can fully comprehend it, as explained in detail in other treatises (etc.).
The Buddha fundamentally has no body and no lifespan; as they are immeasurable, by what could they be defined?

While it would be appropriate not to speak of the measure of his lifespan, since he accords with worldly convention, it is also appropriate to employ various definitions and distinctions—though he has no body, he manifests a body, and though he has no lifespan, he manifests a lifespan.
Among these various bodies, let us clarify the meaning by way of the three bodies (*trikāya*): first, the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is the "lifespan" that receives [the fruits of merit].
Regarding the meaning of the *dharmakāya*: True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not separated from the myriad phenomena; the capacity to express and measure according to reality constitutes its life-force.

Whether a Buddha appears or not, the nature and characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) remain eternally as they are. It is neither associated nor dissociated, neither finite nor infinite—what is called "neither identical nor different," and so forth.
To express and measure it in this way is precisely the measure of the *dharmakāya*. Regarding the *saṃbhogakāya*, as for the objective realm...
Correspondence with wisdom is the meaning of "receiving" (prāpti). To measure it is to take wisdom as one's life and object;
since that object is immeasurable, boundless, eternally abiding, and indestructible, when the wisdom of suchness accords with the object of suchness, it is likewise so described.

This refers to what is called the light of wisdom obtained through long-cultivated practice, which illuminates the immeasurable and so forth. In the case of the response body (nirmāṇakāya), the retribution obtained for a single lifetime is uninterrupted.

This is the meaning of "receiving" (the teaching), because one takes the principle of commonality as one's life; thus, when conditions are long, they are long together, and when conditions are brief, they are brief together, and so forth.

As for what that means for me—namely, the repeated chanting of arising and chanting of ceasing—the *Śū* (Commentary) explains each of these meanings individually, clarifying them by classifying them according to the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Since this is both concise and explicit, it may well be done even without formal topical divisions.
There is no need for further elaboration.
The Great Sutra uses the metaphor of the sun to illustrate that the perceived lifespan of the Buddha may be long or short; this is cited to demonstrate the Three Bodies.
From the perspective of those who perceive him, although there are differences according to the time, if one examines the very sun that is perceived:
Thus, the sun in summer is the sun, and the sun in winter is also the sun; from the outset, there is no difference in their dual substance.

This may be compared to the Tathāgata’s three bodies, which correspond to the sun as one. It is only according to the capacity of one's wisdom and cognition that the [perceived] length or brevity arises, yet the sun itself never changes.

If one discusses the perception based on the sun, it is not short (if one discusses the sun based on the perception, one perceives it as short); if one discusses the sun itself, it is long, yet it is not long.
It is neither short nor long, yet it appears short and long; the manifestations that respond to capacities have never been fixed as one.
How is it that people of old did not understand to discuss this, but instead sought only the superiority or inferiority of physical forms and debated the difficulties of textual meanings?
Is this not shallow? I have also discussed this elsewhere (as detailed below).

The text briefly explains the three bodies (*trikāya*) through this chapter, encompassing both the general and the specific. Although there are both general and specific aspects, they together include all three bodies;

yet, the specific inclusion of the three bodies is adopted here because it is more convenient for correlating the text with the meaning—this is precisely the primary intent of the current explanation of the chapter.

As for how the text correlates with the meaning and why it is convenient, it refers to the fact that the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* possesses the significance of "above merging with the ultimate and below acceding to the conventional. Furthermore, it also...
The three bodies are fully present; it is appropriate to designate them according to the "Fruit" (vipāka) category.

Regarding the statement in the old treatise that "above one is in accord with the profound and below one accords with the mundane," this does not mean that the path of profound accord consists of something other than the single true wisdom itself.
Therefore, when "above one is in accord with the profound," it is the wisdom of one's own fruition; when "below one accords with the mundane," it is likewise one's own fruition.
Because this wisdom is such, it is called the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*); it is precisely that which "mysteriously accords above and harmonizes below.

How could there be another "reward" or "superior body" capable of harmonizing with inferior capacities? Therefore, one should know that [the former view] is not so. Furthermore, no canonical texts are seen that correctly explain the principle of the Reward Body in such a manner;
this is merely an error inherited from antiquity, and thus I have specifically corrected it.

The beginning of the Essential Gate (Honmon) starts with Maitreya’s emergence from below and his inquiry, proceeding through the formal teaching, the admonition and permission, and the successive layers of doubts arising from the movement of attachments;
it is treated here with great earnestness and gravity until it reaches the point where it is simply stated:

"Since I truly attained Buddhahood, an extremely long time has passed. This is what is called the eternal distinction from the one-period teaching, wherein the trace is transcended and the fundamental is revealed. As it says:
This is all there is; how could this be easily spoken? One must truly know that whatever transformations the Buddhas of the three periods have manifested, none are otherwise than this.
When the conditions and opportunities were not yet ripe, they clung to the traces as being real, such that not even a single word could be revealed.
Once the proper time had arrived, they were able to speak according to the true source, saying "thus and so forth. Only then does one come to know from within.

Everything established following the Trace Gate (Jikimon) is a provisional means (*upāya*). Were it not for the ultimate revelation and manifestation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, how could this point be reached?
What is called the "earnest praise of the provisional means" serves as the verse that distinguishes the fundamental from the trace.
Nevertheless, if someone were to suddenly attain perfect enlightenment here and now, would there still be a long-standing fundamental reality to be revealed? Or would there not?
If one says that the Buddha's path is the same for all, then how could there be anyone who has only recently attained it? If we speak according to principle, what is there that is not possible?
If we discuss those who have only recently attained it today, this is simply because they have realized their original Buddhahood;

it is not merely a matter of having been accomplished for a long time. However, it is simply that the facts and the principle do not yet correspond. But then, by what means can we know that [the Buddha] was not already so from the beginning?
Speaking in terms of principle, the subsequent analogies regarding the events of *dust-point kalpas* (rajas-kalpa) demonstrate that this is not merely explained according to principle alone;
all of these were previously un-discussed, and it is left to those of high intelligence to adjudicate them.

The body and land of Vairocana are one; because they are one, they are both all-pervasive and without spatial direction. The three periods of time—past, present, and future—and the ancient and the modern are likewise one;

because they are one, they enter into one another without obstruction. Precisely because there is no obstruction, although the fundamental and the manifested differ, their inconceivable oneness is the very nature of reality.
As clarified in the "Original Gate," the place where he benefits sentient beings is precisely this Sahā world, which is the fundamental response.
The land where his body resides is none other than the Immovable Original Land;

he manifests this trace-abode to show that although there are differences between the present and the past, those who perceive it as being "burned" are merely seeing what is near, while those who illuminate the fundamental source realize the distant origin—there is no duality between them.
Because that which is called "near" is precisely the quiescent light of the Shared Residence, how could the Three Realms seen as being burned be anything other than "near"?

Only when one who illuminates the source reaches the far-reaching can they realize that Gayā is itself the Land of Quiescent Light; thus, seeing that this land is indestructible—how could it be anything other than "the far-reaching"?
To be eternally present at Vulture Peak, seated solemnly upon a single mat, is all according to this principle.
Therefore it is said: "How could one leave Gayā to seek elsewhere for eternal quiescence? Is there not a Sahā world outside the Land of Quiescent Light? Is this not proof of it? If...

When one examines phenomena to find their principle, the essence is entirely identical to its manifestations; thus, the Dharma-realm of Common Residence and the Dharma-realm of Quiescent Light are not two different natures.
How does the Second Gate differ from the present day? The essence is inconceivable and is simply one.
Regarding the two kinds of birth-bodies (*janma-kāya*) as they appear to those of varying capacities, since even "birth" does not exist for a Buddha, how much less can one speak of "two kinds"?

Regarding the two kinds of dharma-bodies (*dharma-kāya*) as explained through the characteristics of the teachings, since even the "Great" is not applicable to a Buddha, how much less can one speak of the "Small"?
If this is so, one might ask: "If there is no birth at all, from what could a Buddha arise? I say: Not so. It is precisely because there is no birth that [a Buddha] truly begins.
It is called the Buddha-ear; furthermore, that which is termed "non-arising" (anutpāda) is not obstructed by arising.

Thus, it is arising while being non-arising, and non-arising while being arising. Therefore, one who attains the state of non-arising is one for whom arising is non-arising—not a state of absolute non-arising such as that of a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns.
Moreover, as for what is called the "arising of the Dharmakāya," it is the ultimate of the great; yet even regarding this, words still fall short.
If one does not accept the "Great" [Vehicle], what fault could exceed this? In the current text, it says: "The present scripture precisely refutes the *sambhogakāya* and *dharmakāya*, etc.

as stated in the passage. This is certainly one interpretation. Yet, if we speak according to the underlying intent, must it not be said that within the true *dharmadhātu*, there is neither Buddha nor sentient beings?
Furthermore, it says that if these are extinguished, then there is neither birth nor Buddha, and so forth. Is this not so?
How can one speak of the "great" or "small" Dharmakāya? Nevertheless, it cannot be discussed in general terms;
if one grasps the underlying meaning, both "great" and "small" are appropriate, but if one loses that meaning, both "existence" and "non-existence" are incorrect.

Truly, this Dharma-gate within is not something that can be deliberated upon by those who produce understanding based on mere words or cling to literal characters. One should reflect upon this with careful scrutiny.

Regarding the discussion of the real and the provisional according to the four *siddhāntas*, there are many approaches; however, based on the present text, the explanation is specifically given in terms of the doctrinal characteristics (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*) of the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, it is explained directly in terms of the *siddhāntas* themselves; it is simply that the textual expressions are obscure and abbreviated, making them somewhat difficult to perceive.

To say that all four *siddhāntas* are equally real: for the *siddhāntas* each respond to the appropriate capacity of beings, bestowing benefits according to the depth or shallowness of their reception.

Because there is no confusion or error and because all things are real, it is called the "world. Since these are real as persons, how much more so must they be real in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
Otherwise, one could perceive their discrepancies and errors through mere reflection.

Furthermore, it is said that if one discusses them according to their actual reality, the former three are the reality of the mundane world, while the ultimate truth is the reality of the supramundane. When viewed in relation to one another, the former is real.

To be empty first and then real, or to be real in accordance with conditions such that it is not fixed—these may even be the reverse of the above. Furthermore, distinctions are made based on origin and manifestation (*honjaku*), gradual and sudden (*zendo*), and so forth, as explained extensively in the text.

Although there are differences in the teachings heard, the realization attained is without distinction; this is the constant principle. Nevertheless, there are also cases where the teachings differ yet [the realization] is attained...

The reason this text poses the question regarding "different realizations" is as follows: it is said that while the *dharmatā* (real aspect) elucidated in the former teachings was uniquely manifest through the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle], the present teaching speaks solely in terms of opening and revealing. If this is so, should not the realizations attained in the present and the past also differ? In the response, it is merely stated that there are gradual and sudden ways of entering, but it never says whether those who enter are identical or different. Regarding the passage beginning with "The reason this text poses the question," the meaning is that the *dharmatā* clarified in the previous teachings was exclusively revealed through the Perfect and Sudden approach; however, the present teaching explains matters solely by way of "opening" (*kai*) and "revealing" (*ken*). Thus, one might ask: do the awakenings attained in the present and the past necessarily differ? In the answer, the text only mentions that there are gradual and sudden modes of entry, but it does not address whether those who enter are the same or different. There is also a slight difference: one who enters suddenly is not equal to one who enters gradually, and entering gradually is not equal to entering through the revelation [of the truth].
Although the Middle Way entered is one and the same, there are nonetheless slight intervals between those who enter; therefore, there are likewise distinctions of superiority and inferiority.

The reason these are not explicitly stated is precisely because [the Buddha] did not wish to diminish the majesty of the Sūtra—for example, as in the case of "entering the True Truth" (*satyadharma*).

By observing whether these have substantiality or are merely analytical constructs, their relative depth and shallowness can be known. This should also be illustrated by applying the two gates of the Distinct (Bie) and the Perfect (Yuan);

however, it is not so, because both the gradual and the sudden proceed from the Perfect, and thus they differ only in this regard. The rest is as explained in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary), where the similarities and differences are detailed at length (*yún yún*).

The purport of the passage beginning with "The Tathāgata knows and sees as it truly is" constitutes the actual realization of the fundamental ground (*mūla-bhūmi*) and is the very source of this chapter;

this must be investigated and clarified. Although the commentaries and records have already treated this in exhaustive detail, fearing that later students might find it difficult to comprehend, I shall here simply present the literal meaning of the text. Regarding the phrase "knows as it truly is":

"Seeing and so forth" means to accord with reality as it truly is, which is what is meant by "conforming to the nature. Speaking in terms of this nature, the three realms are fundamentally non-existent;

there is only the single true source. Therefore, when observed through the seed-knowledge of the Buddha-eye, one does not see that there is anything to be attained in terms of birth-and-death or nirvana.
Because there is no birth-and-death, there is neither "retrogression" nor "emergence. "Retrogression" refers to its... [text truncated]
When one speaks of "entering" and "leaving," it means they are free from them; there is simply no birth-and-death from which to withdraw.

It is precisely because there is no nirvāṇa that there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has attained extinction. To remain in the world is to contradict nirvāṇa, and to attain extinction is to revert to birth-and-death.

Therefore, it is not real, and thus it is not the true nature of nirvana; it is not unreal, and thus it is not the false nature of saṃsāra.
Since one seeks the real nature within both saṃsāra and nirvana and finds it unobtainable, they are simply of one suchness (*tathatā*).
If even suchness itself cannot be obtained, how much less could that which differs from it be obtained? Hence it is said: "Neither suchness nor difference. Furthermore—

The Sūtra clarifies the merit of hearing [the Dharma] from afar and of longevity in order to encourage its circulation, distinguishing between the shallow and the deep according to whether it occurs during the Buddha’s lifetime or after his parinirvāṇa.
